TReserved_parameter_names:
Reserved parameter names (Technical Reference §2.17) are read-only identifiers that report the refinement's current state -- the observed/calculated pattern, the current hkl, the current iteration, lattice parameters, and so on -- rather than being set by the user like an ordinary keyword. An exception is thrown if a reserved name is used as a user-defined parameter name. Table 2-2, reproduced below, lists them grouped as in the manual; Table 2-3 (not reproduced here) covers which peak-generation keywords can be a function of H, K, L, M, Xo, Th and D_spacing, and Table 2-4 covers phase-intensity-specific reserved names (A01/A11/B01/B11, Iobs_no_scale_pks, I_no_scale_pks, I_after_scale_pks).

#define:
#define $name and #undef $name set/clear a pre-processor flag, checked later with #ifdef/#ifndef (independent of the kernel's prm/local parameters, and evaluated purely at the pre-processor stage). For example:

#ifdef !STANDARD_MACROS
  #define STANDARD_MACROS
  xdd ...
#endif

sets STANDARD_MACROS the first time this text is processed, so a later #ifdef STANDARD_MACROS elsewhere in the file (or in an #include'd file) sees it as defined. #undef reverses this -- after #undef $name, a later #ifdef $name sees it as no longer defined (and #ifndef $name sees it as defined-not, i.e. true again). See also #ifdef, #ifndef, #if/#elseif/#else/#endif.
#if:
#if E; ... [#elseif E; ...] [#else] #endif -- together with #ifdef $name/#ifndef $name -- form the pre-processor's conditional family, evaluated once while the INP file is loaded (entirely separate from any kernel-level conditional). #if/#elseif test a general equation (often built from #prm hash parameters); #ifdef/#ifndef instead test whether a name has (or hasn't) been previously #define'd. #else marks the branch taken when every preceding condition was false; #endif closes the block.

#prm ran = Constant(Rand(0,1));
#if ran < 0.5;
  view_structure
#endif

(wrapping in Constant(...) means every #if referencing ran in the same file sees the same value, rather than a fresh random draw each time it's evaluated). #elseif chains additional branches:

#prm space_group_number = 4;
#if And(space_group_number >= 75, space_group_number <= 142);
  ...
#elseif And(space_group_number >= 16, space_group_number <= 74);
  ...
#endif

#ifdef/#ifndef test a flag instead of an equation:

#ifdef STANDARD_MACROS
  xdd ...
#endif

includes the xdd keyword only if STANDARD_MACROS was previously #define'd. Prefixing the name with '!' inverts the test, so these two forms are equivalent 'define once' guards:

#ifdef !STANDARD_MACROS
  #define STANDARD_MACROS
  xdd ...
#endif

#ifndef STANDARD_MACROS
  #define STANDARD_MACROS
  xdd ...
#endif

See also #m_if/#m_elseif/#m_else/#m_endif, the equivalent conditional family used specifically during macro expansion.
#include: #include $file, #ingest $file and #external_INP $file all pull text from another file at the pre-processor stage, but differ in what happens to it. #include inserts the named file's raw text in place before parsing continues -- e.g. #include "my include file.inc"; the standard macro library Topas.inc is always included by default, with no explicit #include needed for its macros. #ingest instead treats the ingested file as if its text were literally part of the original INP file, so any refined parameters within it are updated in place and the OUT file contains the ingested text with those parameters replaced by their refined values -- e.g. xdd... str... #ingest common_str.txt; #ingest calls can be nested. #external_INP designates the named file as a wholly separate INP file, e.g. xdd... #external_INP instrument.inp #external_INP str.inp (see test_examples\external_INP\ext_inp.inp); it can also be nested (an #external_INP file may contain further #external_INP commands), and when running Launch mode from the GUI (TA.EXE), all #external_INP OUT files are renamed to INP files if the prompt on refinement termination is answered affirmatively. In all three cases $file can be a function of macros.
#list:
#list $macro_name1 [& $macro_name2 [, & $extra_arg]]... { row1_values row2_values ... } defines an array of per-row macros from a table of values given in curly braces -- each named column ($macro_name1, $macro_name2, ...) becomes a callable macro whose first (implied) argument is a #type equation evaluating to an integer row number, returning that column's value on the corresponding row. For example:

#list File_Name & Temperature(, & la) Time {
   File0001.xy 300 0.0
   { File0002 .xy } 320 10.2
   File0003.xy 340 21.0
   File0017.xy { 360 + la } 28.9
   File0107.xy 380 101.2
}

makes File_Name(#row), Temperature(#row[, extra]) and Time(#row) all available -- e.g. xdd File_Name(Run_Number) expands to the file name on row Run_Number. Curly braces `{ }` also delimit a value containing spaces (e.g. `{ File0002 .xy }`) or an expression to be substituted verbatim into that row's value (e.g. `{ 360 + la }`, giving Temperature(3, Get(la)+0.01) => (360 + (Get(la)+0.01))); Temperature's extra trailing argument after the row number substitutes into that braced expression. #list_n $list returns, during the pre-processor phase, the number of rows in the named #list -- e.g. #list Files { file1.xdd file2.xdd file3.xdd } Create_XDDs(#list_n Files) expands #list_n Files to 3.
#m_argu:
#m_argu c, #m_unique_not_refine c and #m_first_word $v, used during macro expansion, each change the value of one macro argument in place, according to which directive is used:

#m_argu c -- changes argument c to an auto-generated unique parameter name if c's first character is '@' (the usual TOPAS '@' auto-naming convention, scoped to a macro argument)
#m_unique_not_refine c -- the same unique-naming as #m_argu, but marks the resulting parameter as not to be refined
#m_first_word $v -- replaces the string argument $v with the first word occurring in it, useful for extracting a single identifier out of a longer string-shaped argument

See also #m_unique (section 21.1.5), a related but distinct directive for naming a NEW parameter declared inside a macro body, rather than transforming an existing macro argument.
#m_if:
#m_if E; ... [#m_elseif E; ...] [#m_else] #m_endif is the macro-expansion-time counterpart to the plain pre-processor's #if/#elseif/#else/#endif -- invoked while a specific macro is being expanded, rather than at general pre-processor scope. For example:

macro Ex1(a) { #m_if a == "b"; Yes b #m_elseif a == "c"; Yes c #m_endif }
Ex1("b")

expands to:

Yes b

#m_elseif chains additional conditions (evaluated only if the preceding #m_if/#m_elseif were false), #m_else marks the fallback branch, and #m_endif closes the block -- same structure as the plain #if family. See also #m_ifarg, which specifically tests a property of one of the macro's own arguments (whether it's an equation, a bare code/parameter name, a single word, or equal to a literal string) rather than a general condition, and is commonly used as the condition inside #m_if.
#m_ifarg:
#m_ifarg c $test, used during macro expansion, tests a property of macro argument c against one of a fixed set of $test forms (evaluating to true/false, for use as a condition in #m_if/#m_elseif):

#m_ifarg c #m_code -- true if argument c starts with a letter or '!' and is not an equation
#m_ifarg c #m_eqn -- true if argument c is an equation
#m_ifarg c #m_code_refine -- true if argument c starts with a letter and is not an equation
#m_ifarg c "some_string" -- true if argument c == "some_string"
#m_ifarg v #m_one_word -- true if argument v consists of exactly one word

This lets a macro branch its expansion based on how it was called -- e.g. was a refinable code name passed, or a bare equation, or a specific literal string. #m_code, #m_eqn, #m_code_refine and #m_one_word only ever appear as this second, test-selecting argument to #m_ifarg; they aren't standalone directives.
#seed: #seed [#number] initializes the random number generator at the pre-processor stage (as opposed to the plain seed keyword, which does so at the kernel stage, based on the computer clock unless given an explicit integer). Use #seed specifically when pre-processor-stage randomization -- e.g. inside a #prm equation using Rand(), or a macro expanded differently depending on a pre-processor random draw -- needs to be reproducible run to run.
Other items can be placed here.
A0_matrix_is_constant: A0_matrix_is_constant signals to the program that the A0 matrix (the observed-data contribution to the least-squares normal-equations matrix of Eq. (4-4)) does not change between iterations, so it is calculated only once instead of being recalculated every iteration. This is valid specifically for the deconvolution method of Coelho (2018), implemented via the TOPAS.INC macros Deconvolution_Init, Deconvolution_Bkg_Penalty and Deconvolution_Intensity_Penalty (see test_examples\deconvolution\pbso4-decon.inp), where only linear parameters -- peak intensities and background coefficients -- are refined, and whose derivatives are therefore constant. Because it assumes every refined parameter is linear, using A0_matrix_is_constant together with quick_refine, approximate_A, chi2, or while any genuinely non-linear parameter is being refined will throw an exception, since those all depend on the A0 matrix being recalculated (or being approximated in a way incompatible with a fixed A0). It is a minimization-level optimization, unrelated to any particular phase type, which is why it belongs alongside the other TMinimization keywords rather than under any specific phase.
AB_Cyl_Corr: AB_Cyl_Corr(R) returns the AB term used in the cylindrical-sample intensity correction of Sabine et al. (1998), as a function of sample radius R; used internally by the Cylindrical_I_Correction macro (see cylcorr.inp). Its companion function is AL_Cyl_Corr(R); for a more accurate alternative to both Sabine corrections, see the capillary_diameter_mm convolution.
AL_Cyl_Corr: AL_Cyl_Corr(R) returns the AL term used in the cylindrical-sample intensity correction of Sabine et al. (1998), as a function of sample radius R; used internally by the Cylindrical_2Th_Correction macro (see cylcorr.inp). Its companion function is AB_Cyl_Corr(R); for a more accurate alternative to both Sabine corrections, see the capillary_diameter_mm convolution.
A_matrix:
A_matrix, C_matrix, A_matrix_normalized and C_matrix_normalized generate the un-normalized and normalized least-squares A matrix (the A matrix of Eq. (4-4), A = A0 + AP + AR) and its corresponding correlation matrix. A_matrix and A_matrix_normalized output the un-normalized and normalized forms of the A matrix; C_matrix and C_matrix_normalized output the un-normalized and normalized correlation matrix respectively.

If do_errors is defined, C_matrix_normalized is automatically generated and appended to the OUT file even without being explicitly requested, since it is what do_errors uses to compute and report parameter errors -- the correlation matrix identified by C_matrix_normalized is appended to the OUT file if it does not already exist, or updated if it does. This correlation (covariance) matrix Cov is also used to propagate errors to dependent parameters: for a dependent parameter D = f(a, b, c),

Error(D)^2 = GOF * ( (dD/da)^2 Cov(a,a) + (dD/db)^2 Cov(b,b) + (dD/dc)^2 Cov(c,c)
  + 2 (dD/da)(dD/db) Cov(a,b) + 2 (dD/da)(dD/dc) Cov(a,c) + 2 (dD/db)(dD/dc) Cov(b,c) )

where dD/da etc. are the partial derivatives of D with respect to each independent parameter. See also out_A_matrix, which writes the A matrix to a separate file (optionally filtered via A_matrix_prm_filter) rather than generating it for internal/OUT-file error reporting.
A_matrix_elements_tollerance:
A_matrix_elements_tollerance #tol removes elements from the approximated A matrix (used when approximate_A is defined) whose values fall below #tol, forcing the matrix to be stored sparsely. The comparison is made against A matrix elements normalized such that Aii = 1, so #tol is a relative rather than absolute threshold; typical values range from 0.0001 to 0.01. It can be used simultaneously with A_matrix_memory_allowed_in_Mbytes, combining a magnitude-based and a memory-based criterion for what gets kept in the sparse matrix.

This is intended for refinements with very large numbers of independent parameters, where retaining every small, numerically-insignificant off-diagonal element would waste memory without materially affecting convergence. A_matrix_report_on displays the resulting percentage of non-zero elements in the A matrix, useful for tuning #tol.
A_matrix_memory_allowed_in_Mbytes:
A_matrix_memory_allowed_in_Mbytes limits the memory (in megabytes) used by the approximated A matrix when approximate_A is defined, forcing it to be stored sparsely once that limit would otherwise be exceeded. It can be used simultaneously with A_matrix_elements_tollerance -- the two together keep the sparse A matrix within both a memory budget and an element-magnitude threshold. This is specifically aimed at refinements with very large numbers of independent parameters (thousands of xdds and/or structural parameters), where a dense A matrix would be impractical to hold in memory.

A_matrix_report_on can be used alongside it to display the resulting percentage of non-zero elements retained in the A matrix, which is useful for judging whether the memory limit is set sensibly. Without approximate_A defined, this keyword has no effect, since the exact (non-approximated) A matrix does not go through this sparsification path.
A_matrix_report_on:
A_matrix_report_on displays the percentage of non-zero elements in the A matrix when approximate_A is defined, and in particular when A_matrix_memory_allowed_in_Mbytes and/or A_matrix_elements_tollerance are being used to sparsify it. This provides a direct, quantitative way to check whether the chosen memory limit or element tolerance is producing the intended level of sparsity for a given refinement. It is purely diagnostic/reporting -- it does not change how the A matrix is calculated or stored.

It is most useful when tuning A_matrix_elements_tollerance for a new, very large refinement (thousands of xdds and/or structural parameters), since the appropriate tolerance is problem-dependent and not obvious in advance. See also approximate_A_check_for_must_be_zero, which additionally invokes sparse matrix methods by explicitly zeroing elements known to be exactly zero rather than merely small.
Abs: Abs(x) returns the absolute value of x.
Add: + adds two values: a + b. One of TOPAS's four basic arithmetic operators (alongside -, * and /), usable anywhere inside an equation.
And: And(a, b, ...) returns 1 if every argument is non-zero, 0 otherwise.
Apply_Brindley_Spherical_R_PD: Apply_Brindley_Spherical_R_PD(& R, & PD) is a topas.inc convenience macro that sets brindley_spherical_r_cm as the product of a particle radius R (in cm) and a packing density PD: brindley_spherical_r_cm = R * PD. brindley_spherical_r_cm feeds the Brindley microabsorption correction Bp used in the weight_percent calculation (a function of the difference between a phase's own linear absorption coefficient and the mixture's, scaled by brindley_spherical_r_cm) -- see Phase_LAC_1_on_cm/Mixture_LAC_1_on_cm for the LAC side of that same correction.
ArcCos: ArcCos(x) returns the arc cosine of x, valid for -1 <= x <= 1.
ArcSin: ArcSin(x) returns the arc sine of x, valid for -1 <= x <= 1.
ArcTan: ArcTan(x) returns the arc tangent of x.
ArcTan2: ArcTan2(y, x) returns the arc tangent of y/x -- the two-argument form, which correctly resolves the quadrant from the signs of y and x individually, unlike ArcTan(y/x) alone.
Break: Break terminates the implied loop in an atomic_interaction, box_interaction or grs_interaction equation.
Break_Cycle: Break_Cycle terminates the current refinement cycle -- e.g. atomic_interaction ai = (R - 1.3)^2; penalty = If(ai > 5, Break_Cycle, 0); stops the cycle once ai exceeds 5.
Charge_Flipping.INC: Charge_Flipping.INC is the include file containing the macros that support protein charge-flipping strategies (such as the S0/S1/S1T strategies described in Coelho, 2021) -- see test_examples\CF-PROTEIN\ for the worked solve.inp examples that use them.
Concat: Concat(a, b, c, ...) concatenates its arguments as strings; a parameter argument is converted to its value's string form first.
Constant: Constant(expression) evaluates expression once and permanently replaces Constant(expression) with that fixed numeric value -- useful when a small expected change in a parameter would otherwise insignificantly perturb a dependent equation on every iteration (see the TOF_Exponential macro).
Cos: Cos(x) returns the cosine of x.
Cosh: Cosh(x) returns the hyperbolic cosine of x.
Divide: / divides a by b: a / b.
Equal_to: a == b returns 1 if a equals b, 0 otherwise.
Erf_Approx: Erf_Approx(x) returns an approximation to the error function of x.
Erfc_Approx: Erfc_Approx(x) returns an approximation to the complementary error function of x, i.e. 1 - Erf_Approx(x).
Error: Error(p) returns the refinement error (standard uncertainty) associated with parameter p.
Exp: Exp(x) returns e raised to the power x.
Flack: For single crystal data and for non-centrosymmetric structures the Flack parameter (Flack, 1983) scales F2(h) and F2(-h) as follows (see the test example ylidma.inp).
For: For(Mi = 0, Mi < M, Mi = Mi+1, ...) is a C-style for-loop usable directly inside an equation: an initializer, a continuation test and an increment expression, followed by the loop body -- each argument evaluated the same way a for(;;) loop would be in C.
Gamma_Approx: Gamma_Approx(x) returns an approximation to the Gamma function of x.
Gamma_Ln_Approx: Gamma_Ln_Approx(x) returns the natural logarithm of the Gamma function of x.
Gamma_P: Gamma_P(a, x) returns the (regularized) incomplete Gamma function P(a, x).
Gamma_Q: Gamma_Q(a, x) returns the (regularized) incomplete Gamma function Q(a, x) = 1 - P(a, x).
Get: Get($keyword) returns the value of the parameter associated with $keyword, resolved via the same ancestor-search rule used throughout TOPAS's own Get() path search.
Get_Element_Weight:
Get_Element_Weight(atom) (used as 'prm = Get_Element_Weight(atom);', a str-dependent equation function) returns the weight of the named element/species (atom, e.g. Zr) present in the current phase's structure, computed from that phase's scale, cell_mass, cell_volume and site occupancies/atom types. Used to build an elemental-weight-percent constraint when an element's overall weight percent is known independently (e.g. from XRF) and several phases in the mixture contain it -- e.g. for three Zr-bearing phases:

str ... prm z1 = Get_Element_Weight(Zr); MVW(!m1 0, !v1 0, 0)
str ... scale s2 0.001 prm z2 = Get_Element_Weight(Zr); MVW(0, !v2 0, 0)
str ... scale s3 0.001 prm z3 = Get_Element_Weight(Zr); MVW(0, !v3 0, 0)

Rearranging the element-weight-percent formula lets the first phase's own scale factor be solved directly from a known overall Zr content known_Zr and the other phases' contributions:

scale = (0.01 known_Zr Get(sum_smvs_minus_this) - s2 v2 z2 - s3 v3 z3) / (v1 (z1 - 0.01 known_Zr m1));

See quant-3.inp, and 11-quantitative-analysis.md.
Greater_than: a > b returns 1 if a is greater than b, 0 otherwise.
Greater_than_or_equal: a >= b returns 1 if a is greater than or equal to b, 0 otherwise.
I_parameter_names_have_hkl: I_parameter_names_have_hkl $start_of_parameter_name, a child of hkl_Is, assigns names to the generated intensity (I) parameters that start with $start_of_parameter_name and end with the corresponding hkl indices, instead of leaving them with the default auto-generated internal parameter names. This makes it possible to reference a specific reflection's intensity parameter directly by name elsewhere in the INP file -- for example, in an equation, restraint, or penalty that needs to target a particular hkl's intensity -- without having to hunt through the generated parameter list to find its default name. It is used alongside lp_search and hkl_m_d_th2, which are the other children of hkl_Is controlling how the hkl set and its intensities are generated.
If: If(conditional_test, true_eqn, false_eqn) returns true_eqn if conditional_test is non-zero, otherwise false_eqn. If statements can be nested, e.g. update = If(Val < 10, 10, If(Val > 10000, 10000, Val));. For those who prefer if/else syntax, Topas.inc defines IF/THEN/ELSE/ENDIF macros wrapping this: IF a > b THEN a ' true_expr ELSE b ' false_expr ENDIF.
Include_Charge_Flipping: Include_Charge_Flipping is a bodiless topas.inc MACRO, not a keyword -- confirmed directly from its real definition: `macro Include_Charge_Flipping { #include Double_Quote##ROOT##Charge_Flipping.inc##Double_Quote }`. It's a thin convenience wrapper around the #include preprocessor directive that pulls in Charge_Flipping.inc (the file containing the charge-flipping macros, such as the S0/S1/S1T protein-solving strategies described in Coelho, 2021) using the correct ROOT-relative path, so an INP file doesn't need to know or type that path. Same pattern as the sibling macros Include_GUI_PDF and Include_PDF_Generate. Seen preceding the charge_flipping keyword block in the 'Solving proteins at atomic resolution' worked example, where a structure generated via pdb_cif_to_str_file is then solved/refined using charge flipping.
Known_Weight_Percent:
Known_Weight_Percent(& w) is a str-scoped topas.inc macro that constrains a phase's scale factor so its weight_percent comes out equal to a known value w (e.g. from XRF), rather than being left as a free Rietveld-refined quantity:

scale = (w/(100-w)) * Get(sum_smvs_minus_this) / (Get(cell_mass) * Get(cell_volume))

where Get(sum_smvs_minus_this) is the sum of every other phase's SMV (Sp*Mp*Vp) in the mixture. It is commonly used on a dummy_str describing an amorphous or otherwise unmodeled phase whose weight fraction is known independently -- see test_examples\quant\quant-2.inp (constraining a weight percent to a known value) and quant-4.inp (the same, applied to an hkl_Is phase).
Less_than: a < b returns 1 if a is less than b, 0 otherwise.
Less_than_or_equal: a <= b returns 1 if a is less than or equal to b, 0 otherwise.
Ln: Ln(x) returns the natural logarithm of x.
Ln_Normal_x_at_CD: Ln_Normal_x_at_CD(u, s, v, toll) returns the x value of a log-normal distribution (mean u and standard deviation s of the variable's natural logarithm) at cumulative distribution value v, computed to a tolerance toll in v (see test_examples\wppm\ln-normal-1.inp).
Load_Eval: a = Load_Eval(b) evaluates b once, at load time, and stores the resulting fixed value in a, rather than re-evaluating b on every subsequent iteration.
MM_Cartesian_Display:
MM_Cartesian_Display(mxc, myc, mzc) is a site-dependent, display-only topas.inc macro that converts a site's magnetic moment m = {mlx, mly, mlz} into Cartesian coordinates, using the standard crystallographic-to-Cartesian convention where a lies along the Cartesian x-axis and b lies in the xy-plane:

ax = a, bx = b*Cos(ga), by = b*Sin(ga)
cx = c*Cos(be), cy = c*(Cos(al) - Cos(be)*Cos(ga))/Sin(ga), cz = Sqrt(c^2 - cx^2 - cy^2)

The Cartesian moment components are then:

mxc = mlx*ax + mly*bx + mlz*cx, myc = mly*by + mlz*cy, mzc = mlz*cz

It does not refine anything -- see MM_Cartesian_Refine for the refinable counterpart, and MM_CrystalAxis_Display/MM_CrystalAxis_Refine for the equivalent pair expressed along the crystal axes instead of in Cartesian coordinates.
MM_Cartesian_Refine:
MM_Cartesian_Refine(mxc, mxv, myc, myv, mzc, mzv, mlx_v, mly_v, mlz_v) is a site-dependent topas.inc macro that lets a site's magnetic moment be refined directly in Cartesian coordinates rather than as mlx/mly/mlz. mxc/myc/mzc are refined (each via If_Prm_Eqn_Rpt against a value parameter mxv/myv/mzv), then mlx/mly/mlz are recovered by inverting the same crystallographic-to-Cartesian axis transformation used in MM_Cartesian_Display:

ax = a, bx = b*Cos(ga), by = b*Sin(ga)
cx = c*Cos(be), cy = c*(Cos(al) - Cos(be)*Cos(ga))/Sin(ga), cz = Sqrt(c^2 - cx^2 - cy^2)

mlz = mzc/cz, mly = (myc - mlz*cy)/by, mlx = (mxc - mly*by - mlz*cx)/ax

with the resulting values reported through the equation-name outputs mlx_v/mly_v/mlz_v. This is the refinable counterpart to MM_Cartesian_Display, and is the Cartesian analogue of MM_CrystalAxis_Refine.
MM_CrystalAxis_Display:
MM_CrystalAxis_Display(mxc, myc, mzc) is a site-dependent, display-only topas.inc macro that reports a site's magnetic moment components scaled along the crystal axes:

mxc = mlx*a, myc = mly*b, mzc = mlz*c

(Get(mlx)/Get(mly)/Get(mlz) multiplied by the corresponding lattice parameter). It does not refine anything -- see MM_CrystalAxis_Refine for the refinable counterpart, and MM_Cartesian_Display/MM_Cartesian_Refine for the equivalent pair expressed in Cartesian coordinates instead of along the (possibly non-orthogonal) crystal axes.
MM_CrystalAxis_Refine:
MM_CrystalAxis_Refine(mxc, mxv, myc, myv, mzc, mzv, mlx_v, mly_v, mlz_v) is a site-dependent topas.inc macro that lets a site's magnetic moment be refined in terms of crystal-axis-scaled components rather than mlx/mly/mlz directly. mxc/myc/mzc are refined (each via If_Prm_Eqn_Rpt against a value parameter mxv/myv/mzv), then mlx/mly/mlz are derived from them by dividing out the corresponding lattice parameter:

mlx = mxc/a, mly = myc/b, mlz = mzc/c

with the resulting values reported through the equation-name outputs mlx_v/mly_v/mlz_v. This is the refinable counterpart to MM_CrystalAxis_Display, and is the crystal-axis analogue of MM_Cartesian_Refine.
Max: Max(a, b, c, ...) returns the maximum of all arguments.
Min: Min(a, b, c, ...) returns the minimum of all arguments.
Mixture_LAC_1_on_cm: Mixture_LAC_1_on_cm(0), an xdd-scoped macro, calculates the linear absorption coefficient (LAC) of the whole mixture, in 1/cm, assuming a packing density of 1 -- e.g. 'xdd ... Mixture_LAC_1_on_cm(0)'. It is derived from mixture_MAC (the mixture's mass absorption coefficient in cm^2/g) combined with mixture_density_g_on_cm3, and its estimated error is also calculated and reported alongside the value. It is the mixture-level counterpart of Phase_LAC_1_on_cm, and both feed into the Brindley correction Bp, which is a function of (LAC_phase - MAC_mixture) * brindley_spherical_r_cm for each phase p -- since Bp in turn affects each phase's weight fraction wp, this makes the weight-fraction calculation dependent on itself and it is therefore solved numerically via an iterative procedure rather than analytically. Mass absorption coefficients used in this calculation come from NIST (http://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef).
Mod: Mod(x, y) returns x modulo y; Mod(x, 0) returns 0.
Multiply: * multiplies two values: a * b. The multiplication operator is optional between two sub-expressions -- x*y can equally be written x y (implicit multiplication by juxtaposition).
Obj_There: Obj_There(a) returns 1 if an object named a exists within the current scope, 0 otherwise.
Or: Or(a, b, ...) returns 1 if one or more arguments is non-zero, 0 otherwise.
PV_Lor_from_GL: PV_Lor_from_GL(gauss_FWHM, lorentzian_FWHM) returns the Lorentzian-contribution FWHM of the pseudo-Voigt approximation to a true Voigt profile formed by convolving a Gaussian and Lorentzian with the given FWHMs.
Phase_Density_g_on_cm3: Phase_Density_g_on_cm3(0), a str-scoped macro, calculates the density of an individual phase, in g/cm^3, from its cell_mass and cell_volume -- e.g. 'str ... Phase_Density_g_on_cm3(0)'. Its estimated error is also calculated and reported alongside the value. It is the phase-level counterpart of mixture_density_g_on_cm3, and is used together with phase_MAC to derive Phase_LAC_1_on_cm, the phase's linear absorption coefficient. See example under mixture_MAC / Mixture_LAC_1_on_cm / Phase_LAC_1_on_cm, where all three macros are used together to report phase and mixture absorption/density quantities for a multi-phase refinement.
Phase_LAC_1_on_cm: Phase_LAC_1_on_cm(0), a str-scoped macro, calculates the linear absorption coefficient (LAC) of an individual phase, in 1/cm, assuming a packing density of 1 -- e.g. 'str ... Phase_LAC_1_on_cm(0)'. It is derived from that phase's own phase_MAC (mass absorption coefficient in cm^2/g) combined with its density (see Phase_Density_g_on_cm3), and its estimated error is also calculated and reported. It is the phase-level counterpart of Mixture_LAC_1_on_cm, and the difference between a phase's LAC and the mixture's MAC (LAC_phase - MAC_mixture), scaled by brindley_spherical_r_cm, is what determines the Brindley correction Bp used in the weight-fraction (weight_percent) calculation for that phase. Mass absorption coefficients used in this calculation come from NIST (http://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef).
Phase_LAC_Eqn_1_on_cm: Phase_LAC_Eqn_1_on_cm is the underlying equation macro used by Phase_LAC_1_on_cm to compute a phase's own linear absorption coefficient (LAC) at packing density 1, in 1/cm: Get(phase_MAC) * Phase_Density_Eqn_g_on_cm3 (phase_MAC, its mass absorption coefficient in cm^2/g, times its density in g/cm^3 -- see Phase_Density_g_on_cm3, 1.6605402 * Get(cell_mass) / Get(cell_volume)). Phase_LAC_1_on_cm(u) assigns this equation's value to a local named u: local = Phase_LAC_Eqn_1_on_cm; : u -- so Phase_LAC_Eqn_1_on_cm can be used directly wherever the bare equation value is needed instead of a reported/output local, e.g. inside a further equation.
Power: x^y raises x to the power y. Its precedence binds to the left rather than the right: x^y^z evaluates as (x^y)^z (not x^(y^z)), and x^y*z / x^y/z evaluate as (x^y)*z / (x^y)/z.

Rand: Rand(a, b) returns a uniformly distributed random number between a and b.
Rand_Normal: Rand_Normal(mean, std) returns a normally-distributed random number with the given mean and standard deviation std.

Rs: Primary and secondary instrument radii (mm). For most diffractometers Rp = Rs.
Sign: Sign(x) returns the sign of x (1 or -1), or 0 if x = 0.
Sin: Sin(x) returns the sine of x.
Sinh: Sinh(x) returns the hyperbolic sine of x.
Sites_Geometry_Angle: Sites_Geometry_Angle($Name) returns the angle measurement computed by the sites_geometry object named $Name.
Sites_Geometry_Dihedral_Angle: Sites_Geometry_Dihedral_Angle($Name) returns the dihedral-angle measurement computed by the sites_geometry object named $Name.

TCharge_flipping: TCharge_flipping collects the keywords that configure a charge_flipping object: the charge-flipping cell (a/b/c/al/be/ga), break_cycle_if_true's cycle-termination test, cf_hkl_file/cf_in_A_matrix input files, cf_percent_ED_ge_H's electron-density threshold, cf_plot_fit/cf_plot_histo display toggles, delete_observed_reflections, extend_calculated_sphere_to, f_atom_type/f_atom_quantity (declaring the atom types and quantities present, needed since charge flipping has no a-priori structural model), and find_origin. Together these drive TOPAS's ab-initio structure-solution algorithm (see 22-charge-flipping.md).
TEnergy_minimization:
TEnergy_minimization (see Chapter 14, 'Energy Minimization') groups the keywords for evaluating and minimizing the lattice/electrostatic energy of a structure, as a complement to (or substitute for) refining against diffraction intensities: madelung reports the Madelung constant of a structure, co (site-dependent) reports the Coulomb potential at a site (the sum of all co values equals the Madelung constant), and grs_interaction defines a general repulsion-sum (GRS) interaction between two named sites that can be driven into a genuine energy-minimization mode via repulsion_refine.

Madelung constant and Coulomb potential: madelung uses the method of Coelho & Cheary (1997) to calculate electrostatic potentials, with atomic charges taken from each site's occ keyword; co reports the per-site Coulomb potential whose sum equals the Madelung constant. Both are independent of grs_interaction.

The GRS interaction and its potential form: grs_interaction defines an interaction between sites $site_1/$site_2 with equation E, a function of R (the interatomic distance, in Angstrom, updated as fractional coordinates change); qi/qj are the valence charges of the two sites used in its Coulomb term. A typical two-term potential (Coulomb plus a short-range repulsion) takes the form:

Uij = qi*qj/R + si*sj/R^n

where si/sj are the site-dependent s (scale) parameters and n is the repulsion exponent. Setting the force-balance/equilibrium condition at the minimum-energy separation Ro:

dUij(R=Ro)/dR = 0

gives:

Ro = [ (n-1) si*sj / (qi*qj) ]^(1/(n-1))

i.e. si/sj can be derived directly from a known equilibrium bond distance Ro rather than fit freely. no_coulomb, defined on a grs_interaction, drops the qi*qj/R Coulomb term entirely so the interaction uses only its own equation part -- useful for partly-ionic structures (e.g. AlVO4, via test_examples\grs-alvo4\rep-2.inp) built from several no_coulomb interactions with different R^-n forms, or for splitting a dipole's nucleus and shifted electron-cloud sites into two interactions, one for the nucleus:

= 0;

and one for the shifted cloud:

= 1/R^9; no_coulomb

repulsion_refine mode: when repulsion_refine is defined, every grs_interaction switches from returning its energy value to returning the sum of the squared derivatives of the interaction with respect to atomic coordinates:

Sum((d(grs_interaction)/dfi)^2, i)

where fi ranges over the x/y/z coordinates of the interaction's sites. In this mode fractional coordinates are NOT refined; instead, refinement adjusts the repulsion parameters themselves (qi, qj, q, s, and any other parameters in the grs_interaction equation) so that those derivatives are minimized -- fitting the repulsion model so the Rietveld-refined structure sits at (or near) a force-balance equilibrium. The site-dependent s parameter scales the equation part of a grs_interaction, letting several similar interactions collapse into one shared equation driven by per-site scale factors -- e.g. three separate Al-O/V-O/Al-V interactions, each with its own coefficient B1/B2/B3, become a single:

grs_interaction * * c = 1/R^9;

with B1 = s1*s3, B2 = s2*s3, B3 = s1*s2 (s1/s2/s3 the per-site s values for Al/V/O respectively) -- letting the program cache equation values independent of the refined repulsion parameters for a large speed-up. The site-dependent g keyword reports the difference between the sum of all grs_interactions with a given site included versus excluded -- i.e. that site's contribution to the total.

Including lattice parameters: by default, repulsion_refine's derivative minimization does NOT include lattice parameters. For repulsion_refine mode, adding them requires:

penalty = Get(grs_lp_rep);

the equivalent for ordinary (non-repulsion_refine) refinement, so that lattice parameters flagged for refinement are included in the grs_interaction derivatives, is:

penalty = Get(grs_lp_refine);

See test_examples\alvo4-grs-auto.inp, grs-alvo4\solve-1.inp, grs-alvo4\rep-1.inp and grs-alvo4\rep-2.inp for worked examples spanning structure solution by energy minimization, non-ionic R^-4/R^-9 potentials, and lattice-parameter-inclusive refinement.
TMagnetism:
TMagnetism (see Chapter 12, 'Magnetic Structure Refinement' -- thanks to Branton Campbell and John Evans for expert assistance during the implementation) groups the keywords for refining a magnetic structure alongside (or instead of) the ordinary nuclear one, on a str: mag_space_group $symbol switches on magnetic refinement for that str by declaring its magnetic (Shubnikov) space group, and the site-dependent mlx, mly, mlz (the Cartesian components of a site's magnetic moment vector m = {mlx, mly, mlz}) and mg (the Lande splitting factor) supply the actual magnetic parameters. mag_only_for_mag_sites (str-level) and mag_only (site-level) suppress the ordinary nuclear/structural intensity contribution -- for every magnetic site in the str, or for just one site, respectively -- leaving only the magnetic scattering. See examples in test_examples\mag, and the tutorial by John Evans at http://www.dur.ac.uk/john.evans/topas_workshop/tutorial_lamno3_magnetic.htm.

Core equations: the magnetic intensity is |Fmagcperp|, the component of the magnetic structure factor Fmagc perpendicular to the scattering vector Q:

Fmagcperp = Fmagc - (Fmagc . Qhat) Qhat

where Q = (L^-1)^T * h (L the Cartesian lattice-parameter matrix, h the Miller indices as a vector, so (L^-1)^T is the reciprocal-lattice transform) and Qhat = Q/|Q|. In Cartesian terms Fmagc = L * Fmag, where Fmag for a single site, summed over its equivalent positions j, is:

Fmag = Sum_j (Bj * m) Exp(2*Pi*i*Uj)

with Uj = h.Rj.x + h.tj (x the site's fractional coordinates, Rj/tj the rotation/translation parts of space-group operator j), and Bj = sj*det(Rj)*Rj the magnetic transformation matrix (sj the site's magnetic 'colour' sign). Magnetic form-factor data comes from MAGDATA.DAT (a GSAS-format file, used by permission of Robert Von Dreele); mg defaults to the value MAGDATA.DAT supplies for that ion but can be refined like any other parameter. Shubnikov groups come from shubnikovgroups.txt. Magnetic moments are displayed as arrows (Occupancy*Bj*m) when view_structure is used -- reduce the 'Atom size' display setting if atom balls hide the arrows.

Why two magnetic space groups matter (not in the Technical Reference manual -- Dinnebier, Leineweber & Evans, 2018, section 9.3): a magnetic moment is an axial vector, not a polar one -- it transforms oppositely to an ordinary vector under mirror reflection (a moment perpendicular to a mirror is preserved, one parallel to it is flipped, the reverse of how an atomic displacement transforms). Combining the 230 crystallographic space groups with time reversal (spin reversal, 1', which flips a moment without any accompanying rotation/translation) produces the 1651 magnetic (Shubnikov) space groups, falling into four types: Type 1 (G = F, no time reversal involved), Type 2/'grey' (G = F + F.1', the paramagnetic/disordered case), Type 3 'black-white, first kind' (magnetic cell same size as the nuclear cell -- handled with a single mag_space_group str carrying both nuclear and magnetic scattering), and Type 4 'black-white, second kind' (magnetic cell larger than the nuclear cell -- handled as separate nuclear and magnetic phases, the magnetic one using mag_only_for_mag_sites in its larger cell). mag_space_group expects the BNS (Belov-Neronova-Smirnova) serial number, not the OG (Opechowski-Guccione) one -- the two conventions can assign different numbers/symbols to the same group (e.g. BNS Camma, serial 67.509 = OG Pcmmm', serial 47.11.357); shubnikovgroups.txt lists BNS numbers with their BNS symbols.

Refinement warnings: 'Warning: Magnetic moment mlx of site ... has no contribution to Fmag' and 'Magnetic moment mlx of site ... cannot be refined as it has no derivative' (equivalently for mly/mlz) arise when, for a group of equivalent positions of a special position, the first row of Sum_j(Bj*m) (summed over that group's equivalent positions) comes out zero -- a direct consequence of the moment being an axial vector, since whether a component survives depends on how it transforms under the site's local symmetry. The first message can still appear even when the component isn't being refined; the second terminates refinement if that component IS being refined.

Decomposing Fmag for speed: when a magnetic space group's equivalent positions (other than for group 1.1) are written in terms of others, TOPAS reuses partial sums rather than recomputing Exp(i U) per equivalent position. With Cj = Cos(Uj), Sj = Sin(Uj), and Euler's formula Exp(iU) = Cj + i*Sj: for two equivalent positions sharing U1 = U2 = U,

Fmag1 + Fmag2 = (s1*det(R1)*R1 + s2*det(R2)*R2) m Exp(iU) = c m Exp(iU)

where c doesn't depend on x (a given special position can have many equivalent positions). If instead R1 = -R2 and t1 = -t2 (so U1 = -U2 = U), the s1 = s2 and s1 = -s2 cases reduce respectively to:

Fmag1 + Fmag2 = s1*det(R)*R m (2 Cj)   or   s1*det(R)*R m (2i Sj)

If R1 = R2 (only the translations t1/t2 differ):

Fmag1 + Fmag2 = det(R)*R m (s1 Exp(i.h.t1) + s2 Exp(i.h.t2)) Exp(i.h.R.x) = c Exp(i.h.R.x)

where c again doesn't depend on x and is calculated only once -- many R's can repeat across a space group with only the t's changing. Generally:

Exp(i(h.Rx + h.t)) = Exp(i.h.Rx) Exp(i.h.t)

and Exp(i.h.t) is constant for a given h and calculated once; only the unique Exp(i.h.Rx) values are computed, using trigonometric recurrence so each unique equivalent position costs three cosine and three sine operations rather than a fresh sin/cos per h (a sin or cos costs roughly 40-60 multiplies).

Ambiguities in magnetic structure determination (not in the Technical Reference manual -- Dinnebier, Leineweber & Evans, 2018, section 9.4), genuine information-content limits of powder magnetic diffraction rather than modeling mistakes: genuinely degenerate models can produce identical powder patterns differing only by a scale factor (e.g. a uniform-moment block arrangement vs. a sqrt(2)-times-larger moment on every second site, zero on the rest); multi-k structures (needing more than one propagation vector) can't have their spin configuration uniquely determined from powder data alone; and by Shirane's rule (1959), for collinear magnetic structures how well the moment DIRECTION can be pinned down depends on crystal system -- no information at all for cubic, only the angle to the c-axis for tetragonal/rhombohedral/hexagonal (nothing about orientation within the ab-plane), with full direction information only recoverable for orthorhombic-or-lower symmetry (and the same ambiguity can reappear even there if the true metric symmetry is only slightly distorted from something higher, since peak overlap reintroduces the same information loss).
TMinimization:
TMinimization collects keywords controlling the least-squares minimization engine: A0_matrix_is_constant and approximate_A (with its A_matrix_elements_tollerance/A_matrix_memory_allowed_in_Mbytes/A_matrix_report_on) trade A-matrix accuracy for speed/memory on large refinements; approximate_A_check_for_must_be_zero sanity-checks that approximation; bootstrap_errors (with determine_values_from_samples/fraction_of_yobs_to_resample/resample_from_current_ycalc) estimates parameter errors by resampling rather than from the covariance matrix; chi2 and chi2_convergence_criteria control the refinement objective function and when it's considered converged.

The objective function minimized (Eq. 4-1/4-2/4-3 in 03-minimization-and-convergence.md -- the manual's own typeset equations weren't captured in extraction, but are fully specified by the surrounding text) is:

S = Sum_m[ wm (Yo,m - Yc,m)^2 ] + K1 KP Sum_p[ Pp^2 ] + K1 KR Sum_r[ Rr^2 ]

where Yo,m/Yc,m are the observed/calculated data at data point m (M points total), wm is the weight given to point m (wm = 1/sigma(Yo,m)^2 for counting statistics); Pp are the Np penalty functions (defined via penalty) and Rr the NR restraints (defined via restraint); KP/KR are weights applied to the penalty/restraint sums, automatically computed by default (see pen_weight/Pen_Wt) but overridable; K1 is the user-settable penalties_weighting_K1 (default 1, typically 0.1-2). With no observed data, or when only_penalties is defined, only the penalty/restraint terms remain and BFGS is used by default instead of Newton-Raphson/Marquardt (see example onlypena.inp).

Non-linear least squares uses Newton-Raphson by default, with the Marquardt (1963) method for stability, generating a linear matrix equation each iteration (Eq. 4-4/4-5) from a first-order Taylor expansion of Yc,m (second-order for penalties, first-order for restraints) around the current parameter vector p. Off-diagonal penalty A-matrix terms are always set to zero (restraint off-diagonal terms are calculated unless approximate_A/BFGS is in use -- see restraint/penalty for that distinction).
TMisc_keywords: TMisc_keywords is a small catch-all of top-level keywords that don't belong to any more specific type: aberration_range_change_allowed and default_I_attributes are global tolerances/defaults; load/move_to/for is a looping construct for repeating a block of INP text; new declares a fresh object; dummy/dummy_prm declare placeholder words/parameters with no functional effect, useful for commenting out or stubbing part of an INP file without deleting it.
TMolecular_dynamics:
TMolecular_dynamics (see Chapter 15, 'Molecular dynamics (MD)') places TOPAS in a non-refinement mode where parameters of any type -- not just ones typically associated with molecular dynamics -- are updated in a time-dependent manner using the Verlet (1967) algorithm, driven by grs_interaction (see TEnergy_minimization) supplying the forces. It is conceptually a steepest-descent method, but new parameter values are accepted regardless of whether they improve the objective function (Rwp): relating this to the Newtonian equations of motion for iteration k and parameter p,

Force(k) = m*a(k) = dRwp/dp
Velocity(k+1) = Velocity(k) + (dRwp(k)/dp)/m

The Verlet algorithm avoids computing velocity explicitly and instead updates p directly:

p(k+1) = 2*p(k) - p(k-1) + a(k)*t^2 = 2*p(k) - p(k-1) + (1/m)*(dRwp(k)/dp)*t^2

where t is md_time_step and mass m is set via the _mass parameter attribute. TOPAS generalizes this further to:

p(k+1) = (p(k) - p(k-1) + (_md_k/_mass)*(dRwp(k)/dp)*t^2)*md_scale + p(k)

which reduces to the plain Verlet algorithm when _md_k, _mass and md_scale all take their default value of 1. md_time accumulates simulated time, advancing by md_time_step each MD iteration; md_scale is a means of increasing or decreasing atomic movement per step (effectively temperature).

Defaults for atomic coordinates: in the absence of _mass, mass is instead looked up from the ISOTOPES.TXT file based on the site's occ species (weighted across species for mixed occupancy). In the absence of _md_k, it defaults for x/y/z coordinate parameters to a lattice-geometry correction rather than 1:

md_k for x = ax, for y = by, for z = cz
ax = 1, bx = Cos(Get(ga) Deg), by = Sin(Get(ga) Deg)
cx = Cos(Get(be) Deg), cy = (Cos(Get(al) Deg) - cx*bx)/by, cz = Sqrt(1.0 - cx^2 - cy^2)

so forces are automatically corrected for non-orthogonal lattice parameters without setting _md_k/_mass by hand, e.g.:

x @ # _mass = 26.981; _md_k = ax;

is equivalent to leaving _mass/_md_k unset for that coordinate.

Worked examples (test_examples\grs-alvo4\md-1.inp through md-4.inp, grs-0.inp): md-1.inp operates in P-1, convertible to P1 via p1_fractional_to_file for a 2x2x2 (288-atom) supercell (md-2.inp), where an Al1 atom offset by 2.92 A is shown migrating back to its lowest-energy position over the simulation (tracked via track_buffer/track). md-3.inp displaces an atom 4 A in a random direction (rand_xyz) and uses:

md_scale = If(Cycle_Iter < 2, 0.1, 1);

to damp the resulting chaotic motion for the first two cycles -- since repulsion terms like 1/R^9 blow up at small R, grs-0.inp instead rewrites the grs_interaction as a yobs_eqn that flattens U below a minimum-distance cutoff rsm: for X < rsm, U is a quadratic continuation rather than the raw 1/R^n singularity, avoiding unrealistic large values at small bond distances. Finally, the site-dependent _md_force attribute (default 0) applies an external force to an atom while the simulation maintains overall energy conservation by adjusting the system's kinetic energy to compensate; md-4.inp shows that for AlVO4 under the crude potential used, a force along the a-axis on an Al+3 atom preserves structural integrity, while the same force along c causes the structure to lose it.
TOperators_functions: Toperators_functions collects every operator and built-in function usable inside a TOPAS equation (`= ... ;`), all case sensitive; an equation can also freely mix in any user-defined parameter name alongside these. Click any entry below for its description.
TQuantitative:
TQuantitative collects the per-xdd keywords used for quantitative phase analysis: mixture_MAC and mixture_density_g_on_cm3 supply the mass-attenuation-coefficient and density of the whole mixture (needed to convert Rietveld scale factors into weight percents), weight_percent_amorphous reports the amorphous/unmodeled fraction, elemental_composition reports a per-element weight-percent breakdown, element_weight_percent/element_weight_percent_known report or fix individual element weight percents, and the prm = Get(...) lines expose sum_smvs/mixture_MAC/mixture_density_g_on_cm3 as equation-accessible values. See 11-quantitative-analysis.md.

Worked examples: QUANT-1.INP shows the use of element_weight_percent_known etc. QUANT-2.INP uses the Known_Weight_Percent macro. QUANT-3.INP uses elemental constraint using Get_Element_Weight. QUANT-4.INP uses Known_Weight_Percent on a hkl_Is phase. QUANT-5.INP uses a dummy_str to describe an amorphous phase. QUANT-6.INP uses a hkl_Is phase; links a dummy_str to the hkl_Is phase. QUANT-7.INP uses a fit_obj that is a function of a user_y object to describe a phase; links a dummy_str to a fit_obj to get QUANT info.
TRefinement_control: TRefinement_control collects file-scope controls that apply to the whole refinement, independent of any particular phase or pattern: A_matrix/C_matrix/A_matrix_normalized/C_matrix_normalized request the least-squares/correlation matrices; conserve_memory trades speed for a smaller memory footprint; fft_max_order caps FFT size; file_name_for_best_solutions records the best solutions found (e.g. during simulated annealing); force_positive_fwhm prevents a refined FWHM going negative; inp_text/inp_text_insert lets INP text defined in one place be inserted elsewhere and updated on termination; iters/num_cycles/num_runs control how many refinement iterations, cycles and repeated runs to perform; load_save_locals and no_LIMIT_warnings and out_A_matrix round out file-level behavior.
TReuse_bins:
TReuse_bins (see Chapter 6, 'Reusing objects in large refinements') groups four keywords -- lat_prms, str_dets, phase_dets and use -- that let large numbers of similar phases share common lattice parameters, structural details, and phase-level details (peak shape, transform_X, etc.) instead of each phase recalculating and storing its own copy. This substantially reduces memory usage and speeds up refinement when hundreds of thousands of phases are present, since derivatives of the shared item are also calculated only once.

lat_prms $name { ... }, str_dets $name { ... } and phase_dets $name { ... } each define a named, reusable bin: lat_prms holds a set of lattice parameters (see Tlat_prms); str_dets holds a full structural definition -- space_group and site declarations -- for cases where two phases have similar but not identical lattice parameters yet should still share one set of structure factors (something the program's automatic common-item search cannot do on its own, since it requires identical hkls); phase_dets holds phase-level peak-shape/transform details (lor_fwhm, gauss_fwhm, th2_offset, scale_pks, transform_X, stretch_pks). A phase then pulls in one or more of these named bins with use { name1 name2 ... } inside its str, e.g. str scale @ 1 load use { l0 s0 pd0 ze0 }. Without str_dets, structural details differing only slightly between phases (yet whose hkl sets would otherwise differ) cannot be shared; defining them once in a str_dets object allows a common structure to be reused regardless. For phases with similar lattice parameters, a common set of hkls can likewise be shared via lat_prms.

Worked example (see test_examples\xrd-ct\xrd-ct-0.inp and xrd-ct-1.inp): two strs across two xdds share one str_dets (one set of hkls/structure factors generated instead of two) while using two different lat_prms (since their lattice parameters differ) and two different phase_dets (different lor_fwhm crystallite-size values). The refinement log reports which items were shared via lines like 'Num hkl-sets/unique: 2 1' and 'Num structure-factors-sets/unique: 2 1', and warns if the lattice parameters are not similar enough to justify sharing structure factors. The companion example xrd-ct-1.inp scales this to 150,000 strs and 163,150 independent parameters, completing 20 iterations in ~60s on an 8-core laptop using ~3.1 GB of memory -- impossible without this reuse mechanism (and approximate_A_check_for_must_be_zero). Objects that can be reused this way include hkls, lattice parameters, Ycalc, peak buffers, structure factors, th2_offset, transform_X, stretch_pks, gauss_fwhm, other common arrays such as (Sin(Th)/Lam)^2, and derivatives for common refined parameters.
Tadditional_prm_attributes: Tadditional_prm_attributes adds three extra per-parameter attributes used in molecular- dynamics-driven refinement: _md_k (a parameter's force-field spring constant), _mass (its effective mass in the MD integration) and _md_force (its accumulated force each MD step). See 16-molecular-dynamics.md.
Tan: Tan(x) returns the tangent of x.
Tanh: Tanh(x) returns the hyperbolic tangent of x.
Tcf_GUI_Related: Tcf_GUI_Related collects charge-flipping keywords that only affect the TA.EXE GUI's live display, with no effect on the flipping algorithm: add_to_cloud_N/add_to_cloud_when control how often electron-density points are added to the displayed 3D cloud, pick_atoms_when controls when the GUI attempts to pick atom positions from that cloud, and view_cloud toggles the cloud display.
Tcf_miscellaneous: Tcf_miscellaneous collects further charge-flipping controls not grouped elsewhere: apply_exp_scale (see its entry), correct_for_atomic_scattering_factors/correct_for_temperature_effects toggle structure-factor corrections, hkl_plane declares specific reflections for special treatment, randomize_initial_phases_by sets the random-phase spread used to start flipping (default Rand(-180,180)), scale_E/scale_F/scale_F000/scale_weak_reflections/user_threshold tune how structure-factor magnitudes and weak reflections are weighted during flipping, and verbose controls console output detail.
Tcolour_line_width_point_size: Tcolour_line_width_point_size supplies a single shared attribute, _clp (four numbers: color, line width, and point size settings), mixed into any object whose plotted curve appearance (in the GUI) needs to be customizable -- e.g. a phase's calculated curve, or a fit_obj's curve.
Tcomm_1: Tcomm_1 collects convolution-related keywords shared across many contexts: axial_conv (axial divergence, with filament_length/sample_length/receiving_slit_length and primary/secondary_soller_angle), capillary_diameter_mm (capillary absorption correction, with capillary_u_cm_inv and the convergent/divergent/parallel-beam geometry choice), circles_conv, and exp_conv_const (a general exponential convolution term with its exp_limit cutoff). These are the fundamental-parameters-style instrumental convolutions layered onto a calculated peak shape.
Tcomm_1_2_phase_1_2: Tcomm_1_2_phase_1_2 is a pure aggregator with no keywords of its own -- it bundles Tcolour_line_width_point_size, Tcomm_1, Tcomm_2, Tphase_1 and Tphase_2 together as one unit wherever it's mixed in, so a phase-level object gets all five families of keywords in one step rather than listing each type mixin individually.
Tcomm_2: Tcomm_2 collects a broad second set of commonly-mixed-in keywords: existing_prm references an already-defined parameter; lam (with la/lo/lh/lg/lo_ref) defines the radiation wavelength table; out/out_dependences/out_dependences_for control writing values to an output file (with the nested Tout_record sub-block for custom formatted lines); penalty adds a soft restraint to the objective function; prm|local defines a refinable/local parameter with its full attribute set (min/max/del/update/stop_when/val_on_continue/...); scale_phase_X and scale_pks scale individual phases or peaks.
Telectron_density_perturbations: Telectron_density_perturbations collects charge-flipping keywords for deliberately perturbing the electron-density map mid-refinement to escape local minima: flip_equation/flip_regime_2/flip_regime_3 control the flipping threshold's behavior, histogram_match_scale_fwhm (with hm_size_limit_in_fwhm/hm_covalent_fwhm) matches the density histogram to expected atomic peak shapes, and pick_atoms (with activate/choose_from/choose_to/choose_randomly/with_symmetry) targets specific candidate atom sites for perturbation.
Tf0_f1_f11_atom: Tf0_f1_f11_atom lets an individual atom's f0/f1/f11 scattering-factor values be overridden directly (f0_f1_f11_atom, with per-atom f0/f1/f11 sub-attributes) instead of using the values TOPAS would otherwise compute from the atom's element and radiation.
Tfit_obj: Tfit_obj defines a fit_obj -- a named target curve equation (optionally restricted to an [min_X, max_X] range via fit_obj_phase/fo_transform_X) that a refinement can fit against, with its plotted-curve appearance via the mixed-in Tcolour_line_width_point_size. Used e.g. for PDF fitting and other non-standard fit targets.
Tgenerate_stack_sequences: Tgenerate_stack_sequences configures generate_stack_sequences, which randomly generates layer-fault sequences for stacking-fault modeling: number_of_sequences/number_of_stacks_per_sequence set how many sequences of what length to generate; save_sequences/save_sequences_as_strs write the results out as plain text or as ready-to-use .str files; layers_tol/n_avg/num_unique_vx_vy tune the generation; match_transition_matrix_stats and transition (one per named transition) supply the layer-to-layer transition probabilities the sequences are generated to match. See 10-stacking-faults.md.
Thkl_lat: Thkl_lat collects lattice- and reflection-level controls: the cell (via the mixed-in Tlat_prms), normals_plot/normals_plot_min_d for plotting reflection normals, omit_hkls to exclude specific reflections, phase_penalties to restrain specific hkl_Re_Im values, spherical_harmonics_hkl for texture/preferred-orientation correction, and str_hkl_angle for reporting the angle to a given hkl.
TIndexing: TIndexing collects the controls for powder-pattern indexing: index_lam sets the wavelength; index_max_Nc_on_No/index_max_number_of_solutions/index_max_th2_error/index_max_zero_error bound the search; index_min_lp/index_max_lp bound the figure-of-merit; index_th2/index_d (with per-peak index_I) supply the observed peak list to index; index_x0/index_zero_error handle the pattern's zero-point offset; ndx_sg reports a found candidate cell/space-group solution; no_extinction_subgroup_search disables an optional part of the search. See 14-indexing.md.
Tlat_prms: Tlat_prms is the standard unit-cell definition shared across many object types: a, b, c (lengths) and al, be, ga (angles, each defaulting to 90 degrees).
Tmin_max_r: Tmin_max_r is a shared min_r/max_r pair defining a radial (r) range, e.g. the real-space range considered in a PDF-related calculation.
To_Prm: To_Prm(a, b, c, ...) concatenates its arguments into a parameter name and returns that parameter's value; a parameter argument is converted to its value's string form first.
To_String: To_String(a) evaluates parameter a and converts the result to a string.
Tout_record: Tout_record defines one custom-formatted line inside an out block: out_eqn supplies the value (an equation), out_fmt (and out_fmt_err for its uncertainty) supplies the C-style printf format string used to render it.
Tpdf: Tpdf collects pair-distribution-function (PDF) keywords: pdf_scale_simple/pdf_zero/pdf_ymin_on_ymax control basic PDF scaling and baseline; pdf_info reports PDF-generation diagnostics; the mixed-in Tpdf_convolute applies broadening; pdf_for_pairs (with pdf_only_eq_0/pdf_gauss_fwhm and its own Tpdf_convolute) computes a partial PDF restricted to a specific pair of site sets; pdf_partial_1/pdf_partial_2/pdf_partial_when select which partial PDF to compute and when. See 08-pdf-generation.md and 09-pdf-refinement.md.
Tpdf_convolute: Tpdf_convolute applies a broadening convolution to a PDF: pdf_convolute supplies the convolution term, min_X/max_X restrict the X-range it's applied over, and convolute_X_recal controls whether that range is recalculated each iteration.
Tpeak_stack: Tpeak_stack collects keywords for manipulating a stack of trial peaks during interactive peak-shape work: push_peak adds the current peak to the stack, bring_2nd_peak_to_top/bring_n_peak_to_top reorder it, add_pop_1st_2nd_peak combines/removes peaks, and scale_top_peak/set_top_peak_area adjust the topmost peak's scale or area.
Tphase_1: Tphase_1 collects phase-level output and scaling controls: atom_out/mag_atom_out write a phase's atom (or magnetic-moment) list to file (each with its own Tout_record for custom formatting); auto_scale toggles automatic scale-factor estimation; del_approx tunes an approximation's step size; transform_X applies an X-axis transform local to this phase; phase_name labels the phase for reporting; phase_out/phase_out_X write the phase's calculated pattern (or its X-axis) to file; brindley_spherical_r_cm applies the Brindley correction for spherical-particle microabsorption.
Tphase_2: Tphase_2 collects phase-level peak-shape controls: peak_buffer_step/peak_buffer_based_on tune the internal peak-shape lookup buffer's resolution and trigger; peak_type selects the peak-shape model (with its sub-attributes -- pv_lor/pv_fwhm for pseudo-Voigt, h1/h2/m1/m2 or spv_h1/spv_h2/spv_l1/spv_l2 for split/super pseudo-Voigt variants); numerical_area forces numerical (rather than analytical) peak-area integration.
Tphase_perturbations: Tphase_perturbations collects tangent-formula/charge-flipping phase-perturbation controls: add_to_phases_of_non_weak_reflections/add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections and cf_set_phases nudge or directly set specific reflection phases; modify_initial_phases and randomize_phases_on_new_cycle_by control how starting phases are perturbed; set_initial_phases_to loads a starting phase set from file; tangent_num_h_read/tangent_num_k_read/tangent_num_h_keep/tangent_max_triplets_per_h/tangent_min_triplets_per_h/tangent_scale_difference_by tune the tangent-formula phase-extension algorithm.
Tr_wp: Tr_wp collects the standard Rietveld figure-of-merit R-factors reported after a refinement: r_p/r_wp/r_exp/gof and their background-subtracted 'dash' counterparts r_p_dash/r_wp_dash/r_exp_dash, plus weighted_Durbin_Watson, a statistic testing for serial correlation in the fit residuals.
Trigid: Trigid defines a rigid-body group (rigid) moved and rotated as a single unit: point_for_site assigns each site's local (u) coordinates within the body, z_matrix instead builds it from internal coordinates (bond length/angle/torsion to three reference atoms), and rotate/translate apply the body's orientation and position parameters. See 13-rigid-bodies.md.
Tscr_1: Tscr_1 collects single-crystal-refinement controls: Flack refines the Flack parameter (absolute structure); dont_merge_equivalent_reflections/dont_merge_Friedel_pairs/ignore_differences_in_Friedel_pairs control how symmetry-equivalent and Friedel-pair reflections are combined; i_on_error_ratio_tolerance filters weak/unreliable reflections by their I/sigma(I) ratio; num_highest_I_values_to_keep caps how many of the strongest reflections are retained.
Tspace_group: Tspace_group supplies a single keyword, space_group, giving the structure's space-group symbol (Hermann-Mauguin or a recognized alias).
Tstr_details: Tstr_details collects structural-model-level controls: append_cartesian/append_fractional and append_bond_lengths append the refined coordinates (or bond lengths) back into the INP/CIF-style output on termination; atomic_interaction/ai_anti_bump (with ai_sites_1/ai_sites_2/ai_no_self_interation/ai_closest_N/ai_radius/ai_exclude_eq_0/ai_only_eq_0) and box_interaction define site-to-site interaction/anti-bumping restraints (see the ai_closest_N family's entry); cell_mass/cell_volume/weight_percent report the phase's mass, volume and Rietveld weight fraction, with spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent/corrected_weight_percent supporting internal-standard spike correction (see corrected_weight_percent).
Ttop: Ttop is the manual's root data-structure type -- the tree's starting point, from which every keyword in the language is reachable, either directly or via one of its top-level type mixins. Reachable from Ttop is not the same as writable at the literal top level of an INP file, though: most of Ttop's mixins -- TCharge_flipping, Tcomm_1/Tcomm_2 (convolutions, wavelength, output, penalties, parameter attributes -- shared with Txdd and every phase container too), TRefinement_control (file-scope controls like iters/num_cycles/A_matrix), TIndexing, TMinimization (least-squares engine controls), TMolecular_dynamics, TReuse_bins, Tr_wp (the reported R-factors), Txdd (one experimental pattern, the central object most everything else hangs off of) and Txdd_scr (the single-crystal counterpart of xdd) -- do contribute keywords or object declarations genuinely writable bare at the top level. But TEnergy_minimization, TMagnetism and TQuantitative are mixed in only because their outer wrapper is [str].../[xdd]... -- everything useful inside them requires first being inside a str or xdd block, not the bare top level. TOperators_functions is different again: its members (equation operators/functions like Add, Sqrt, Sum, Get, If) aren't 'defined' at any particular scope at all -- they're grammar used inside any equation, wherever that equation happens to sit (top level, str, or xdd). TMisc_keywords and TPre_processor round out Ttop's mixins as a genuine miscellany and the pre-processor's directives respectively -- the latter operate at the text-substitution stage before the kernel ever sees the file, so they can legally appear anywhere, not just the top level. Unlike most other Txx types, Ttop is never reached as a type-mixin from somewhere else -- it's the tree's starting point, not a reusable building block.
Txdd: Txdd defines an xdd -- one powder diffraction pattern to be fit -- and its direct members: the data file/range/format (xye_format/gsas_format/fullprof_format or inline {$data}), xdd_file/xdd_tag for identification, gui_reload/gui_ignore/gui_add_bkg for GUI behavior, cross_corr for cross-correlating with another pattern, d_Is/hkl_Is for Pawley/Le-Bail-style intensity extraction, and element_weight_percent/element_weight_percent_known/elemental_composition for per-pattern quantitative analysis. Most of an xdd's real content comes from the many further type-mixins included alongside these (Tcomm_1, Tcomm_2, Txdd__xdd_scr, one or more str phases, ...).
Txdd__xdd_scr: Txdd__xdd_scr collects controls shared between a normal powder xdd and a single-crystal xdd_scr: bkg supplies the Chebyshev background polynomial; convolution_step tunes convolution resolution; d_spacing_to_energy_in_eV_for_f1_f11 supports energy-dispersive f1/f11 lookup; degree_of_crystallinity (with amorphous_area/crystalline_area) reports the crystalline fraction; exclude cuts out specific X-ranges from the fit; extra_X_left/extra_X_right pad the calculated range beyond the data; the mixed-in Tfit_obj supplies fit_obj targets; neutron_data flags neutron (rather than X-ray) radiation; rebin_with_dx_of/rebin_start_x_at rebin the data onto a new step size; Rp/Rs report single-crystal R-factors.
Txdd_scr: Txdd_scr defines xdd_scr -- a single-crystal reflection-file pattern, structurally parallel to xdd but for hkl-indexed single-crystal data rather than a 2theta scan -- bundling in Tcomm_2 (common output/parameter keywords), Txdd__xdd_scr (the controls shared with powder xdd), Tmin_max_r, and one or more nested str phases.
Voigt_FWHM_GL: Voigt_FWHM_GL(gauss_FWHM, lorentzian_FWHM) returns the FWHM of the Voigt profile formed by convolving a Gaussian and Lorentzian with the given FWHMs.
Voigt_Integral_Breadth_GL: Voigt_Integral_Breadth_GL(gauss_FWHM, lorentzian_FWHM) returns the integral breadth of the Voigt profile formed by convolving a Gaussian and Lorentzian with the given FWHMs.
WPPM_L_max: WPPM_L_max defines the maximum column length (WPPM_L) considered when evaluating a WPPM Fourier-space convolution term such as WPPM_ft_conv_re/WPPM_ft_conv_im -- e.g. WPPM_L_max = D; for a term whose physical extent is set by a size parameter D.
WPPM_break_on_small: WPPM_break_on_small terminates the Fourier-transform summation used in a WPPM calculation once WPPM_ft_conv_re falls below WPPM_break_on_small times its value at WPPM_L=0 -- e.g. WPPM_break_on_small 1e-7. If not defined, no early-termination check is made and the full sum is always evaluated.
WPPM_correct_Is: WPPM_correct_Is, when defined, applies an intensity-scaling correction when a WPPM calculation (carried out in reciprocal-space s or q) is interpolated back onto the pattern's 2Th axis, so that I(s)ds = I(q)dq is preserved. The effect is typically small at low angles and becomes noticeable only at very high angles.
WPPM_ft_conv: WPPM_ft_conv describes a Fourier Transform (FT) in s space and performs a convolution on phase peaks that have been interpolated to s space, for Whole Powder Pattern Modelling (WPPM) microstructure analysis (Scardi & Leoni, 2001; Leoni et al. 2004; David et al. 2010). WPPM_ft_conv is equivalent to using the two keywords [WPPM_ft_conv_re_im WPPM_ft_conv_re].
WPPM_ft_conv_im: WPPM_ft_conv_im (paired with WPPM_ft_conv_re) supplies the imaginary part of a user-defined Fourier-space convolution term for Whole Powder Pattern Modelling (WPPM); together WPPM_ft_conv_re_im is equal to [WPPM_ft_conv_re, WPPM_ft_conv_im].
WPPM_ft_conv_re: WPPM_ft_conv_re (paired with WPPM_ft_conv_im) supplies the real part of a user-defined Fourier-space convolution term for Whole Powder Pattern Modelling (WPPM); together WPPM_ft_conv_re_im is equal to [WPPM_ft_conv_re, WPPM_ft_conv_im]. See WPPM_L_max, WPPM_th2_range, WPPM_break_on_small and WPPM_correct_Is for the surrounding WPPM controls.
WPPM_ft_conv_re_im:
WPPM_ft_conv_re_im (along with the equivalent pair WPPM_ft_conv_re/WPPM_ft_conv_im, commonly invoked via the WPPM_ft_conv macro) describes a Fourier Transform (FT) in s space and performs a convolution on phase peaks that have been interpolated to s space, for Whole Powder Pattern Modelling (WPPM) microstructure analysis (Scardi & Leoni, 2001; Leoni et al. 2004; David et al. 2010) -- for example: WPPM_ft_conv = 1 - 1.5 WPPM_L / D + 0.5 (WPPM_L / D)^3. The result is interpolated back to 2Th space; when WPPM_correct_Is is defined, this interpolation is scaled such that I(s)ds = I(q)dq, an effect that is typically small at low angles but becomes noticeable at high angles.

WPPM_L is a reserved parameter returning the transform parameter; WPPM_L_max defines its maximum value. WPPM_th2_range shortens the long tails of WPPM peaks (often written in terms of the FWHM from the Scherrer equation). WPPM_break_on_small terminates the FT calculation once WPPM_ft_conv_re falls below that fraction of its value at WPPM_L = 0; if left undefined, no such check is made. Get(ft_0) and FT_Break can both be used within WPPM_ft_conv in a manner similar to ft_conv, and when multiple WPPM_ft_conv(s) are defined, the program internally uses the convolution theorem.
WPPM_th2_range: WPPM_th2_range restricts the 2Th extent over which a WPPM peak's long tails are calculated -- WPPM peak tails otherwise extend across almost the whole diffraction pattern, so shortening this range keeps computation tractable, e.g. WPPM_th2_range = 25 .1 Rad Lam / (D Cos(Th));.
Ycalc_at: Ycalc_at(x) returns the calculated intensity (Ycalc) at x-axis position x; returns 0 if x lies outside the pattern's data range (X1..X2).
Yobs_Avg: Yobs_Avg(x1, x2) returns the average observed intensity (Yobs) between x1 and x2, each first snapped to the nearest actual x-axis data point.
Yobs_Min: Yobs_Min(x1, x2) returns the minimum observed intensity (Yobs) between x1 and x2.
Yobs_at: Yobs_at(#x) returns the observed intensity (Yobs) at x-axis position #x; usable in any equation dependent on a sub-xdd.
Yobs_dx_at: Yobs_dx_at(#x) returns the observed data's step size at x-axis position #x; usable in any equation dependent on a sub-xdd. Collapses to a single constant (the step size) when the data's x-axis is equidistant.
_clp: _clp #red #green #blue #line_width #point_size (a phase- or bkg-dependent attribute) sets a plotted curve's color and marker appearance in the GUI: the first three numbers are red/green/blue weightings between 0 and 1, and #line_width/#point_size each range 0 to 15 -- e.g. _clp 0.5 0.5 0.5 3 2 for a grey curve with line width 3 and point size 2. The bundled colours.inc defines standard color presets to use here. See test_examples\zro2.inp.
_mass: _mass !E (default 1) is a per-parameter attribute giving the mass m used by molecular_dynamics in the Verlet-derived update equation p(k+1) = (p(k) - p(k-1) + (_md_k / _mass)(dRwp(k)/dp) t^2) md_scale + p(k) (see Chapter 15, 'Molecular dynamics (MD)'). For atomic coordinate parameters, if _mass is not explicitly set it is instead looked up from the ISOTOPES.TXT file based on the site's occ species (weighted across species if the site has mixed occupancy), so atoms move according to their real atomic mass by default without having to set _mass by hand.
_md_force: _md_force !E (default 0) is a per-parameter attribute used by molecular_dynamics to apply an external force to a parameter -- typically an atomic coordinate -- during an MD simulation (see section 15.3, 'Applying a force on atoms'). The simulation maintains overall energy conservation by adjusting the system's kinetic energy to compensate for the work done by the applied force. MD-4.INP demonstrates this by applying a force along the a-axis to an Al+3 atom in AlVO4: for that particular structure and potential, a force along a preserves the structure's integrity, while an equivalent force along c causes it to lose structural integrity.
_md_k: _md_k !E (default 1) is a per-parameter attribute used by molecular_dynamics as the k factor in the Verlet-derived update equation p(k+1) = (p(k) - p(k-1) + (_md_k / _mass)(dRwp(k)/dp) t^2) md_scale + p(k) (see Chapter 15, 'Molecular dynamics (MD)'). For atomic x/y/z coordinate parameters, if _md_k is not explicitly set it defaults to a lattice-geometry correction factor (ax for x, by for y, cz for z, derived from the cell angles al/be/ga) rather than 1, so that forces are corrected for non-orthogonal lattice parameters automatically. It can be set explicitly on any parameter, e.g. x @ # _mass = 26.981; _md_k = ax;, to reproduce that default behavior manually or override it.
a: The unit cell's lattice parameters: a, b, c are the cell edge lengths (in Angstrom), and al, be, ga are the cell angles alpha, beta, gamma (in degrees). al, be, and ga each default to 90 if omitted -- written as a trailing default value directly on the attribute, e.g. [al !E90], meaning 'this can be a refinable parameter/equation (!E), defaulting to 90 if not given' -- so only a, b, c need to be supplied for an orthogonal/tetragonal/cubic-shaped cell; al/be/ga only need overriding for a monoclinic (one non-90 angle) or triclinic (all three non-90) cell. The exact same six parameters appear in more than one place with slightly different attribute types depending on context -- e.g. Thkl_lat's line uses plain E (a fixed value only, no refinement), while TCharge_flipping's line uses !E (refinable/equation-capable) -- since a str/xdd-level cell is normally refined, whereas some other contexts (like Thkl_lat's generic listing) don't need that. When refining a real structure, a/b/c/al/be/ga are ordinarily written the same way as any other refinable parameter, e.g. `a 5.4306` (fixed) or `a @ 5.4306` (refined).
a_add:
a_add E, a child of a 'to' transition within generate_stack_sequences, defines the x coordinate of the stacking vector RELATIVE to the previous stacking vector, in terms of the crystallographic a axis (b_add is the equivalent for the b axis/y coordinate). This differs from ta/tb, which define the stacking vector's x/y coordinates directly (not relative to the previous vector). For example, in test_examples\stacking_faults\fit-1.inp:

generate_stack_sequences {
  number_of_sequences Nseqs 200
  number_of_stacks_per_sequence Nv 200
  num_unique_vx_vy 6
  Transition(1, lpc)
    to 1 = pa;   a_add = 2/3;  b_add = 1/3;   n !n1 349984
    to 2 = 1-pa; a_add = 0;    b_add = 0;     n !n2 149781
  Transition(2, lpc)
    to 1 = 1-pa; a_add = 0;    b_add = 0;     n !n3 149781
    to 2 = pa;   a_add = -2/3; b_add = -1/3;  n !n4 350254
}

Here the two transitions model DIFFaX-style stacking where each layer either repeats with no lateral shift (a_add = b_add = 0) or shifts by +/-2/3 a, +/-1/3 b, with n1-n4 recording how many of each transition type were generated (from which the probability pa can be recovered as (n1+n3)/(n1+n2+n3+n4)). See also (Examples: fit-1.inp, fit-2.inp).
aberration_range_change_allowed: aberration_range_change_allowed !E describes the maximum allowed change in the x-axis extent of a convolution aberration before a new peak is calculated for the peaks buffer (see also ymin_on_ymax, which determines a peak's x-axis extent, and section 5.1). For example, for axial_conv the spacing between peaks in the peaks buffer should be small at low angles and large at high angles; aberration_range_change_allowed is what controls that spacing, as a dependent of the relevant peak-type parameters/convolutions. Smaller values reduce the spacing between peaks in the peaks buffer, increasing the number of peaks stored (more accurate, more memory/time); defaults are typically adequate and vary by parameter -- 0.05 for m1/m2, 0.01 for pv_lor/spv_l1/spv_l2, and Peak_Calculation_Step for h1/h2/pv_fwhm/spv_h1/spv_h2/hat/axial_conv/whole_hat/half_hat/one_on_x_conv/exp_conv_const/circles_conv/lor_fwhm/gauss_fwhm.
add_pop_1st_2nd_peak: add_pop_1st_2nd_peak (a peaks-buffer stack operation) adds the top entry on the peak stack to the second-most-recent entry, then pops (removes) the top entry, leaving the combined result as the new top.
add_to_phases_of_non_weak_reflections: add_to_phases_of_non_weak_reflections !E, used in protein charge flipping. The manual gives only its bare bracket syntax with no accompanying prose. By direct naming symmetry with add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections -- which, when defined, leaves weak-reflection intensities untouched (set to the values determined by the inverse Fourier transform) rather than zeroing them -- add_to_phases_of_non_weak_reflections most likely applies an analogous phase modification to the non-weak (ordinary/strong) reflections instead. This interpretation is inferred from context and naming convention, not stated directly in the manual.
add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections:
add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections !E allows for modification of the phases of "weak" reflections during charge flipping (see fraction_reflections_weak / extend_calculated_sphere_to for how reflections get flagged weak in the first place). For example, to add pi/2 (i.e. 90 degrees) to the phases of weak reflections:

add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections 90

When add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections is defined, the intensities of weak reflections are NOT set to zero; instead they are left untouched, meaning their intensities are set to whatever value the inverse Fourier transform determines. This is often ramped down over a run:

add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections = 90 Ramp(1, 0, Nr);

or randomized instead of fixed:

add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections = Rand(-180, 180);
