(the latter is required rather than a fixed 90 when symmetry_obey_0_to_1 is also in use, since a fixed 90 causes the electron-density origin to shift, which symmetry_obey_0_to_1 otherwise prevents). See also scale_weak_reflections, which instead rescales weak-reflection intensities.
adps:
adps generates the unn anisotropic atomic displacement parameters (ADPs) for a site, with considerations made for special positions (see test_examples\single-crystal\AE14-ADPS.INP). On termination of refinement, the adps keyword is replaced in the INP file with the resulting u11/u22/u33/u12/u13/u23 parameters themselves (see example ae1-adps.inp); alternatively, these unn parameters can be entered manually from the start instead of using adps to generate them. u11, u22 and u33 are the diagonal elements of the anisotropic displacement tensor -- the mean-square atomic displacements along the a*, b* and c* reciprocal-axis directions respectively; u12, u13 and u23 are the off-diagonal elements, capturing correlation between pairs of axes (i.e. anisotropy/tilt of the displacement ellipsoid away from the reciprocal axes).

Together they enter the anisotropic temperature factor as the standard exponential Debye-Waller term:

T = Exp[-2*Pi^2 (h^2 a*^2 u11 + k^2 b*^2 u22 + l^2 c*^2 u33
  + 2hk a* b* u12 + 2hl a* c* u13 + 2kl b* c* u23)]

used in the structure-factor calculation (Eq. 19-1); this generalizes the simpler isotropic beq case,

T = Exp(-beq Sin(2*Theta/Lambda)^2)

to a full 6-parameter displacement ellipsoid per site. The unn matrix can be kept positive definite (a physical requirement for a valid displacement ellipsoid) using the site-dependent macro ADPs_Keep_PD, applied after the unn parameters have been created, which can help stabilize refinement. For determining ADP constraints, the 3x3 eigenvalue-determination routine of Kopp (2006) is used.
adps_scale:
adps_scale E, used in PDF refinement, scales a site's Uij anisotropic displacement parameters (entered via u11/u22/u33/u12/u13/u23, generated the same way as in reciprocal-space refinement via adps) and can itself be a function of X, where X is the distance between atoms -- for example:

adps_scale = 2 aa (Abs(1 - delt1/X - delt2/X^2 + Qb^2 X^2))

This PDF-refinement ADP implementation follows the same approach as PDFgui (Farrow et al., 2007), in which peaks are treated as Gaussian even at low r, so ADPs correct for PDF peak width but not asymmetry -- real asymmetry does occur and becomes noticeable when the atomic displacement geometry is extreme. The FWHM of a PDF peak arising from a pair of atoms i and j is given by:

FWHMij = Sqrt(adps_scale_i * Ucart,i + adps_scale_j * Ucart,j)

where Ucart is Uij expressed in Cartesian coordinates -- so adps_scale directly controls how strongly each atom's displacement parameters broaden the PDF peaks it takes part in, and its X-dependence lets that broadening vary with interatomic distance rather than being fixed. See also the ADP_5 and ADP_7 macros for a multi-atom approach to ADPs in PDF refinement.
al: Lattice angle (default 90 degrees when part of the charge_flipping a/b/c/al/be/ga line).
amorphous_area: amorphous_area is a reported child of degree_of_crystallinity, giving the sum of the numerical areas under all phases in the xdd that ARE marked amorphous_phase. It is used together with crystalline_area to compute degree_of_crystallinity as '100 * Get(crystalline_area) / (Get(crystalline_area) + Get(amorphous_area))'. See degree_of_crystallinity for the overall calculation.
append_bond_lengths:
append_bond_lengths [consider_lattice_parameters] appends bond lengths (and the angles between them) to the *.OUT file at the end of refinement, for a site's nearest neighbours. consider_lattice_parameters includes lattice-parameter errors in the calculated bond-length/bond-angle errors. A number corresponding to the site's equivalent position (as found in the *.SG space group files in the SG directory) is appended after each site name following a ':'. Example output for a reference site Y1 with three neighbours O1, O2, O3:

Y1:0    O1:0    2.23143
        O2:0    2.23143    88.083
        O3:0    2.28045    109.799    99.928

Each row after the first adds one more neighbour: the first number in a row is always the bond length from Y1 to that row's neighbour (2.23143 A to O1, 2.23143 A to O2, 2.28045 A to O3); every number after that is the angle at Y1 between that neighbour and each of the neighbours listed in the earlier rows, in order -- so row 2's 88.083 is the O1-Y1-O2 angle, and row 3's 109.799/99.928 are the O1-Y1-O3 and O2-Y1-O3 angles respectively. In short: bond lengths are always the first number on a line, and bond angles are every number after it.
append_fractional: For the case of append_fractional, in_str_format produces output in INP format.
apply_exp_scale:
apply_exp_scale !E (default on) determines two internal coefficients a and b each charge-flipping iteration such that:

R-factor = Sum| a * Exp(b / D_spacing^2) * Fc - Fo |

is minimized, where Fc and Fo are the calculated and observed structure-factor moduli respectively. It corrects R-factors for an incorrect temperature-factor correction applied when normalizing structure factors, and typically increases the contrast between R-factors before and at convergence (most of that increase is usually realized from d-spacings less than 1 Angstrom) -- setting it to zero disables this correction. apply_exp_scale changes R-factors only, not the phases, so the direction taken by charge flipping is unaffected by it.
approximate_A: approximate_A approximates the A matrix of Eq. (4-4) without calculating the expensive A matrix dot products, using the BFGS method (Broyden 1970; Fletcher 1970; Goldfarb 1970; Shanno 1970). It is useful when calculating the A matrix dot products is expensive, and can also improve convergence when penalties dominate the refinement. approximate_A cannot be used together with line_min or use_extrapolation. When approximate_A is used, the resulting A matrix can additionally be made sparse via A_matrix_memory_allowed_in_Mbytes and/or A_matrix_elements_tollerance, which together allow refinements with very large numbers of independent parameters. approximate_A_check_for_must_be_zero further improves convergence in very large problems (thousands of xdds) by explicitly zeroing A-matrix elements that must be zero (parameters from different xdd patterns) but that the BFGS approximation may otherwise leave non-zero. Examples ae14-approx-a.inp and ae1-approx-a.inp show approximate_A achieving convergence faster than the fully calculated A matrix for single-crystal refinement.
approximate_A_check_for_must_be_zero:
approximate_A_check_for_must_be_zero #n tests A-matrix elements that must be zero (Aij where parameter pi and parameter pj come from different xdd patterns) and explicitly sets them to zero, correcting for the fact that the BFGS approximation used by approximate_A can otherwise leave such elements as small but non-zero values. This improves convergence in large problems comprising thousands of xdds, and importantly it also invokes sparse matrix methods so that only the genuinely non-zero A-matrix elements are stored, reducing memory usage -- in cases with thousands of xdds, this often removes the need to additionally define A_matrix_memory_allowed_in_Mbytes.

Because checking for zero elements has a modest computational cost, the check is only performed up to the nth refinement-cycle iteration, where #n is the value given after the keyword, e.g.:

approximate_A_check_must_be_zero = Cycle_Iter < 4;

after the nth iteration, elements that must be zero are set to whatever they were determined to be at the nth iteration. See example test_examples\XRD-CT\XRD-CT-1.inp.
atom_out: Used for writing site dependent details to file. See out for a description of out_record. The Out_CIF_STR macro uses atom_out. mag_atom_out selects magnetic sites.
auto_scale: auto_scale rewrites the scale parameter in terms of F2; this eliminates the need for the scale parameter. The value determined for auto_scale is updated at the end of refinement.
axial_conv:
axial_conv implements TOPAS's full axial divergence model, using the method of Cheary & Coelho (1998b), to correct for the axial-plane instrumental aberration common in laboratory and synchrotron diffractometers. Its children filament_length, sample_length and receiving_slit_length define the lengths of the tube filament, sample, and receiving slit in the axial plane, in mm. primary_soller_angle and secondary_soller_angle define the Soller slit angles, in degrees. axial_n_beta defines the number of rays emanating from a point X-ray source in the axial plane; larger values increase both accuracy and calculation time.

The Full_Axial_Model macro simplifies the use of axial_conv by wrapping these parameters into a single call. Internally, axial_conv is one of the response functions calculated using a mixture of analytical and straight-line-segment convolution (along with one_on_x_conv and circles_conv), and is evaluated at twice the normal Peak_Calculation_Step resolution (Step = Peak_Calculation_Step / 2) for accuracy.
axial_n_beta: axial_n_beta defines the number of rays emanating from a point X-ray source in the axial plane; larger values increase both accuracy and calculation time.
b:
b E is one of the six lattice parameters -- a, b, c (in Angstroms) and al, be, ga (lattice angles alpha, beta, gamma, in degrees) -- that define a structure's unit cell. It can be refined like any other parameter:

b @ 5.4102

fixed to a known value, or constrained via an equation -- e.g. for a tetragonal/hexagonal cell where b is tied to a:

b = a;

Convenience macros such as Cubic(), Tetragonal(), Hexagonal() and Orthorhombic() set up the appropriate a/b/c/al/be/ga constraints for common crystal systems automatically rather than needing b written out by hand.
b_add: a_add, b_add define the stacking vector's x and y coordinates relative to the previous stacking vector, in terms of the crystallographic a and b axes. tz defines the stacking vector's z coordinate along the crystallographic c axis, in Å. (Examples: fit-1.inp, fit-2.inp)
be: Lattice angle (default 90 degrees when part of the charge_flipping a/b/c/al/be/ga line).
bkg: bkg [@] # # #... defines a Chebyshev polynomial background, where the number of coefficients equals the number of numeric values given after bkg. The Chebyshev background function can sometimes misbehave during Pawley, Le Bail or deconvolution refinements, since it is only loosely constrained by the fit and can develop unphysical excursions between data features. For xdd deconvolution refinements specifically, the Deconvolution_Bkg_Penalty macro stabilizes bkg in most cases. In other cases of instability, the Bkg_at(x) function can be used inside penalty equations to directly guide the shape of bkg -- see Bkg_at for the mechanism and a worked example.
bootstrap_errors: bootstrap_errors !Ecycles invokes the bootstrap method of error determination (Efron & Tibshirani 1986; DiCiccio & Efron 1996; Chernick 1999), performing a series of refinements each with a fraction of Yobs replaced to form a new bootstrap sample; the standard deviations of the refined values across all these cycles become the bootstrap errors, written to the OUT file. !Ecycles gives the number of refinement cycles to perform (default 200). fraction_of_yobs_to_resample sets the fraction of observed data replaced each cycle (default 0.37); replacement data is, by default, drawn randomly from the Ycalc of the first refinement cycle, or from the currently completed cycle if resample_from_current_ycalc is defined -- either way, the updated Yobs is further adjusted so that the change in Rwp stays consistent with the current Ycalc. Parameter values at the start of each cycle come from the end of the first refinement cycle (modifiable via val_on_continue); if determine_values_from_samples is defined, final parameter values are instead derived from the full set of bootstrap-cycle results. Per-cycle results are streamed to disk in binary format and processed at the end without being held in memory, giving bootstrapping a small memory footprint; bootstrap_errors are generally considered more accurate than SVD/matrix-inversion errors because they respect parameter limits (e.g. that intensities cannot be negative), which matrix inversion does not.
box_interaction:
box_interaction [from_N #] [to_N #] [no_self_interaction] $site_1 $site_2 N E defines a site interaction named N between sites identified by $site_1 and $site_2. E is the interaction equation, a function of R (the distance in Angstrom between the two atoms, updated as fractional coordinates change) and Ri; N can then be used elsewhere, including in penalty equations. no_self_interaction prevents interactions between equivalent positions of the same site -- useful when a general position is used to describe what is really a special position.

from_N/to_N restrict the interaction to a distance-sorted range: when either is defined, interactions between $site_1 and $site_2 are sorted by distance and only those between the from_N and to_N ranks are kept (counting starts at zero). For example, to soft-constrain a site Si1's three nearest oxygen neighbours to 2 A:

box_interaction Si1 O* to_N 2 !si1o = (R-2)^2; penalty = !si1o;

to_N 2 reaches the third-nearest atom since counting starts at 0. The wildcard 'O*' matches every site name starting with 'O'; site names can instead be listed explicitly in double quotes, e.g.:

box_interaction Si1 \"O1 O2 O3\" to_N 3 ...

The order of $site_1 and $site_2 matters whenever from_N/to_N is used, because sorting-and-ranking is done from $site_1's own point of view: e.g. if Si1's four nearest neighbours (by equivalent position) are O1,1 at 1.0 A, O2,3 at 1.1 A, O2,1 at 1.2 A and O1,2 at 1.3 A, then:

box_interaction Si1 \"O1 O2 O3\" to_N 3

only reaches the two equivalent positions of O1 and the two of O2 -- O3 is never reached at all. Swapping the argument order:

box_interaction \"O1 O2 O3\" Si1 to_N 0

instead ranks from each oxygen's own point of view, ensuring every one of O1/O2/O3 gets an interaction with its own nearest Si1.

When from_N/to_N is used, the reserved parameter Ri gives the index of the current interaction (starting at 0), and Break can be used to terminate the implied loop early. box_interaction is used internally by, for example, the Anti_Bump macro.
break_cycle_if_true: Interrupts charge flipping to execute randomize_phases_on_new_cycle_by. Cycle_Iter is set to zero and Cycle is incremented.
brindley_spherical_r_cm: brindley_spherical_r_cm !E is a str-scoped keyword that supplies the phase's particle radius-times-packing-density value used by the Brindley microabsorption correction Bp in the weight_percent calculation (see weight_percent for how Bp is used). It's normally set via the Apply_Brindley_Spherical_R_PD(& R, & PD) macro rather than directly: 'macro Apply_Brindley_Spherical_R_PD(& R, & PD) { brindley_spherical_r_cm = R PD; }', where R is the spherical particle radius in cm and PD is the packing density. For example, two phases each correcting with their own radius/packing-density parameters: 'xdd ... str Apply_Brindley_Spherical_R_PD(R, PD) MVW(0,0,0) str Apply_Brindley_Spherical_R_PD(R, PD) MVW(0,0,0)', or with literal values: 'xo_Is Apply_Brindley_Spherical_R_PD(0.002, 0.6) MVW(654, 230, 0) phase_MAC 200'.
bring_2nd_peak_to_top: bring_2nd_peak_to_top (a peaks-buffer stack operation, alongside push_peak/bring_n_peak_to_top/add_pop_1st_2nd_peak/scale_top_peak/set_top_peak_area) brings the second entry on the peak stack to the top, swapping it with the current top entry.
bring_n_peak_to_top: bring_n_peak_to_top !E (a peaks-buffer stack operation) brings the nth entry on the peak stack to the top, where n=0 is the stack's current top entry.
c:
c E is one of the six lattice parameters -- a, b, c (in Angstroms) and al, be, ga (lattice angles alpha, beta, gamma, in degrees) -- that define a structure's unit cell. It can be refined like any other parameter:

c @ 25.1091

fixed to a known value, or constrained via an equation. In stacking-fault work (generate_stack_sequences), Get(generated_c) reports the average thickness of the generated stacking sequences and is commonly assigned to c to keep the cell consistent with the generated stacking:

c = Get(generated_c);

Convenience macros such as Cubic(), Tetragonal(), Hexagonal() and Orthorhombic() set up the appropriate a/b/c/al/be/ga constraints for common crystal systems automatically rather than needing c written out by hand.
capillary_convergent_beam:
capillary_convergent_beam selects the focusing-convergent-beam variant of the capillary convolution (Coelho & Rowles, 2017), one of three mutually exclusive beam-geometry options alongside capillary_divergent_beam and capillary_parallel_beam. It's used together with capillary_diameter_mm, capillary_u_cm_inv, capillary_focal_length_mm and capillary_xy_n. For example, using a str phase where capillary_u_cm_inv is set from the calculated linear absorption coefficient times a packing density:

prm packing_density 0.31208
capillary_diameter_mm @ 0.57313
capillary_u_cm_inv
  = Get(mixture_MAC) Get(mixture_density_g_on_cm3) packing_density;
capillary_focal_length_mm @ 197.89657
capillary_convergent_beam

If capillary_focal_length_mm is not defined, it defaults to the diffractometer radius Rs. See examples LAB6-STOE.INP and LAB6-D8.INP in test_examples\capillary.
capillary_diameter_mm: capillary_diameter_mm is the top-level keyword for TOPAS's capillary convolution (Coelho & Rowles, 2017), used to model the peak-shape effects of capillary/Debye-Scherrer geometry. Examples are lab6-stoe.inp and lab6-d8.inp, found in the test_examples\capillary directory. If using a str phase, capillary_u_cm_inv can be set to the calculated linear absorption coefficient multiplied by a packing density.
capillary_focal_length_mm:
capillary_focal_length_mm E gives the focal length (in mm) used by the focusing convergent-beam capillary convolution (see capillary_convergent_beam, Coelho & Rowles, 2017). If not defined, it defaults to the diffractometer radius Rs. For example:

prm packing_density 0.31208
capillary_diameter_mm @ 0.57313
capillary_u_cm_inv
  = Get(mixture_MAC) Get(mixture_density_g_on_cm3) packing_density;
capillary_focal_length_mm @ 197.89657
capillary_convergent_beam

See examples LAB6-STOE.INP and LAB6-D8.INP in test_examples\capillary.
capillary_u_cm_inv: capillary_u_cm_inv E, a child of capillary_diameter_mm, is the linear absorption coefficient (in 1/cm) used by the capillary convolution -- the sample's mass absorption coefficient times its density at the actual packing density of the capillary, not the fully-dense value. If using a str phase, it can be set directly from the phase's computed quantities times a packing density, e.g.: 'prm packing_density 0.31208 capillary_diameter_mm @ 0.57313 capillary_u_cm_inv = Get(mixture_MAC) Get(mixture_density_g_on_cm3) packing_density; capillary_focal_length_mm @ 197.89657 capillary_convergent_beam'. See mixture_MAC and mixture_density_g_on_cm3 for those two Get() targets. The capillary convolution (including the focusing-convergent-beam extension of Coelho & Rowles, 2017, enabled via capillary_convergent_beam/capillary_divergent_beam/capillary_parallel_beam) is demonstrated in test_examples\capillary\lab6-stoe.inp and lab6-d8.inp. If capillary_focal_length_mm is not defined, it defaults to the diffractometer's secondary radius Rs.
capillary_xy_n: capillary_xy_n #, a sibling of capillary_diameter_mm/capillary_u_cm_inv/capillary_focal_length_mm under the capillary convolution (see capillary_convergent_beam, capillary_divergent_beam, capillary_parallel_beam -- Coelho & Rowles, 2017). The manual does not describe its exact mechanics in prose beyond listing it in the keyword tree; by its name and position alongside capillary_diameter_mm, it most likely sets the number of grid points used across the capillary's circular cross-section (x,y) when numerically integrating the beam-path-length/absorption contribution for the convolution -- more points give a more accurate but slower calculation, similar in spirit to convolution_step for other convolutions. Treat this as inference rather than confirmed documented behavior. LAB6-STOE.INP uses 'capillary_xy_n 40'. See also examples LAB6-D8.INP in test_examples\capillary.
cf_hkl_file: cf_hkl_file $file defines the input hkl file for charge flipping. If space_group is also defined, cf_hkl_file is assumed to comprise merged hkls corresponding to that space group; otherwise it is assumed to be of space group type P1. See use_Fc, whose implied *.FC file name is derived from cf_hkl_file's (or cf_in_A_matrix's) file name with the extension replaced by FC.
cf_percent_ED_ge_H: cf_percent_ED_ge_H # returns the percentage of electron-density (ED) pixels greater than 1, where the maximum of the ED is normalized to the number of electrons in the heaviest atom defined via f_atom_type. Values less than 1 often signal a spurious high-density ('uranium atom') solution, where a single ED peak dominates rather than the density being spread realistically across the true atomic sites. cf_percent_ED_ge_H is displayed during charge flipping in the Fit Dialog, giving a running indication of whether the current solution is trending toward that failure mode.
cf_plot_fit: cf_plot_fit !E, used alongside cf_plot_histo in charge flipping, plots a fitted curve over the electron density pixel-intensity histogram, letting the actual distribution be compared visually against an expected/model distribution.
cf_plot_histo: cf_plot_histo !E plots a frequency distribution (histogram) of the electron density pixel intensity during charge flipping. See also cf_percent_ED_ge_H, which reports a single summary statistic derived from that same distribution.
cf_set_phases: cf_set_phases !E { #h #k #l #Re #Im } sets the phases for the family of reflections (#h, #k, #l) to the phase corresponding to #Re and #Im, when the leading !E equation is non-zero; it additionally scales the intensities of those reflections by the value !E evaluates to. This is useful when phases are already known from another source, or for fixing origin-defining phases -- for triclinic structures, up to three independent origin-defining phases are possible and can be set this way.
charge_flipping: charge_flipping declares a charge-flipping object, implementing the method of Oszlanyi & Suto (2004) as adapted by Coelho (2007), optionally combined with the tangent formula (Hauptman & Karle, 1956) applied iteratively during flipping. It takes its own cell (a/b/c/al/be/ga) and the rest of the TCharge_flipping keyword family (cf_hkl_file, cf_in_A_matrix, f_atom_type/f_atom_quantity, find_origin, ...). At the end of a run, a file with the same name as cf_hkl_file but a .FC extension is written out. See 22-charge-flipping.md.
chi2_convergence_criteria:
chi2_convergence_criteria sets the tolerance used to decide when refinement has converged: convergence is reached when the change in chi2 is less than chi2_convergence_criteria for three consecutive refinement iterations, together with the satisfaction of any stop_when parameter attributes. It can be an equation, for example:

chi2_convergence_criteria = If(Cycle_Iter < 10, 0.001, 0.01);

to relax the tolerance once a cycle has run for a while.

It is particularly relevant to simulated annealing and structure solution in real space, where continue_after_convergence repeatedly restarts refinement once this criterion (and stop_when) is met, so a looser chi2_convergence_criteria directly increases the rate at which new refinement cycles are attempted. Along with quick_refine and yobs_to_xo_posn_yobs, it is one of the keywords that most directly trades off computational speed for a more careful convergence, and its appropriate choice can change structure-solution speed by a factor of 20 or more.
choose_from: choose_from !E, a child of pick_atoms, limits the range of picked atoms operated on, given that picked atoms are sorted in decreasing intensity order -- together with choose_to it selects a contiguous slice of that sorted list (e.g. 'choose_from 4 choose_to 20' skips operating on the first three atoms and stops after the 20th). See pick_atoms for the overall mechanism.
choose_randomly: choose_randomly !E, a child of pick_atoms, further reduces the set of atoms operated on after choose_from/choose_to have already been applied, by randomly selecting from what remains. See pick_atoms for the overall mechanism.
choose_to: choose_to !E, a child of pick_atoms, is the upper bound (in decreasing-intensity rank) of which picked atoms are operated on -- used together with choose_from to select a range, e.g. 'pick_atoms * choose_to 5' operates on just the 5 highest-intensity picked atoms. See pick_atoms for the overall mechanism.
circles_conv: circles_conv E defines εm in the convolution function (1 − εm/√ε), for ε = 0 to εm, that is convoluted into phase peaks. εm can be greater than or less than zero. circles_conv is used, for example, by the Simple_Axial_Model macro, which uses it as the generic convolution underlying the 'simple' axial divergence model (see Table 19-1 for the other instrument convolutions built the same way); the full axial divergence model of Cheary & Coelho (1998a, 1998b) is available separately via axial_conv/Full_Axial_Model.
co: The site dependent keyword co reports on the Coulomb potential at a site. The sum of all co values equates to the Madelung constant.
conserve_memory: Deletes temporary arrays used in intermediate calculations as often as possible; memory savings of up to 70% can be expected on some problems with subsequent lengthening of execution times by up to 40%. When approximate_A is used on dense matrices then conserve_memory can reduce memory usage by up to 90%.
continue_after_convergence:
continue_after_convergence restarts refinement immediately after convergence, rather than stopping, and is the mechanism used to implement simulated annealing (Coelho, 2000) -- it is not specific to structure solution, but is used there heavily (see onlypena.inp and rosenbrock-10.inp). Before each restart, val_on_continue equations for independent parameters are evaluated, followed by any randomize_on_errors processes and any rand_xyz processes; a parameter with val_on_continue defined is not additionally randomized by randomize_on_errors.

Combined with a defined temperature regime, this produces a full simulated-annealing scheme; the Auto_T macro bundles continue_after_convergence with quick_refine, randomize_on_errors and a temperature regime into a single, broadly-applicable setup (see cime-z-auto.inp). Whether values saved at the very end of refinement are the last iteration's or the best encountered also depends on whether save_best_chi2 is defined alongside continue_after_convergence -- see save_best_chi2.
convolution_step: convolution_step defines an integer corresponding to the number of calculated data points per measurement data point used to calculate the peaks in the peaks buffer, see x_calculation_step. Increasing the value for convolution_step improves accuracy for data with large step sizes or for peaks that have less than 7 data points across the FWHM.
correct_for_atomic_scattering_factors: Structure factors are normalized when correct_for_atomic_scattering_factors is non-zero and when f_atom_type’s are defined. Structure factors are normalized by default.
correct_for_temperature_effects: Attempts to remove isotropic temperature effects from the structure factors. correct_for_temperature_effects is ON by default, setting it to zero will prevent this correction. Normalized structure factors are realized when correct_for_temperature_effects is ON and the unit cell contents are defined using f_atom_type and f_atom_quantity.
corrected_weight_percent:
corrected_weight_percent is the spike-corrected counterpart of weight_percent for a phase whose spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent has been defined (see Chapter 11, 'Quantitative Analysis'). Internally it is computed as:

q = spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent / spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent_wt;
corrected_weight_percent = q * Get(weight_percent)

i.e. the raw Rietveld weight_percent scaled by the ratio of the KNOWN (true) spike amount to the spike's own Rietveld-determined weight percent, removing the distortion the spike introduces into every other phase's apparent weight fraction. weight_percent_amorphous is then 100*(1 - q). elemental_composition's 'Corrected' column reports elemental weight percents built from corrected_weight_percent rather than the raw 'Rietveld' column.
create_pks_name: create_pks_name is a xo_Is dependent keyword that creates a peak at each step x-axis step, with peak intensity parameter names prefixed by $a_name. Peaks are not created if they already exist for the xo_Is phase.
cross_corr: cross_corr calculates the cross-correlation function for a triangle of x-axis width cross_corr_s. cross_corr_s can be an equation that can be a function of Cycle_Iter which allows for changing the width of the triangle in situ. (Examples: cross-corr\cross.inp, CROSS.INP)
cross_corr_s: cross_corr_s !E (a cross_corr dependent) sets the x-axis width of the triangular window cross_corr uses when calculating its cross-correlation function; it can be an equation depending on Cycle_Iter, allowing the triangle's width to change in situ over the course of a refinement.
crystalline_area: crystalline_area is a reported child of degree_of_crystallinity, giving the sum of the numerical areas under all phases in the xdd that are NOT marked amorphous_phase. It is used together with amorphous_area to compute degree_of_crystallinity as '100 * Get(crystalline_area) / (Get(crystalline_area) + Get(amorphous_area))'. See degree_of_crystallinity for the overall calculation.
current_peak: Get(current_peak) is a reserved FUNCTION, not a keyword -- it is only ever used as a function call inside an equation, never declared or assigned to directly. Valid inside a modify_peak_eqn equation, it returns the current (not-yet-modified) intensity of the emission-profile peak at the point being calculated, letting that equation build the actual modified peak shape by combining this value with a correction factor. For example, `modify_peak_eqn = Get(current_peak) / Get(current_peak_x);` (test_examples\wppm\gamma.inp) divides the current peak height by its own position, and test_examples\dispersion\disp.inp multiplies Get(current_peak) by a conditional dispersion-correction factor built from Get(current_peak_x).
current_peak_max_x:
current_peak_max_x !E, a sibling of current_peak_min_x and modify_peak_eqn under modify_peak, sets the upper x-axis bound (in wavelength, when no_th_dependence is not defined, or in the x-axis unit otherwise -- see Get(current_peak_x)) over which the modify_peak mechanism is applied to a peak. modify_peak lets you rewrite a phase's peak profile, either before or after convolutions, using the internal objects Get(current_peak_x) (the x-axis/wavelength point currently being processed) and Get(current_peak) (the calculated peak intensity at that point) inside a modify_peak_eqn equation.

A real usage, from the Absorption_Edge_Correction macro in topas.inc (used by the AL2O3-PAM.INP and SPINEL-PAM.INP examples to model an absorption edge in the emission profile):

current_peak_max_x = max_lam;
modify_peak_eqn =
  (Get(current_peak) + a_white Exp(-b_white (Get(current_peak_x) - edge)^2) / Tan(Th))
  (edge_extra + 0.5 (1 + Erf_Approx(a_erf (Get(current_peak_x) - edge))));

Here current_peak_max_x caps how far in wavelength the absorption-edge correction is evaluated (max_lam), analogous to how min_X/max_X bound other user-defined equations (e.g. user_defined_convolution) elsewhere in TOPAS.
current_peak_min_x: current_peak_min_x !E is the lower-bound counterpart to current_peak_max_x -- both are siblings of modify_peak_eqn under modify_peak, and set the x-axis range (in wavelength, when no_th_dependence is not defined, or in the x-axis unit otherwise) over which the modify_peak mechanism is applied to a peak; see current_peak_max_x for the full modify_peak mechanism, the AL2O3-PAM.INP/SPINEL-PAM.INP absorption-edge example, and Get(current_peak_x)/Get(current_peak). Note: the manual's Absorption_Edge_Correction macro (topas.inc), the primary real-world use of this mechanism, only sets current_peak_max_x (to max_lam) and leaves current_peak_min_x undefined -- when omitted, modify_peak appears to apply from the natural start of the peak's x-axis extent rather than requiring an explicit lower bound.
current_peak_x: Get(current_peak_x) is a reserved FUNCTION, not a keyword -- it is only ever used as a function call inside an equation, never declared or assigned to directly. Valid inside a modify_peak_eqn equation, it returns the x-axis position of the point currently being calculated within that peak -- specifically the wavelength of that point when no_th_dependence is not defined, or the plain x-axis value when no_th_dependence is defined. Used alongside Get(current_peak) to build a modified emission-profile peak shape, e.g. as a dispersion or absorption-edge correction that depends on position within the peak -- see test_examples\absorption-edge\ and test_examples\dispersion\disp.inp.
d: Defines a phase type that uses d-spacing values for generating peak positions. d corresponds to the peak position in d-space in Å and I is the intensity parameter before applying any scale_pks equations.
d_Is: Declares a phase type that generates peaks from user-supplied d-spacing values rather than from a crystal structure or hkls -- each member is a `[d E I E]...` pair: d is the peak position in d-spacing (Angstrom) and I is the intensity parameter, both before any scale_pks equation is applied. TOPAS converts each d-spacing to the pattern's x-axis position internally (via the wavelength/geometry already in scope), so unlike xo_Is (positions given directly in x-axis units) this is the right choice when the peak list is naturally in d-spacing, e.g. from an external indexing/peak-search tool. Also mixes in Tcomm_1_2_phase_1_2 (so it can carry its own peak-shape/background/phase-level settings like any other phase type) and supports lebail for a Le-Bail-style intensity extraction rather than fixed intensities.
d_spacing_to_energy_in_eV_for_f1_f11: Used for refining on energy dispersive data (see example ed_si_str.inp). Can be a function of the reserved parameter D_spacing. f' and f" (see section 19.12) values used corresponds to energies given by d_spacing_to_energy_in_eV_for_f1_f11. For example: (Examples: ed_si_str.inp)
default_I_attributes:
default_I_attributes E changes the attributes of the reserved intensity parameter I -- the auto-generated refined intensity that TOPAS creates internally for each reflection/peak (named e.g. xo_Is... I) -- rather than leaving it at its normal default attributes. For example:

xo_Is... default_I_attributes 0 min 0.001 val_on_continue 1

sets a starting value of 0, a minimum of 0.001, and re-randomizes to 1 each time continue_after_convergence restarts the refinement. This is useful when randomizing lattice parameters during Le Bail refinements with continue_after_convergence, since each restart needs the I parameters to be re-seeded rather than staying frozen at their previous converged values.
degree_of_crystallinity: degree_of_crystallinity # reports on the degree of crystallinity of an xdd pattern, calculated as '100 * Get(crystalline_area) / (Get(crystalline_area) + Get(amorphous_area))'. crystalline_area and amorphous_area are its two children: crystalline_area is the sum of the numerical areas under phases NOT marked amorphous_phase, and amorphous_area is the sum of the numerical areas under phases that ARE marked amorphous_phase. A phase is treated as amorphous in this calculation purely by having amorphous_phase defined on it -- degree_of_crystallinity does not distinguish amorphous from crystalline phases by any other means. degree_of_crystallinity is therefore only meaningful when the xdd contains a mix of phases, some flagged amorphous_phase and some not.
del_approx: del_approx # (a phase dependent) groups nearby peaks in the peaks buffer while summing them into Ycalc: peaks whose 2Th positions all fall within (-del_approx * Peak_Calculation_Step) to (del_approx * Peak_Calculation_Step) of each other are grouped, and only the group's smallest- and largest-2Th peaks are kept, the rest merged in. This trades a small amount of accuracy for significantly faster computation; a value between 1 and 3 (depending on Peak_Calculation_Step) is typically acceptable.
determine_values_from_samples:
determine_values_from_samples, used with bootstrap_errors, causes the final parameter values at the end of bootstrapping to be updated using values determined from the individual bootstrap-cycle refinements, rather than keeping the parameter values obtained from the very first (non-resampled) refinement cycle. Each bootstrap cycle's parameter values are written to disk in binary format as the cycles complete; determine_values_from_samples causes these stored per-cycle values to be read back and processed (without ever holding the full set in memory at once) to derive the final reported values, in addition to the usual bootstrap standard-deviation errors.

Without determine_values_from_samples defined, only the standard deviations of the bootstrap cycles are used (as the errors), while the reported parameter values themselves still come from the initial, non-resampled refinement. This is useful when the distribution of bootstrap-sample values is expected to give a better central estimate than a single refinement against the original (un-resampled) data.
displace: displace !E, a child of pick_atoms, displaces picked atom positions by the given amount in Angstrom; it is evaluated before insert. For example, 'displace = Rand(0.4, 0.6); insert 1' randomly displaces picked atoms by 0.4-0.6 Angstrom before inserting them back. See pick_atoms for the overall mechanism.
do_errors:
do_errors instructs the program to calculate estimated standard deviations (errors) for refined independent parameters at the end of refinement, using the correlation matrix -- created and appended to the OUT file, or updated if it was already defined via C_matrix_normalized. With plain do_errors, neither penalties nor restraints are included in the A matrix used for this error calculation, even if they were present during refinement.

Errors are determined by default using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), which closely resembles the boot strap method; use_LU_for_errors can force LU-decomposition instead, though LU-decomposition gives very large errors for intensities that are 100% correlated. See do_errors_include_restraints and do_errors_include_penalties for the variants that do fold restraints or penalties into this error calculation, and bootstrap_errors for an alternative, potentially more accurate error-determination method that respects parameter limits (e.g. that intensities are positive). Example refinements comparing the three error-determination approaches are y2o3a-lu.inp, y2o3a-svd.inp and y2o3a-boot.inp in test_examples\svd-errors.
do_errors_include_penalties: do_errors_include_penalties calculates estimated standard deviations for refined independent parameters at the end of refinement, including the penalty contribution (the AP off-diagonal terms, which are otherwise always set to zero, of Eq. (4-4)) in the A matrix used for that calculation. This differs from plain do_errors, which excludes both penalties and restraints from the error-calculation A matrix. It is relevant whenever penalties represent real constraining information about the parameters (rather than being purely a numerical device) that should be reflected in the reported parameter uncertainties, analogous to the same reasoning behind do_errors_include_restraints. Note that a penalty's off-diagonal A-matrix terms are approximated as zero during ordinary refinement regardless of this keyword -- do_errors_include_penalties only affects the separate end-of-refinement error calculation, not the refinement.
do_errors_include_restraints:
do_errors_include_restraints calculates estimated standard deviations for refined independent parameters at the end of refinement, including the restraint contribution (the AR off-diagonal terms of Eq. (4-4)) in the A matrix used for that calculation. This differs from plain do_errors, which excludes both restraints and penalties from the error-calculation A matrix entirely. Including restraints in the error calculation is appropriate when the restraints represent genuine additional information about the parameters (such as expected bond lengths) that should legitimately narrow the reported uncertainty, in the same way real observed data would.

It is used, for example, in reproducing ShelX-style restrained refinement behaviour, where:

restraint = Sqrt(w) (yt - y);

is combined with penalties_weighting_K1 set from the ratio of Rwp to Rexp squared. See do_errors_include_penalties for the equivalent option that folds in penalties instead.
dont_merge_Friedel_pairs: For single-crystal data (xdd_scr), prevents merging of Friedel pairs (hkl and -h-k-l) -- normally merged together like other symmetry-equivalent reflections, but kept separate when this is used, which matters when anomalous dispersion makes the two members of a Friedel pair genuinely different in intensity (see also ignore_differences_in_Friedel_pairs).
dont_merge_equivalent_reflections: For single-crystal data (xdd_scr), prevents merging of equivalent reflections -- normally, reflections related by symmetry are merged together into a single averaged intensity before refinement; this keyword keeps them as separate, individual observations instead. See also section 19.9.3.
dont_save_extrapolated_pks: The process of adding peaks to a calculated profile from the peaks buffer can be computationally intensive. This process occurs many times during a refinement iteration when, for example, calculating the derivatives of a site fractional atomic coordinate. An in-between step is therefore performed where interpolated peak data is stored. The memory requirements for the interpolated data can be large and in cases where memory is an issue then the keyword dont_save_extrapolated_pks can be used.
dummy: dummy $word reads a single word from the input stream and ignores it -- a way of consuming placeholder/dummy text so the Kernel skips over it without needing it to be valid syntax of any other kind (see section 2.14, 'dummy and dummy_prm keywords').
dummy_prm: dummy_prm E is similar to dummy but reads parameter-dependent text -- an entire parameter-like block (name, value, min/max, equation, etc.) -- and ignores it, letting a load block skip over parameter declarations it doesn't need to load (see section 2.14, 'dummy and dummy_prm keywords'). For example: load xo dummy_prm I { 10 = 1/Max(0.00023, 0.0001); min 10 max = Val 2; @ 100 ... } loads xo but discards the parameter text that follows dummy_prm I.
element_weight_percent:
element_weight_percent $atom $Name #, an xdd-dependent keyword, tracks the weight percent of one named element ($atom, e.g. Zr+4) summed across all str's of that xdd as a named quantity ($Name), which can then be referenced elsewhere in equations, restraints, or penalties. For example:

element_weight_percent Zr+4 zr 0

creates a tracked quantity named zr for the weight percent of Zr+4; after refinement this updates to the actual computed value (e.g. 65.027), and can be restrained directly to a known value -- such as one obtained from XRF results:

restraint = (zr - 65);

with the restraint's effective strength controlled by penalties_weighting_K1. This is distinct from element_weight_percent_known, which instead supplies a fixed, externally-known elemental weight percent used purely to enrich elemental_composition's reporting (splitting out an 'Other'/amorphous column) rather than creating a restrainable tracked quantity. A phase's overall weight_percent (rather than one element's contribution to it) can similarly be named and restrained via MVW's third argument:

MVW(0,0, !Cubic_Zirconia_wt_percent 0)
restraint = (Cubic_Zirconia_wt_percent - 36);

See elemental_composition for the related keyword that reports on every element's weight percent across all phases at once, rather than tracking one specific named element as a standalone restrainable quantity.
element_weight_percent_known:
element_weight_percent_known $atom # supplies an independently-known elemental weight percent for the whole sample -- typically from XRF (X-ray fluorescence) analysis -- for example 'element_weight_percent_known Zr 63' and 'element_weight_percent_known O 24'. Unlike element_weight_percent, which tracks an element's weight percent as a refinable/restrainable quantity for named str's, element_weight_percent_known is not refined -- it is a fixed input value used purely to enrich the reporting of elemental_composition. When one or more element_weight_percent_known keywords are defined (together with spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent for the spiking correction), elemental_composition gains an extra 'Other' column, reporting -- per element -- the difference between the known (XRF) value and the value attributable to the refined crystalline phases, i.e. the elemental content apparently residing in the amorphous/undefined portion of the sample.

A negative value in the 'Other' column for a given element (e.g. O) reflects that the known/measured value for that element is lower than what the Rietveld refinement accounts for; it is not an error condition. See test_examples\quant\quant-1.inp for a worked example combining element_weight_percent_known with a dummy_str used to describe the amorphous phase's composition.
elemental_composition:
elemental_composition is an xdd-dependent keyword that reports on the elemental composition of atoms within all the structures of that xdd, appending a table to the OUT file on refinement termination listing each element found and its weight percent with error, e.g.:

elemental_composition { Rietveld  AL 0.875`_0.021  O 26.135`_0.009  SI 0.090`_0.003 Y 6.289`_0.012  ZR 66.612`_0.029 }

If spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent is defined (an internal-standard/spiking quant correction), elemental_composition instead reports three columns -- 'Rietveld' (the raw Rietveld-determined values for the spiked phase), 'Corrected' (spike-corrected values) and 'Original' (values for the original, un-spiked sample) -- each of which sums to 100%. If element_weight_percent_known keywords are additionally defined (known elemental contents, e.g. from XRF results), a fourth 'Other' column is added reporting the elemental content attributable to whatever amorphous/undefined phase content remains: the last row of the 'Corrected' column gives Get(weight_percent_amorphous), and the last row of 'Other' is the portion of that amorphous content not accounted for by any known element.

A dummy_str phase (void of MVW, so it takes no part in the ordinary quantitative-analysis scale calculation) can be used to describe this amorphous content with a real chemistry and lattice parameters -- combined with Known_Weight_Percent to fix its weight percent -- which then correctly folds its composition into the 'Rietveld'/'Corrected'/'Original' columns (and, via the Brindley correction, into Mixture_LAC_1_on_cm and phase_LAC) instead of leaving it in a separate 'Other' column. The related, also xdd-dependent element_weight_percent (distinct from element_weight_percent_known) reports the weight percent of one named element across all str's of the xdd as its own tracked quantity, e.g.:

element_weight_percent Zr+4 zr 0

which can then be restrained directly to a known value (such as an XRF measurement):

restraint = (zr - 65);

with the restraint's strength controlled via penalties_weighting_K1. A phase's weight_percent can similarly be restrained by naming it via MVW's third argument:

MVW(0,0, !Cubic_Zirconia_wt_percent 0)
restraint = (Cubic_Zirconia_wt_percent - 36);

See test_examples\quant\quant-1.inp through quant-7.inp for worked examples covering element_weight_percent_known, Known_Weight_Percent, Get_Element_Weight elemental constraints, and dummy_str-based amorphous-phase descriptions (including one linked to an hkl_Is phase and one linked to a fit_obj).
exclude: Excludes an x-axis region between #x1 and #x2. The macro Exclude simplifies usage; see example ceo2.inp.
exp_conv_const: exp_conv_const (εm) defines a response function that is convoluted into phase peaks, following the aberration function A = Exp(Ln(0.001) × ε / εm), for ε = 0 to exp_limit. It is used by the Absorption and Absorption_With_Sample_Thickness_mm macros. The valid range of ε for A is (0 < ε < exp_limit) for εm < 0, or (exp_limit < ε < 0) for εm > 0, where A(exp_limit) = 0.001; exp_limit can also be set directly via the exp_limit keyword.
extend_calculated_sphere_to: Used to sharpen electron density clouds by filling in missing reflections; added reflections are given the status of “weak”. extend_calculated_sphere_to can be used in conjunction with scale_weak_reflections and add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections to modify “weak” reflection magnitudes and phases respectively (see section 23.2.6); here’s an example: (Examples: fourier-map-cime.inp)
extra_X_left: Determines the extra x-axis range for hkl generation (both default to 0.5). For TOF data extra_X_left is typically used; for x-ray data extra_X_right is typically used.
extra_X_right: Determines the extra x-axis range for hkl generation (both default to 0.5). For TOF data extra_X_left is typically used; for x-ray data extra_X_right is typically used.

f_atom_type: f_atom_type $type f_atom_quantity !E, used in pairs (e.g. 'load f_atom_type f_atom_quantity { Ca 2 O 10 C 12 }'), defines the atom types present and their quantity within the unit cell for charge flipping. It is used by the tangent formula in determining Eh values, by correct_for_atomic_scattering_factors / correct_for_temperature_effects to normalize structure factors (normalization happens when correct_for_atomic_scattering_factors is non-zero and f_atom_type's are defined -- see also the Oszlanyi & Suto (2005/2006) algorithm), and by the OpenGL display and pick_atoms when picking atoms, where the picking routine locates atom types based on picked-atom intensities weighted by each type's scattering power.
