fft_max_order: fft_max_order # (default 22, a Tglobal keyword) caps the maximum FFT order TOPAS will use internally, bounding the largest FFT size considered during calculations that rely on Fourier transforms.
filament_length: filament_length, sample_length and receiving_slit_length define the lengths of the tube-filament, sample and receiving slit in the axial plane in mm. primary_soller_angle and secondary_soller_angle define Soller slit angles in degrees.
file_name_for_best_solutions: Appends INP file details to $file during refinement with independent parameter values updated. The operation is performed when convergence results in the best Rwp.
find_origin: If defined and non-zero, then origin finding is turned ON. symmetry_obey_0_to_1 defines find_origin by default. symmetry_obey_0_to_1 can be used without find_origin by defining and setting find_origin to zero.
fit_obj: fit_obj E defines a user-defined function that is added to Ycalc, and can be a function of X (see example pvs.inp). min_X and max_X define the x-axis range over which the fit_obj is calculated; if min_X is omitted the fit_obj is calculated from the start of the x-axis, and if max_X is omitted it is calculated to the end of the x-axis. fo_transform_X is a dependent of fit_obj used to transform X as used within the fit_obj equation. By default, in the GUI, phases are plotted on top of background, where background comprises all fit_obj's plus bkg; fit_obj_phase (defaulting to 1) and the xdd-dependent gui_add_bkg control this plotting behaviour -- see fit_obj_phase.
fit_obj_phase: fit_obj_phase !E controls, for GUI plotting purposes only, whether a given fit_obj is treated as part of the background that phases are plotted on top of; it defaults to 1. When the xdd-dependent gui_add_bkg is also 1 (its default), the plotted background comprises 'bkg + (any fit_obj's that have fit_obj_phase = 1)'; setting gui_add_bkg to 0 stops phases being plotted above background at all, regardless of fit_obj_phase. fit_obj_phase is useful for the opposite case too -- treating a fit_obj as if it were a phase, rather than as background, for display purposes. Example quant\quant-7.inp demonstrates this: a fit_obj that is a function of a user_y object and is meant to represent a phase is plotted on top of background using a dummy_str, where the dummy_str checks the fit_obj's fit_obj_phase status to decide how to render it.
flip_regime_2:
flip_regime_2 E; is one of the two built-in charge-flipping perturbation regimes (the other is flip_regime_3; a third option is the fully user-written flip_equation -- only one of the three can be active at a time). The electron density is first modified by the standard flip rule (negate density below the threshold, see flip_equation for that default equation), and then further modified using (rho = electron density, rho_max = the maximum density):

rho = rho - Get(flip_regime_2) * rho^3 / rho_max^2

(reconstructed from the manual's typeset equation -- treat the exact exponents as approximate, but the cubic-damping shape is correct). This pulls high-density peaks down more strongly than low ones, damping runaway single-atom ("uranium atom") solutions. flip_regime_2 is typically ramped from 1 to 0 over the course of a run, e.g.:

flip_regime_2 = Ramp(1, 0, Nr);

alongside the other CF perturbation ramps. If flip_regime_2 still produces uranium-atom solutions, flip_regime_3 is recommended instead.
flip_regime_3:
flip_regime_3 E; is the second of the two built-in charge-flipping perturbation regimes (the other is flip_regime_2; a third option is the fully user-written flip_equation -- only one of the three can be active at a time). The electron density is first modified by the standard flip rule (see flip_equation for that default equation), and then further modified using (rho = electron density, rho_max = the maximum density, delta = the flip threshold):

rho stays rho, for rho < delta
rho becomes Min(rho, rho_max * Get(flip_regime_3)), for rho >= delta

(reconstructed from the manual's typeset equation -- treat the exact form as approximate, but the cap-above-threshold shape is correct). A value of 0.5 for flip_regime_3 introduces little perturbation whilst reducing the occurrence of uranium-atom solutions; it is recommended in cases where flip_regime_2 still produces uranium-atom solutions. An additional perturbation may be necessary alongside it, such as:

add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections = 90;
fo_transform_X: fo_transform_X !E (a fit_obj dependent) transforms the X value used when evaluating its parent fit_obj's equation -- letting a fit_obj be expressed in terms of a transformed x-axis rather than the pattern's native X directly.
for: for $object_type { ... } (e.g. for strs { ... }) is a pre-processor loop that expands its body once for every existing instance of the given object type. Use of $ inside the loop controls whether a macro-generated parameter is SHARED across all iterations or given a UNIQUE value per iteration: an @-based auto-name (e.g. CS_L(@, 100)) produces one shared parameter reused by every str in the loop, while a $-based auto-name (e.g. CS_L($cs, 100)) produces a distinct, uniquely-named parameter per str. The $-named form's drawback is that only one of the resulting unique values is written to the OUT file at the end of refinement -- the rest are lost -- which load_save_locals can remedy.
force_positive_fwhm:
force_positive_fwhm forces every lor_fwhm and gauss_fwhm value in the refinement to stay positive, by wrapping their equations in Abs(...) internally. The following two INP snippets are equivalent:

force_positive_fwhm
xdd ...
str ...
lor_fwhm = Rand(-1,1);

xdd ...
str ...
lor_fwhm = Abs(Rand(-1,1));

(the manual's second snippet prints as 'Abs(Rand(-1.1,))', which is almost certainly a typo/OCR artifact for 'Abs(Rand(-1,1))' -- the point of the example is that force_positive_fwhm at the top of the file saves having to wrap every individual FWHM equation in Abs() by hand). This is useful when randomizing FWHM starting values (e.g. across multiple phases or a Create_XDDs loop), since a plain Rand(-1,1) can otherwise produce a negative FWHM that TOPAS would then need to recover from during refinement.
fraction_of_yobs_to_resample:
fraction_of_yobs_to_resample sets the fraction of the observed data (Yobs) that is replaced with a new bootstrap sample during each refinement cycle of bootstrap_errors; it defaults to 0.37. By default the replacement values are drawn randomly from the Ycalc determined during the first refinement cycle of the bootstrapping process, unless resample_from_current_ycalc is defined, in which case replacement values instead come from the currently completed cycle's Ycalc.

In both cases, the updated (resampled) Yobs data is further adjusted so that the resulting change in Rwp remains consistent with the current Ycalc, rather than introducing an artificial Rwp shift purely from resampling. This keyword only has meaning in the context of bootstrap_errors -- see that keyword for the overall bootstrap procedure and the meaning of the resulting errors.
fraction_reflections_weak: Defines the fraction of observed reflections to flag as “weak”. When scale_weak_reflections, add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections and extend_calculated_sphere_to are all not defined then intensities of weak reflections are set to zero effectively removing them from the charge flipping process. Otherwise, intensities of weak reflections are not set to zero; instead, they are left untouched prior to scale_weak_reflections and add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections and space group family averaging.
ft_conv: ft_conv defines a Fourier Transform (FT) of a response function that is convoluted into phase peaks using a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) -- for example, to convolute a Voigt into a phase: ft_conv = Exp(-(Pi FT_K gfwhm)^2 / (4 Ln(2)) - Pi FT_K lfwhm). ft_conv is equivalent to using the two keywords [ft_conv_re_im ft_conv_re] (see ft_conv_re_im for the FT_K/ft_x_axis_range/ft_min mechanics they share). More than one transform can be defined at either the xdd or phase level; when defined at the xdd level, the convolution applies to all phases of that xdd. Get(ft_0) returns FT(k=0) for use within the transform equation, and If(,,) constructs can be used within it for further control, e.g. to terminate the calculation early via FT_Break.
ft_conv_re_im:
ft_conv_re_im (also written as the equivalent pair ft_conv_re/ft_conv_im, and commonly invoked via the ft_conv macro) defines a Fourier Transform (FT) of a response function that is convoluted into phase peaks using a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) -- for example, to convolute a Voigt into a phase. FT_K is a reserved parameter that returns the transform k divided by the peak's x-axis range. ft_x_axis_range is a mandatory equation defining that range, set such that the transform decays to near zero (a Lorentzian needs a large ft_x_axis_range for accurate tails, since peak tails are otherwise incorrect). ft_min (default 1e-8) is the smallest value the transform is calculated to before being set to zero for larger k.

Multiple transforms can be defined at either the xdd or phase level; when defined at the xdd level, the convolution applies to all phases of that xdd. (Examples: ft\alvo4a.inp, ft\voigt.inp)
g: The site dependent keyword g reports the difference in value between the sum of all grs_interactions with the site included, and the site excluded. In other words, it reports the site’s contribution to all grs_interactions.
ga: Lattice angle (default 90 degrees when part of the charge_flipping a/b/c/al/be/ga line).
gauss_fwhm: Defines the FWHM of a Gaussian function convoluted into phase peaks; see CS_G and Strain_G macros.
generate_name_append:
The supercell approach to stacking faults has been implemented. layer identifies a site as belonging to a layer called $layer; stack applies a stacking vector {sx, sy, sz} to the named layer. Structure factors are generated in the usual manner, with a shift applied corresponding to the stacking vector. stack operates in any space group. Sites that do not belong to a layer are treated as un-stacked, and their structure factors are generated in the usual manner. generate_these generates the sites found in $sites for the stack, with coordinates reflecting the original $sites positions plus the stacking vector. generate_name_append appends $append_to_site_name to the generated site.

The generated sites have occupancies set to zero, which signals a dummy site. Dummy sites do not take part in structure factor calculations, so speed is not affected. The dummy sites allow for graphical display of the layers, i.e.
generate_stack_sequences: generate_stack_sequences { ... } generates random sequences of stacked layers from the transition probabilities described by the enclosed transition keywords (Coelho et al., 2016), enabling stacking-fault analysis at practical speeds. Keywords inside the braces (number_of_sequences, save_sequences, layers_tol, n_avg, ...) are local to this block and cannot be used outside it; after generation, Get(generated_c) reports the generated sequences' average thickness. See 10-stacking-faults.md.
generate_these: generate_these generates the sites found in $sites for the stack, with coordinates reflecting the original $sites positions plus the stacking vector. generate_name_append appends $append_to_site_name to the generated site.
gr_to_fq: gr_to_fq !E, a child of pdf_generate, reverses the usual PDF-generation direction when non-zero: instead of generating G(r) from reciprocal-space data, it regenerates F(Q) from an already-generated G(r). This is used to verify that PDF generation round-trips correctly -- see LIFEPO4\GR-TO-FQ.INP, which generates G(r) from an original F(Q) at Run_Number 0, then uses gr_to_fq to reproduce that original F(Q) from the newly-created G(r) at Run_Number 1, and compares the two. See pdf_generate for the overall PDF-generation process.
grs_interaction:
Defines a GRS interaction with the name N between sites identified by $site_1 and $site_2. E represents the GRS interaction equation that can be a function of R; R returns the distance in Å between two atoms; these distances are updated when dependent fractional atomic coordinates are modified. The name N of the grs_interaction can be used in equations including penalty equations. When either from_N or to_N are defined, the interactions between $site_1 and $site_2 are sorted by distance and only the interactions between the from_N and to_N are considered. no_self_interaction prevents any interactions between equivalent positions of the same site.

This is useful when a general position is used to describe a special position. qi and qj corresponds to the valence charges used to calculate the Coulomb sum for the $site_1 and $site_2 sites respectively. (Examples: grs-alvo4\solve-1.inp, grs-alvo4\Rep-1.inp)
gui_add_bkg: gui_add_bkg !E is an xdd-dependent keyword controlling, for GUI plotting purposes only, whether phases are drawn on top of the background curve. By default, phases are plotted on top of background, where the plotted background comprises bkg plus any fit_obj's that have their fit_obj_phase set to 1 (fit_obj_phase defaults to 1). gui_add_bkg defaults to 1; setting it to 0 stops phases being plotted above background entirely, regardless of any fit_obj_phase settings. It is purely a display option -- it does not affect the calculated pattern, Ycalc, or the refinement, only how phases are rendered relative to background in the GUI's scan window. See fit_obj_phase for the complementary, fit_obj-scoped control over which fit_obj's are counted as part of that background.
gui_ignore: gui_ignore is an xdd-dependent keyword that tells the GUI to ignore that xdd's data file entirely -- Ycalc, the difference curve, and other items associated with the data file are no longer retrieved from the Kernel for display purposes. It's useful for xdds that don't need to be shown/plotted in the GUI, avoiding the cost of retrieving and rendering their results.
gui_reload: gui_reload is an xdd-dependent keyword that forces the GUI to reload that xdd's data file. When in Launch mode, data files are by default NOT reloaded if already loaded into the GUI -- they are only loaded/reloaded when the data file isn't loaded into the GUI yet, or when one of gui_reload, rebin_with_dx_of, smooth, yobs_eqn or yobs_to_xo_posn_yobs has been used at the xdd level. gui_reload is useful when the data file has been changed on disk by some other process not already covered by that list, ensuring the GUI picks up the new file content rather than continuing to display what it already had loaded.
h1:
h1, h2, m1 and m2 are the parameters of the Split-PearsonVII (spvii) peak_type, which forms a peak from two independent PearsonVII half-profiles either side of the peak position. The sum of h1 and h2 gives the FWHM of the composite peak:

fwhm1 = 2*h1, fwhm2 = 2*h2, fwhm = h1+h2

m1 and m2 are the PearsonVII exponents of the left (x<0) and right (x>0) half-profiles respectively. Each half is:

PVIILeft(x) = a*(1+b1*x^2)^(-m1), for x<0
PVIIRight(x) = a*(1+b2*x^2)^(-m2), for x>0
b1 = (2^(1/m1)-1)/h1^2, b2 = (2^(1/m2)-1)/h2^2

(chosen so each half reaches half-maximum exactly at x=-h1/x=h2), and a is a shared normalization constant involving Gamma functions of m1, m2, b1 and b2 chosen to give the composite peak unit area. See peak_type for the full Table 5-2 formulas.
half_hat: half_hat (a stacked_hats_conv dependent) defines one asymmetric hat-shaped term in a summation-of-hats aberration convolution: its x-axis range runs from half_hat to zero if half_hat<0, or zero to half_hat if half_hat>0. hat_height sets the hat's height (default 1). Its symmetric counterpart is whole_hat; stacked_hats_conv is used, for example, by the Tube_Tails macro to describe X-ray tube tails.
hat: Defines the x-axis extent of an impulse function that is convoluted into phase peaks. num_hats correspond to the number of hats to be convoluted. hat is used for example by the Slit_Width and Specimen_Tilt macros. (Examples: Fullerene\DECON.INP, LIFEPO4\DECON.INP, Silicon\DECON.INP)
height: height E (a stacking-fault layer dependent) sets a layer's height along the stacking direction, usable in place of the z_add keyword; refining parameters that height (or z_add) depends on lets layer heights be refined (see fit-3.inp).
histogram_match_scale_fwhm: An implementation of Histogram Matching (Baerlocher et al., 2007), where the distribution of pixels within the unit cell is restrained to one that matches Gaussian atoms with intensities corresponding to the atoms defined by f_atom_type's. The histogram-matching operation is performed when histogram_match_scale_fwhm evaluates to a non-zero value; the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the Gaussians (obtained from the file atom_radius.def) is then scaled by histogram_match_scale_fwhm. hm_size_limit_in_fwhm corresponds to the extent to which the Gaussians are calculated, in units of FWHM; hm_covalent_fwhm selects covalent radii (when non-zero) versus ionic radii (when zero/undefined). A typical usage is 'histogram_match_scale_fwhm = If(Mod(Cycle_Iter, 3), 0, 1); hm_size_limit_in_fwhm 1 hm_covalent_fwhm 1'. What is reported is the fraction of pixels modified; values of 1 for both histogram_match_scale_fwhm and hm_size_limit_in_fwhm seem optimal, where typically ~15 to 20% of pixels are modified. Using histogram matching should produce R-factors at convergence that are equal to or better than R-factors produced without it; it sharpens the electron density cloud for data at poor resolution (see examples cf\cf-cime-histo.inp and cf\cf-cime-poor-histo.inp).
hkl_Is: Declares a phase type that generates peaks from hkls -- either derived from the space group and cell (the normal case), or given explicitly via a `load hkl_m_d_th2 I { h k l m d th2 I ... }` block -- rather than from a real atomic structure (no sites are needed; hkl_Is is a Pawley-/Le-Bail-style intensity-extraction phase). If no hkl_m_d_th2 entries are given, TOPAS generates them from the space group, and writes the generated hkl_m_d_th2 list back into the OUT file (placed right after space_group) on convergence, with intensity parameters seeded at 1 and given the refinable `@` code unless lebail is set. Each hkl_m_d_th2 entry's six leading numbers are h, k, l (Miller indices), m (multiplicity), and d/th2 (d-spacing and 2-theta), followed by the intensity parameter I (the peak's intensity before any scale_pks equation). lp_search runs a dedicated indexing algorithm here that works directly off the figure-of-merit for a candidate cell rather than requiring d-spacings to be extracted from the pattern first (avoiding the usual difficulty of resolving overlapped lines) -- see test_examples\indexing\lp-search-pbso4.inp. I_parameter_names_have_hkl gives each generated intensity parameter a name of the form $start_of_parameter_name followed by its hkl, instead of an anonymous auto-generated name. Even with no sites defined, weight_percent still works off whatever cell_mass is set to. Also mixes in Tspace_group, Tcomm_1_2_phase_1_2, and Thkl_lat.
hkl_m_d_th2:
[hkl_m_d_th2 # # # # # # I E]... is a child of hkl_Is; it defines a phase type that uses explicit hkls for generating peak positions rather than deriving them from a space group. The six numbers after hkl_m_d_th2 give h k l m d and 2Th for that reflection, where:

h, k, l : Miller indices
m : multiplicity
d and th2 : d-spacing and 2Th value
I : the peak intensity parameter, before any scale_pks is applied

If no hkl_m_d_th2 lines are defined, hkls are instead generated automatically from the space group, and the resulting hkl_m_d_th2 details are appended after the space_group keyword on refinement termination (intensity parameters start at 1, and get the @ refine code unless lebail is defined). For example, given:

xdd quartz.xdd
...
hkl_Is
  Hexagonal(4.91459, 5.40603)
  space_group P_31_2_1

the OUT file will contain generated lines like:

load hkl_m_d_th2 I {
  1   0   0   6    4.25635   20.85324 @ 3147.83321
  1   0   1   6    3.34470   26.62997 @ 8559.23955
  1   0  -1   6    3.34470   26.62997 @ 8559.23955
  ...
}

The Create_hklm_d_Th2_Ip_file macro creates an hkl file in this same 'load hkl_m_d_th2 I' format. Even with no sites defined, weight_percent can still be used on such a phase -- it falls back to whatever value cell_mass provides. See also lp_search, an indexing algorithm usable alongside hkl_Is that works independently of d-spacing extraction, and I_parameter_names_have_hkl, which names the generated I parameters after their hkl.
hkl_plane: hkl_plane $hkl, used by the OpenGL viewer to display specific hkl planes overlaid on the structure (see the CeO2.STR file in the rigid directory) -- for example 'hkl_plane 1 1 1' or 'hkl_plane "2 -2 0"' (quoted when an index is negative). More than one hkl_plane can be defined to display multiple planes simultaneously.
hm_covalent_fwhm: hm_covalent_fwhm, a child of histogram_match_scale_fwhm, selects which radii are used when building the Gaussian atoms for histogram matching: covalent radii are used if hm_covalent_fwhm evaluates to a non-zero value, otherwise ionic radii are used. See histogram_match_scale_fwhm for the overall histogram-matching mechanism.
hm_size_limit_in_fwhm: hm_size_limit_in_fwhm, a child of histogram_match_scale_fwhm, sets the extent to which each Gaussian atom is calculated, in units of FWHM (default 1). See histogram_match_scale_fwhm for the overall histogram-matching mechanism.
i_on_error_ratio_tolerance: i_on_error_ratio_tolerance # (an xdd_scr/single-crystal keyword) filters out weak or unreliable reflections that fail the condition |Fo| > i_on_error_ratio_tolerance * |Sigma(Fo)| -- e.g. i_on_error_ratio_tolerance 4 discards any reflection whose observed structure factor isn't at least 4 times its estimated standard deviation.
ignore_differences_in_Friedel_pairs: For single-crystal data (xdd_scr), forces the use of Eq. (19-12) for calculating F2, which ignores any anomalous-dispersion-driven intensity difference between the two members of a Friedel pair (hkl and -h-k-l) rather than accounting for it.
in_cartesian: in_cartesian, a child of insert_atoms, signals that the x/y/z coordinates given for each insert_atom are Cartesian coordinates rather than fractional atomic coordinates. See insert_atoms for the overall mechanism.
index_I: index_I is typically set to the area under the peak; it is used to weight the reflection. good signals that the corresponding d-spacing is not an impurity line. (Examples: ex13.inp)
index_lam:
index_lam !E, a TIndexing keyword, defines the wavelength in Angstroms used for indexing; it defaults to 1.540596 (Cu Ka1). For example:

seed index_lam 0.79776 index_zero_error index_max_Nc_on_No 6 try_space_groups 3
load index_th2 dummy dummy index_I dummy {
  ' d (A)  2Theta     Height      Area     FWHM
  1.724  26.50645    2758.3   23303.7    0.0450
  ...
}

See examples indexing\ex10.inp and ex13.inp.
index_max_Nc_on_No: Determines the maximum ratio of the number of calculated to observed lines. The value of 6 allows for up to 83% of missing lines.
index_max_number_of_solutions: index_max_number_of_solutions #3000, used during indexing (TIndexing), sets the number of best trial solutions retained and reported at the end of an indexing run. A larger value keeps a longer list of candidate unit cells and figures of merit to inspect, which is useful for difficult indexing problems where the correct solution may not rank first; a smaller value reduces the memory and reporting overhead when a large number of candidate solutions are being explored internally. It only controls how many of the internally-explored candidates are kept and written to the *.NDX/*.DET output -- it does not change how many candidate cells the search algorithm considers.
index_max_th2_error: index_max_th2_error !E (default 0.05) is used to determine which lines are treated as impurity lines (unindexed 'UNI' lines in the *.NDX file) versus real lines belonging to the phase being indexed. A larger value, e.g. 1, forces more observed lines to be considered indexable rather than flagged as impurities -- useful (and faster) when it's already known there are few or no impurity lines, since the search doesn't need to explore as many impurity-vs-real assignments.
index_max_zero_error: Excludes solutions with zero errors greater than index_max_zero_error.
index_min_lp: index_min_lp !E2 and index_max_lp !E define the minimum and maximum lattice parameter values (in Angstrom) considered during indexing (TIndexing). index_min_lp defaults to 2; index_max_lp has no fixed default and is typically determined automatically from the observed d-spacings (the largest observed d-spacing implies a lower bound on how large the true cell could plausibly be). Narrowing this range when the approximate cell dimensions are already known -- for example, from a related structure or a rough unit-cell estimate -- reduces the search space and can significantly speed up indexing, as well as reduce the chance of the search converging on a spuriously small or large false solution. See also index_x0, which can directly seed a plausible reciprocal-lattice starting point rather than only constraining the overall range.
index_th2: index_th2 or index_d defines a reflection entry in 2θ degrees or d-spacing in Å. index_I is typically set to the area under the peak; it is used to weight the reflection.
index_zero_error: index_zero_error, used during indexing (TIndexing), includes a zero error (a constant offset in 2*Theta or d) as part of the indexing search, rather than assuming the input peak positions are free of any systematic zero-point shift. This is important because an unaccounted-for zero error can otherwise masquerade as an inconsistency in the lattice parameters, making indexing fail or converge on an incorrect cell even when the true cell is close to a correct match. It is distinct from index_max_zero_error, which instead bounds how large a zero error is allowed to be when excluding candidate solutions -- index_zero_error switches the zero-error search on in the first place, while index_max_zero_error constrains it once it is being searched.
inp_text:
inp_text $name { ... } defines a named block of INP text at one place in a file, which is then inserted at another place in the same INP file, or in an #include file, using inp_text_insert $name. This is useful for simplifying complicated INP files by moving control parameters (such as background coefficients) to the top of the file, away from where they are used -- for example: 'inp_text back_ground { bkg @ 17.365576` 14.5555883` 14.038067` } xdd ... inp_text_insert back_ground'. The inp_text block is updated on refinement termination, so refined values placed there (as in the bkg example) are written back in place.

More than one inp_text can share the same $name; in that case, inp_text_insert uses whichever inp_text of that name was most recently defined.
inp_text_insert:
inp_text $name { ... } defines a named block of INP text at one place in a file; inp_text_insert $name then pastes that same text in at another place in the file, or in an #include file. The pasted-in inp_text is updated on refinement termination (so refined values written back into it stay in sync). This is useful for simplifying complicated INP files by collecting control parameters (e.g. a shared background) at the top of the file rather than repeating or scattering them. For example:

inp_text back_ground {
  bkg @ 17.365576` 14.5555883` 14.038067`
}
xdd ...
inp_text_insert back_ground

More than one inp_text can share the same $name; each inp_text_insert of that name always uses the most recently defined inp_text block above it in the file.
insert_atom: insert_atom, a child of insert_atoms, defines one explicit atom to insert into the electron density during protein charge flipping, given its x, y, z position (Cartesian or fractional depending on whether in_cartesian is set) and occ (occupancy/intensity). Multiple insert_atom entries can be listed within a single insert_atoms block. See insert_atoms for the overall mechanism.
insert_atoms: insert_atoms { ... } inserts one or more explicit atoms into the electron density during protein charge flipping, listed as insert_atom entries each with their x/y/z/occ. activate controls when the insertion runs (evaluated non-zero to trigger it, like the activate used elsewhere in pick_atoms), and in_cartesian signals that the given x/y/z coordinates are Cartesian rather than fractional. This is distinct from pick_atoms/insert, which re-inserts electron density derived from atoms already picked from the existing density, whereas insert_atoms places brand-new, explicitly-positioned atoms directly.
insert_fwhm: insert_fwhm !E1, a child of pick_atoms (protein charge flipping), sets the FWHM (full width at half maximum) of the Gaussian used when insert re-inserts a picked atom's electron density -- the protein-charge-flipping counterpart of pick_fwhm/omit_fwhm, applied specifically to the insert operation. See pick_atoms and insert for the overall mechanism.
inter: [inter !E #] is a site attribute (alongside num_posns and rand_xyz) used within energy minimization/GRS-interaction setups (TEnergy_minimization). inter holds the sum of all grs_interaction contributions that are a function of this site -- i.e. every GRS interaction defined between this site and another via grs_interaction gets summed into inter for that site. Depending on the type of GRS interaction defined (e.g. a Coulomb-sum term using qi/qj valence charges), inter can represent something physically meaningful such as the site's electrostatic potential. Like num_posns, it is a computed/reported value rather than something you set directly, and it updates as the refinement/minimization proceeds.
iters: The maximum number of refinement iterations, default is 109. (Examples: lpsd-simulated.inp)
la: Defines an emission profile (see section 5), where each la determines an emission profile line: la is the area under the line, lo its wavelength in Å, lh the HW in mÅ of a Lorentzian convoluted into it, and lg the HW in mÅ of a Gaussian convoluted into it. By default the reserved parameter Lam (used to determine the Bragg angle) is taken from the emission profile line with the largest la value; if la parameters are refined, the reference wavelength could then change and cause confusion. lo_ref marks a specific line's lo as the one to use as the reference wavelength instead, avoiding that ambiguity.
lam: lam defines the emission profile (wavelength) used for a phase, comprising one or more la lines. ymin_on_ymax determines the x-axis extent to which an emission profile line is calculated (default 0.001). no_th_dependence defines an emission profile that is 2θ independent, allowing the use of non-X-ray data or fitting to negative 2θ values. By default, the program calculates d-spacings using the wavelength of the emission profile line with the highest la parameter; if la parameters are refined, this reference wavelength could change, causing confusion -- lo_ref can be used to identify the reference wavelength directly. Lam defines the value used for the reserved parameter Lam; when not defined, Lam is set to the wavelength of the emission profile line with the largest la value (Lam is used to determine the Bragg angle).
lat_prms: lat_prms $name { ... } defines a named, reusable set of lattice parameters (see Tlat_prms and Chapter 6, 'Reusing objects in large refinements') that one or more phases can share via use { name }, instead of each phase carrying its own copy -- letting phases with similar lattice parameters also share a common set of generated hkls, reducing memory usage and recalculation cost when many phases are present.
layer: layer $layer (a site dependent, stacking-fault modeling) marks a site as belonging to the named layer $layer, for use with the supercell approach to stacking faults. A site marked with layer cannot take part in restraints and is not displayed graphically (a site generated from it via generate_these can, however, take part in restraints). See stack, sx/sy/sz, and 10-stacking-faults.md.
layers_tol: layers_tol !#0.5 (a generate_stack_sequences dependent, default 0.5) corresponds to the tolerance q described in Coelho et al. (2016) Fig. 1 -- it sets the termination condition used while generating each stacking sequence.
lebail: Use the following input segment for Le Bail intensity extraction (see example lebail1.inp): (Examples: lebail1.inp)
line_min: line_min invokes line minimization (also known as the steepest descent method) for solving the normal equations. It uses a direction in parameter space given by delta_pi = Yi / Aii to minimize chi2 by adjusting a single scalar step lambda along that direction. Line minimization with the full A matrix calculated (approximate_A not defined) can increase the rate of convergence on problems like Pawley refinement. It has a relatively small memory footprint compared to full A-matrix methods, making it useful when the A matrix would otherwise consume too much memory -- approximate_A is the alternative approach for that same memory concern. When used together with use_extrapolation, oscillatory behaviour in chi2 during refinement can be reduced. line_min cannot be used together with approximate_A.
load_save_locals:
load_save_locals automatically saves and reloads parameters that were given unique names via local (typically the $-prefixed local coordinates/values created inside a 'for strs {}' or 'for xdds {}' loop), so that their refined values persist across separate runs of the same INP file. Without load_save_locals, a for-loop that assigns a value to a local parameter using the $ character across multiple str's or xdd's only has its LAST such value saved to the OUT file, since all instances share the same underlying local name; load_save_locals instead saves every instance's value.

Values are written to a file named INP_File.out_sl (note the .out_sl extension); on rerunning the INP file, the program checks for a matching .sl file and, if found, reads parameter values back from it. The GUI copies inp_file.out_sl to inp_file.sl when parameter values are kept after refinement, making this a normal keep/rerun cycle rather than something that needs manual file management. Each saved local parameter is identified internally by its xdd file name and phase name (and, for raw files, its range number); phase names within a given xdd must be unique for this identification to work correctly.

When multiple xdd's share the same file name -- for example, two XDD(..\ceo2) entries with different start_X/finish_X ranges -- the xdd-dependent xdd_tag keyword can be used instead to give each xdd instance a distinct identifying tag, typically set via Load_Eval so it is evaluated once at load time, e.g.:

xdd_tag = Load_Eval(Concat("tag", i));

with i incremented via existing_prm across the loop. lor_fwhm: Defines the FWHM of a Lorentzian that is convoluted into phase peaks; see for example the CS_L and Strain_L macros.
lp_search:
lp_search !E, used on an hkl_Is phase, defines a phase type that uses hkls (rather than extracted d-spacings) for generating peak positions, using an indexing algorithm that is independent of d-spacing extraction (Coelho, 2017; see lp-search-pbso4.inp). It minimizes on a figure-of-merit function that measures the correctness of a set of trial lattice parameters directly against the raw pattern. This avoids the difficulties of conventional d-spacing-extraction-based indexing on complex patterns with heavily overlapped lines, where the primary problem is ascertaining how many lines are present -- lp_search sidesteps that problem entirely by not requiring d-spacings to be extracted first.

If no hkl_m_d_th2 keywords are defined, hkls are generated automatically from the space group; the resulting hkl_m_d_th2 details are written back after the space_group keyword on refinement termination. Generated intensity parameters start at 1, and are given the '@' refine-code automatically unless lebail is defined. I_parameter_names_have_hkl can be used to name the generated intensity parameters starting with $start_of_parameter_name and ending with the corresponding hkl, making them easier to identify individually.

lp_search cannot be applied directly to time-of-flight (TOF) data, since it operates in 2*Theta space; TOF data must first be converted to 2*Theta before lp_search can be used, as demonstrated in test_examples\tof\tof-to-q.inp. The conversion follows from I(Q) = Intensity(TOF) * dTOF/dQ, with:

Q = 2*Pi/d, TOF = t0 + t1*d + t2*d^2

differentiating and substituting d = 2*Pi/Q gives:

dTOF/dQ = -t1*2*Pi/Q^2 - 2*t2*(2*Pi)^2/Q^3

(assuming t0/t2 corrections as needed), which for the common case of t0 = t2 = 0 simplifies to:

dTOF/dQ = -t1 * D_spacing^2 / (2*Pi)

giving a direct Jacobian factor for converting TOF intensities to equivalent 2*Theta/Q-space intensities before running lp_search on the transformed data.
lpsd_th2_angular_range_degrees: Convolutes the aberration for a Linear Position Sensitive Detector (Cheary & Coelho, 1994) into phase peaks. lpsd_th2_angular_range_degrees corresponds to the angular range of the LPSD in 2Th degrees. lpsd_equitorial_divergence_degrees is the equatorial divergence in degrees of the primary beam and lpsd_equitorial_sample_length_mm the length of the sample in the equatorial plane. lpsd_th2_angular_range_degrees corrects peak shapes, intensities and 2Th shifts, see example lpsd-simulated.inp. (Examples: lpsd-simulated.inp)
macro:
macro $user_defined_macro_name { ... } (or macro $name(args) { ... } with arguments) defines a reusable text-substitution macro, expanded by the pre-processor before the kernel ever sees the file -- see TPre_processor for the full family of related directives. For example:

macro Cubic(cv) { a cv b = Get(a); c = Get(a); }

Macros can take multiple arguments or none. Some example uses of Cubic:

Cubic(4.50671)
Cubic(a_lp 4.50671  min 4.49671  max 4.52671)
Cubic(!a_lp 4.50671)

The first defines a, b, c with no parameter name; the second names/refines a_lp; the third prefixes a_lp with '!' so it's not refined (but can still be used in equations). A macro's definition need not precede its use anywhere in the file -- macros are fully collected before expansion begins. Multiple macros can share the same name as long as they take different numbers of arguments; TOPAS resolves which one to expand purely by matching the argument count at the call site (see topas.inc's Beq(...) for a real 2-arg/3-arg example) -- a call that matches no defined arity fails with 'Cannot find match for macro <name>'. Macros can also expand to other macro names (e.g. Crystallite_Size expands to CS, which is itself a macro). See also #m_unique for defining collision-safe parameter names inside a macro body, and the '&' argument-type prefix (section 21.1.6) for controlling how macro arguments get parenthesized on expansion.
madelung: The madelung keyword reports on the Madelung constant of a structure (Madelung, 1918). It uses the method of Coelho & Cheary (1997) for calculating the electrostatic potentials. (Examples: test_examples\Madelung.inp, madelung.inp, Madelung.inp)
mag_only: mag_only, a site-dependent keyword, causes the non-magnetic component of intensity to be ignored for that one site -- only its magnetic scattering (Fmag) contributes to the calculated pattern. See mag_only_for_mag_sites for the str-level equivalent that applies this to every magnetic site at once, and mag_space_group for the overall magnetic-refinement mechanism.
mag_only_for_mag_sites: mag_only_for_mag_sites, defined on a str using mag_space_group, causes the non-magnetic component of intensity to be ignored for ALL magnetic sites within that str -- i.e. those sites contribute only their magnetic scattering (Fmag), not their ordinary nuclear/structural scattering, to the calculated pattern. This differs from the related, site-dependent mag_only, which ignores the non-magnetic component for just the one site it's defined on rather than every magnetic site in the str. See mag_space_group for the overall magnetic-refinement mechanism and the required mlx/mly/mlz/mg parameters.
mag_space_group:
mag_space_group $symbol defines the magnetic (Shubnikov) space group for a str, and is the central keyword that switches on magnetic structure refinement, used together with the site-dependent mlx, mly, mlz and mg parameters (thanks to Branton Campbell and John Evans for expert assistance during this implementation). See examples in the test_examples\mag directory, and the tutorial by John Evans at http://www.dur.ac.uk/john.evans/topas_workshop/tutorial_lamno3_magnetic.htm.

The magnetic intensity is |Fmagcperp|, where Fmagcperp is the component of the magnetic structure factor vector Fmagc perpendicular to the scattering vector Q:

Fmagcperp = Fmagc - (Fmagc . Qhat) Qhat
Q = (L^-1)^T * h, Qhat = Q/|Q|

(L the Cartesian lattice-parameter matrix, h the Miller indices, so (L^-1)^T is the reciprocal lattice). Fmagc = L * Fmag in Cartesian terms, where Fmag for a single site, summed over its equivalent positions j, is:

Fmag = Sum_j(Bj*m) Exp(2*Pi*i*Uj)
Uj = h.Rj.x + h.tj
Bj = sj*det(Rj)*Rj

with x the site's fractional coordinates, Rj/tj the rotation/translation parts of the space-group operator j, m = {mlx, mly, mlz} the magnetic moment, and Bj the magnetic transformation matrix. Magnetic form-factor data comes from MAGDATA.DAT (a GSAS-format file), Shubnikov groups from shubnikovgroups.txt, and the Lande splitting factor can be refined via the site-dependent mg parameter, whose default also comes from MAGDATA.DAT. Magnetic moments are displayed as arrows when view_structure is used; the 'Atom size' display setting can be reduced if atom balls are hiding the arrows.
match_transition_matrix_stats: match_transition_matrix_stats {...} (a generate_stack_sequences dependent) checks that the statistics of the actually-generated stacking sequences match the intended transition probability matrix, reporting any discrepancy.
max_X: min_X and max_X bound the x-axis window [min_X, max_X] that a pdf_convolute equation is evaluated/applied over -- see test_examples\pdf\beq-3.inp. convolute_X_recal, the third member of the same pdf_convolute block, forces that window's resolution to be recalculated rather than reused. The same min_X/max_X pair is also reused elsewhere with the same generic 'x-axis window' meaning (e.g. fit_obj's [min_X !E] [max_X !E]), just scoping a different keyword's x-axis range rather than pdf_convolute's.
md_scale: md_scale !E (default 1) scales the size of each molecular-dynamics parameter update, in the Verlet-derived update equation p(k+1) = (p(k) - p(k-1) + (_md_k / _mass)(dRwp(k)/dp) t^2) md_scale + p(k) (see molecular_dynamics and Chapter 15). It is effectively a way of increasing or decreasing the simulated temperature -- increasing md_scale increases atomic movement per step, decreasing it damps movement. MD-3.INP uses this to tame an initially chaotic simulation after a large random displacement (rand_xyz): md_scale = If(Cycle_Iter < 2, 0.1, 1);, starting with heavily damped motion for the first two cycles before returning to normal scale.
md_time: md_time !E accumulates simulated time during a molecular_dynamics run, advancing by md_time_step each MD iteration (see Chapter 15, 'Molecular dynamics (MD)').
md_time_step: md_time_step !E (default 0.002) is the molecular-dynamics time step t used in the Verlet parameter-update equation (see molecular_dynamics and Chapter 15): p(k+1) = (p(k) - p(k-1) + (_md_k / _mass)(dRwp(k)/dp) t^2) md_scale + p(k).
mg:
mlx, mly and mlz are the site-dependent Cartesian components of a site's magnetic moment vector m = {mlx, mly, mlz}, used (together with mag_space_group) in magnetic structure refinement. They enter the magnetic structure factor as:

Fmag = Sum_j(Bj*m) Exp(2*Pi*i*Uj)

summed over the site's equivalent positions j, where Bj is the magnetic transformation matrix for equivalent position j -- so mlx/mly/mlz are what's refined to determine the size and direction of the magnetic moment on that site.

Like any other parameter, they can be refined, given min/max attributes, or constrained by equation; the site-dependent macros MM_CrystalAxis_Refine and MM_Cartesian_Refine provide convenient ways to refine them either in crystal-axis or Cartesian form. When mlx (or mly/mlz) is being refined but has no derivative for a given group of equivalent positions, TOPAS raises 'Magnetic moment mlx of site ... cannot be refined as it has no derivative' and terminates -- this happens when the first row of Sum_j(Bj*m), summed over the equivalent positions of a special-position group, comes out zero for that component.

Magnetic moments (displayed as Occupancy*Bj*m) are shown graphically as arrows when view_structure is used, with the 'Atom size' display setting reducible if atom balls are hiding them. mg is the site-dependent Lande splitting factor used in calculating magnetic form factors from MAGDATA.DAT (a GSAS-format file); if left undefined it defaults to the value MAGDATA.DAT supplies for that ion, but it can also be refined like any other parameter. See mag_space_group for the full magnetic structure factor derivation and the overall magnetic-refinement mechanism.
min_X: min_X and max_X bound the x-axis window [min_X, max_X] that a pdf_convolute equation is evaluated/applied over -- see test_examples\pdf\beq-3.inp. convolute_X_recal, the third member of the same pdf_convolute block, forces that window's resolution to be recalculated rather than reused. The same min_X/max_X pair is also reused elsewhere with the same generic 'x-axis window' meaning (e.g. fit_obj's [min_X !E] [max_X !E]), just scoping a different keyword's x-axis range rather than pdf_convolute's.
min_d: Determines in Å the resolution of observed reflections to work with; only observed reflections with a d-spacing above min_d are considered. min_d is evaluated each CF iteration. Get(num_observed_reflections_above_d_min) is updated when a change in min_d is detected. See also extend_calculated_sphere_to and delete_observed_reflections.
min_grid_spacing: If defined, then the grid spacing used is set to the smaller of min_d/2 and min_grid_spacing; useful for obtaining many grid points for graphical purposes. (Examples: fourier-map-cime.inp)
min_r: min_r # and max_r # (a Tmin_max_r type-mixin, available at the site level) define the minimum and maximum radii for calculating bond lengths -- only neighbor atoms within this radius range of a site are included when bond lengths/angles are reported (see append_bond_lengths). Defaults are 0 and 3.2 Angstroms respectively.
mixture_MAC:
mixture_MAC # calculates the mass absorption coefficient (MAC) of the whole mixture, in cm^2/g, as:

(mu/rho)_mixture = Sum_i[ (mu/rho)_i * w_i ]

where w_i and (mu/rho)_i are the weight percent and phase_MAC of phase i respectively, summed over all phases in the mixture. Errors are reported for both phase_MAC and mixture_MAC. Mass absorption coefficients are sourced from NIST (http://physics.nist.gov/PhysRefData/XrayMassCoef). mixture_density_g_on_cm3: Calculates the density of the mixture assuming a packing density of 1, see also mixture_MAC.

modify_peak: modify_peak can be used to modify peak profiles either before convolutions or after. Functionality is realized by using the internal data objects Get(current_peak_x) and Get(current_peak); these two objects return the x-axis wavelength being processed and the current calculated peak intensity respectively. When no_th_dependence is defined, Get(current_peak_x) returns the x-axis of the point being calculated; when it is not defined, Get(current_peak_x) returns the wavelength of the point being calculated.
modify_peak_apply_before_convolutions: Controls whether modify_peak's modification (via modify_peak_eqn) is applied before or after peak convolutions are performed.
modify_peak_eqn: The equation used by modify_peak to modify the current peak profile, evaluated using the internal data objects Get(current_peak_x) (the x-axis point being processed) and Get(current_peak) (the current calculated peak intensity).
molecular_dynamics:
molecular_dynamics (see Chapter 15, 'Molecular dynamics (MD)') places TOPAS in a non-refinement mode where parameters of any type -- not just the ones typically associated with molecular dynamics -- can be updated in a time-dependent manner using the Verlet (1967) algorithm. It is conceptually the steepest-descent method of refinement, but new parameter values are accepted regardless of whether they improve the objective function (Rwp): relating this to the Newtonian equations of motion for iteration k and parameter p,

Force(k) = m a(k) = dRwp/dp
Velocity(k+1) = Velocity(k) + (dRwp(k)/dp)/m

The Verlet algorithm avoids computing velocity explicitly and instead updates p directly:

p(k+1) = 2 p(k) - p(k-1) + a(k) t^2 = 2 p(k) - p(k-1) + (1/m)(dRwp(k)/dp) t^2

where t is md_time_step and mass m is set via the _mass parameter attribute. TOPAS generalizes this further to:

p(k+1) = (p(k) - p(k-1) + (_md_k / _mass)(dRwp(k)/dp) t^2) md_scale + p(k)

which reduces to the plain Verlet algorithm when _md_k, _mass and md_scale all take their default value of 1.

For atomic coordinate parameters specifically, mass defaults to the value found in the ISOTOPES.TXT file for the site's occupancy species (weighted by occ if more than one), and _md_k defaults to a lattice-geometry correction for x/y/z (ax for x, by for y, cz for z, derived from the lattice angles) rather than 1, so that forces are corrected for non-orthogonal lattice parameters without the user having to set _md_k/_mass explicitly. grs_interaction can supply the forces driving an MD run (see MD-1.INP). _md_force (see md_force's description) can apply an external force to an atom. See test_examples\grs-alvo4\md-1.inp through md-4.inp and grs-0.inp for worked examples, including a 2x2x2 supercell relaxation, a random-displacement + damped-md_scale recovery, and applying a directional force to an atom to test structural integrity along different crystallographic axes.
move_to: move_to $keyword repositions subsequent input to attach to a different location in the internal data tree, letting you set attributes (e.g. min/max) on a parameter or object without first loading/declaring it explicitly (see section 2.18.2, 'The "move_to $keyword" keyword'). $keyword can be any object in the internal data tree -- for example, move_to u12 followed by min = -Sqrt(Get(u11) Get(u22)); max = Sqrt(Get(u11) Get(u22)); sets those bounds directly on u12 without a preceding load block, as used in the site-dependent ADPs_Keep_PD macro's ADP limits.
more_accurate_Voigt: Fitting to the Voigts using the accurate calibration results in the small difference plots seen in the following: The more_accurate_Voigt calibration is accurate and fast. It fits to each true Voigt the following: (see section 5.6). Three examples in the test_examples\voigt-approx directory compare peak-shape approximations against a true Voigt generated by CREATE.INP: FIT-PV.INP fits an ordinary two-parameter pseudo-Voigt (pv_lor and pv_fwhm both refined) directly to the true-Voigt data, showing the plain PV approximation's accuracy. FIT-MORE.INP fits the same data using more_accurate_Voigt -- peak_type pv is declared but pv_lor/pv_fwhm are held at 0, and lor_fwhm/gauss_fwhm are refined directly instead, letting more_accurate_Voigt's calibration approximate the Voigt profile in place of the standard PV formula. FIT-OBJ.INP fits a sum of four fit_obj basis functions (two Gaussians plus two Lorentzians, refined via simulated annealing over a temperature schedule) directly to the same true-Voigt data, as a more flexible, higher-order benchmark against the simpler PV and more_accurate_Voigt fits.
n: n returns the number of transitions generated for the corresponding "to" transition. height can be used instead of the z_add keyword. (Examples: fit-1.inp, fit-2.inp)
n_avg: n_avg !E (a generate_stack_sequences dependent) controls the averaging used while generating stacking sequences from the transition probability matrix.
ndx_sg: One record from a saved set of indexing solutions, written in the compact row form TOPAS produces at the end of an indexing run and expects back if you paste those solutions into a load block to re-examine or reprocess them later without re-running the search (see the Technical Reference manual, section 22.3). Each record is a single row: ndx_sg (space group symbol) followed by numeric fields -- ndx_status (a solution status/accept-reject flag, present only in the newer 'status-aware' record form), ndx_uni (a uniqueness indicator distinguishing a genuinely distinct cell/space-group solution from a derivative of one already listed), ndx_ze (the refined 2th zero-error for that solution, present only in the 'with zero error' record form), then the cell parameters ndx_alp/ndx_blp/ndx_clp (a, b, c) and ndx_allp/ndx_belp/ndx_galp (alpha, beta, gamma). Rows like this are normally wrapped in one of four topas.inc macros that declare the exact matching field list for a `load dummy ...` block: Indexing_Solutions (sg, uni, vol, gof, alp, blp, clp, allp, belp, galp -- no zero-error, no status), Indexing_Solutions_With_Zero_Error (adds ze), Indexing_Solutions_2 (adds status), and Indexing_Solutions_With_Zero_Error_2 (adds both status and ze). Note the macros' field lists also include ndx_vol (cell volume) and ndx_gof (goodness of fit) between ndx_uni and ndx_ze/ndx_alp, which this line omits -- worth double-checking against whichever macro you're pasting a solution row for.
neutron_data: Signals that the input data is of neutron type. Used in the picking of atoms and additionally Eh values are not corrected from any defined f_atom_type and f_atom_quantity keywords. (Examples: test_examples\mag\occ-merge.inp)
new: new $object creates several instances of a given object type at once, e.g. new(xdd, n) creates n xdds -- see section 19.5, 'Creating many xdds at once using new and xdd_file'. Typically used inside a macro together with move_to to target the array being populated, for example: macro Create_XDDs(n) { move_to xdds move_to xdd_recs new(xdd, n) }.
no_coulomb:
no_coulomb, defined on a grs_interaction, makes that interaction ignore the Coulomb (qi*qj/R) part of the interaction and use only its equation part. This is useful for materials that are not wholly ionic, where a purely Coulombic model isn't appropriate for every interaction. For example, a Lennard-Jones-style potential:

U = A/R^6 + B/R^12

can be built efficiently from two separate grs_interactions, each with no_coulomb defined, e.g. 'grs_interaction ... = 1/R^4; no_coulomb' and 'grs_interaction ... = 1/R^9; no_coulomb' -- the 1/R^4 and 1/R^9 values are then stored in lookup tables calculated once at the start of refinement, rather than being recomputed from atomic charges every time. This potential form is used to describe the partly ionic structure of AlVO4 (see grs-alvo4\rep-2.inp). no_coulomb can also be combined with setting the grs_interaction equation to zero on a different, related interaction -- useful for modeling dipole effects where the electron cloud's centre is displaced from the nucleus, e.g. one grs_interaction with '= 0;' (no repulsion equation) for the nucleus site and a second with '= 1/R^9; no_coulomb' (no Coulomb potential) for the shifted electron-cloud site.
no_extinction_subgroup_search: By default, extinction subgroup determination is performed at the end of an indexing run; this can be negated by defining no_extinction_subgroup_search.
no_f11: no_f11 instructs the program to ignore f11 (the imaginary part of the anomalous dispersion correction) entirely, increasing refinement speed with little change to Ycalc. It is a child of f0_f1_f11_atom, relevant since high correlations exist between f1, f11, scale and beq parameters, making f11 often not worth the extra computational cost of including when its effect on the calculated pattern is small. See f0_f1_f11_atom for the full atomic-scattering-factor mechanism; report_on_str reports the f1/f11 (or neutron scattering length) values used, though not when d_spacing_to_energy_in_eV_for_f1_f11 is in effect.
no_normal_equations: no_normal_equations prevents the use of normal equations (the A p = Y matrix system of Eq. (4-4)) in the minimization routine. It is used together with line_min, which instead solves for each parameter's step directly via delta_pi = Yi / Aii without forming or solving the full normal-equations matrix system. This avoids the cost of assembling and inverting the A matrix, at the expense of the faster convergence that off-diagonal A-matrix terms normally provide. It is most useful in the same memory-constrained situations that motivate line_min in the first place -- refinements with very large numbers of parameters where even a sparse A matrix is impractical. See line_min for the direction used to update each parameter.
normalize_FCs: Normalizes site fractional coordinates. Normalization does not occur for coordinates with min/max limits, that are part of a rigid body, or that are part of a site constraint of any kind. (Examples: test_examples\occ-merge.inp)
num_cycles:
num_cycles # determines the number of convergence cycles to process when continue_after_convergence is defined -- each cycle runs until convergence, then restarts. The number of iterations per cycle, set via iters, is still adhered to independently (iters caps each cycle's iteration count; num_cycles caps how many such cycles run in total). To set the number of cycles to 100, use something like:

continue_after_convergence
iters 1000000000
num_cycles 100

(iters is set very high here so it never terminates a cycle early -- convergence and num_cycles are what stop the refinement).
num_highest_I_values_to_keep: num_highest_I_values_to_keep #num, used with single-crystal data (xdd_scr), removes all hkl's except for the #num hkl's with the highest Fo values -- a way to restrict a single-crystal refinement to only its strongest reflections. See also i_on_error_ratio_tolerance, which filters hkl's by a |Fo| vs Sigma(Fo) ratio instead of by rank.
num_posns: num_posns #, a child of site, is the number of unique equivalent positions generated for that site from the space group; it is calculated and written back into the INP file automatically on refinement termination, so it does not need to be entered by hand. rand_xyz !E introduces a random displacement to the site's fractional coordinates (x, y, z) -- used together with continue_after_convergence for simulated annealing/structure solution, where !E gives the displacement amount (scaled by the current temperature); a value of 1, for example, applies a full-strength random displacement each time rand_xyz processes are triggered after convergence. inter !E #, a site-dependent reserved-parameter-like quantity, is the sum of all GRS interactions (see grs_interaction) that are a function of this site; depending on which GRS interactions are defined, inter can represent the site's electrostatic potential, making it useful for reporting on or restraining the local bonding/Coulomb environment of a site.
num_runs: When num_runs > 0, then, by default, output to TOPAS.LOG (or TC.LOG if running TC.EXE) is suspended after the first run (Run_Number == 0). suspend_writing_to_log_file changes this behaviour.
num_unique_vx_vy: On termination of refinement, num_unique_vx_vy reports the number of unique {sx, sy} stacking vector coordinates for all layer types. transition defines a "from" transition with the name $transition_name; the transition uses the layer defined in use_layer. (Examples: fit-1.inp)
number_of_sequences: number_of_sequences !E (a generate_stack_sequences dependent) sets how many independent stacking sequences to randomly generate from the transition probability matrix.
number_of_stacks_per_sequence:
number_of_stacks_per_sequence !E, a child of generate_stack_sequences, sets how many layers are stacked together to build one generated sequence (i.e. the length/depth of each simulated crystallite in layers). Its sibling number_of_sequences sets how many independent sequences are generated and averaged together -- using more than one (recursive averaging, corresponding to DIFFaX's "recursive" mode) reduces statistical noise compared to relying on a single long sequence (DIFFaX's "explicit" mode). For example, from test_examples\stacking_faults\fit-1.inp:

generate_stack_sequences {
  number_of_sequences Nseqs 200
  number_of_stacks_per_sequence Nv 200
  num_unique_vx_vy 6
  Transition(1, lpc)
    to 1 = pa;   a_add = 2/3;  b_add = 1/3;   n !n1 349984
    to 2 = 1-pa; a_add = 0;    b_add = 0;     n !n2 149781
  ...
}

Here 200 independent sequences (Nseqs) are each generated with 200 layers (Nv), and the diffraction contribution is averaged over all 200 sequences. Increasing either value improves statistical accuracy at the cost of computation time. See examples FIT-1.INP, FIT-2.INP, FIT-3.INP.
numerical_area: Returns the numerically calculated area under the phase.
numerical_lor_gauss_conv: numerical_lor_gauss_conv creates a 'true' Voigt peak shape by numerically convoluting a Gaussian (gauss_fwhm) with a Lorentzian (lor_fwhm), rather than using the faster but approximate analytical pseudo-Voigt. TOPAS performs this convolution via FFT to carry out the underlying double summation; for a Lorentzian fraction greater than 500 (out of 1000, see below) the convolution uses an analytical Lorentzian convoluted with a Gaussian approximated as straight line segments, while for less than 500 it uses an analytical Gaussian convoluted with a Lorentzian approximated as straight line segments. It is used, for example, in test_examples\voigt-approx\create.inp, where the amount of Lorentzian character is entered as a number out of 1000 -- a value of 500 yields a Voigt with both Lorentzian and Gaussian FWHM equal to 0.5. The resulting true Voigt is written to a file named voigtNNNN.xy (NNNN between 0 and 1000), containing 100,000 data points, with a convolution step size as small as 0.0005 when convolution_step is set to 4. This true-Voigt generation is what more_accurate_Voigt's calibration was originally fitted against (the fit_obj-based pseudo-Voigt approximation used by more_accurate_Voigt reduces the error against these true Voigts by roughly a factor of 100 compared to the ordinary pseudo-Voigt). See also fit-pv.inp, fit-more.inp and fit-obj.inp, which each fit a different peak-shape approximation against the generated true Voigt to compare accuracy.
numerical_lor_ymin_on_ymax: numerical_lor_ymin_on_ymax !E0.0001, used together with numerical_lor_gauss_conv, defines the x-axis extent to which the numerical Gaussian/Lorentzian convolution aberrations are calculated, as the ratio of the tail intensity to the peak intensity at which calculation stops (default 0.0001) -- the same ymin_on_ymax convention used elsewhere for emission-profile and convolution extents (e.g. the ordinary ymin_on_ymax on lam). A smaller value extends the calculation further into the peak's tails at the cost of more computation; the default is generally adequate for generating the 'true' Voigt reference peaks that numerical_lor_gauss_conv produces.
occ: occ and beq defines the site occupancy factor and the equivalent isotropic temperature factor respectively. $atom corresponds to a valid atom symbol or isotope contained in the file ATMSCAT.TXT for x-ray data and NEUTSCAT.TXT for neutron_data.
occ_merge:
Rewrites site occupancies of sites defined in $sites in terms of their fractional atomic coordinates (Favre-Nicolin and R. Cerny 2002). This is useful during structure solution for merging rigid bodies such as octahedra. It is also useful for identifying special positions as seen in the example test_examples\occ-merge.inp. In this implementation $sites are thought of as spheres with a radius occ_merge_radius. When two atoms approach with a distance less than the sum of their occ_merge_radius's then the spheres intersect. The occupancies of the sites, occ_xyz, become:

occ_xyz = 1 / (1 + Intersecting_fractional_volumes)

In this way any number of sites can be merged. Sites appearing in $sites cannot have their occupancies refined. On termination of refinement the occ parameter values are updated with their corresponding occ_xyz.
omit_fwhm: omit_fwhm !E1, a child of pick_atoms (protein charge flipping), sets the FWHM (full width at half maximum) of the Gaussian used when omit removes a picked atom's electron density -- the protein-charge-flipping counterpart of pick_fwhm/insert_fwhm, applied to the omit operation. See pick_atoms and omit for the overall mechanism.
one_on_x_conv: one_on_x_conv (εm) defines a response function following the convolution function (4 εm ε)^(-0.5), for ε = 0 to εm, that is convoluted into phase peaks. εm can be greater than or less than zero -- see for example the Divergence macro, which uses one_on_x_conv to implement the Equatorial Divergence aberration. Internally, one_on_x_conv is one of the response functions calculated using a mixture of analytical and straight-line-segment convolution (along with axial_conv and circles_conv).
only_penalties:
only_penalties restricts refinement to minimizing on penalty functions (and restraints) alone, with the observed-data term of the objective function (Eq. (4-1)/(4-3)) effectively absent -- this is the same situation that occurs automatically whenever no observed data is present, and in both cases the BFGS method is used by default for the minimization (overridable with line_min). It is used heavily for structure solution and energy minimization against a purely geometric or interaction-based penalty model, such as GRS-series atomic-interaction penalties (see AlVO4-grs-auto.inp) rather than against diffraction data.

Because only_penalties does not update the xdd-dependent Rwp, Get(non_fit, r_wp) (the global Rwp) must be used instead of Get(r_wp) to monitor progress when reporting results from an only_penalties refinement. It is commonly combined with continue_after_convergence and a temperature regime to perform energy-minimization-style simulated annealing, as in the solve-1.inp and rep-1.inp/rep-2.inp example families.
operate_on_points: operate_on_points $sites (used with rotate/translate on a rigid body) restricts a rigid-body rotation/translation to only the named sites, given as a site-identifying string -- which can use the wildcard character * (e.g. O* matches every site starting with 'O') and the negation character ! (e.g. "Si* O* !O2" matches Si*/O* sites except O2). in_cartesian/in_FC select whether the operation is expressed in Cartesian or fractional coordinates.
out:
out $file [append] opens $file for writing parameter and equation details, one or more out_record blocks at a time; append causes output to be appended to $file rather than overwriting it. Each out_record defines a single line (or field) of output: out_eqn gives the equation or parameter whose value is written, and out_fmt gives the $c_fmt_string -- a C-style format string containing a single format specifier for a double-precision number -- used to format it; out_fmt can also be used without out_eqn to write a literal string. out_fmt_err gives the $c_fmt_string used to format the estimated standard deviation (error) of out_eqn; both out_fmt and out_fmt_err require an out_eqn to be defined, and the order in which out_fmt and out_fmt_err are given determines which is written first.

Multiple out_record blocks can be loaded compactly with 'load out_record out_fmt out_eqn { "%d " = Run_Number; ... }'. The special characters ,(){}[] can be written to $file by wrapping them in double quotes (e.g. Out_String("a,b}c(d")), and a literal apostrophe or double quote is written using the escape sequences %A and %B respectively. See also atom_out, phase_out, phase_out_X and xdd_out, which are phase/site/xdd-scoped variants that reuse the same out_record mechanism.
out_A_matrix: out_A_matrix $file outputs the least-squares A matrix to the file $file; it is used by the Out_for_cf macro (to prepare a Pawley-refinement A matrix for use in charge flipping via cf_in_A_matrix). Output can be limited to specific parameters using A_matrix_prm_filter -- for example, 'out_A_matrix file.a A_matrix_prm_filter q*' outputs only the A-matrix elements corresponding to parameters whose names start with 'q'. This is distinct from A_matrix/A_matrix_normalized/C_matrix/C_matrix_normalized, which instead generate the A matrix and its correlation matrix for internal/OUT-file error-reporting purposes rather than exporting it to a separate file.
out_dependences_for: out_dependences_for $user_string $object_name is similar to out_dependences, but names an object that is not a parameter -- for example, 'out_dependences_for tag_1 rigid' lists the independently refined parameters associated with the most recently defined rigid body. Many $object_name's can be tagged, including x, y, z, occ, beq, u11, u22, u33, u12, u13, u23, a, b, c, al, be, ga, and non-parameter objects such as site, rigid, sites_restrain, lat_prms, gauss_conv, lor_conv, all_scale_pks and th2_offset_eqn.
out_eqn: out_eqn !E (a Tout_record dependent, used inside an out block) supplies the equation or parameter whose value is written to the out file, formatted using the record's out_fmt. out_fmt can also be used without out_eqn, for writing literal strings.
out_fmt: out_fmt $c_fmt_string (a Tout_record dependent) supplies the C-style printf format string (containing a single double-precision format specifier) used to render the value from out_eqn -- or, used without out_eqn, a literal string to write as-is. Where both out_fmt and out_fmt_err are given, their order in the INP determines which is written to the file first.
out_fmt_err: out_fmt_err $c_fmt_string (a Tout_record dependent) supplies the C-style printf format string used to render out_eqn's refinement error/uncertainty; it requires an out_eqn to be defined on the same record, and its order relative to out_fmt determines which value is written to the file first.
out_prm_vals_on_convergence: out_prm_vals_per_iteration $file [append] and out_prm_vals_on_convergence $file [append] output refined independent parameter values, either every iteration or only on convergence respectively, into the file $file. out_prm_vals_filter can be used to filter which parameters are output; $filter can contain the wildcard character '*' and the negation character '!' -- for example, 'out_prm_vals_per_iteration PRM_VALS.TXT out_prm_vals_filter "* !u*"' outputs every parameter except those starting with 'u'. More than one out_prm_vals_per_iteration/out_prm_vals_on_convergence can be defined at once, letting different filtered subsets of parameters be routed to different files. out_prm_vals_dependents_filter additionally allows dependent (non-independent, equation-derived) parameters to be output according to its $filter_dependents. A related keyword, out_prm_vals_on_end $file [append], outputs only once, at the end of refinement -- for example, 'prm wtp = Get(weight_percent); out_prm_vals_on_end aac2.txt append out_prm_vals_filter wtp out_prm_vals_dependents_filter wtp' appends just the final weight_percent value each run. Combined with num_runs and load out_record/out_fmt/out_eqn, out_prm_vals_on_end can build up a per-run summary table (e.g. Cycle, Iter, Rwp, and named parameters) across a whole batch of runs into one results file.
out_prm_vals_on_end:
out_prm_vals_on_end $file [append] outputs refined independent parameter values only once, at the end of refinement, into the file $file (append keeps adding to the file across runs instead of overwriting it) -- unlike out_prm_vals_per_iteration (every iteration) or out_prm_vals_on_convergence (every convergence), which output repeatedly. out_prm_vals_filter can be used to filter which parameters are output; $filter can contain the wildcard character '*' and the negation character '!'. For example:

prm wtp = Get(weight_percent);
out_prm_vals_on_end aac2.txt append out_prm_vals_filter wtp out_prm_vals_dependents_filter wtp

appends just the final weight_percent value each run (out_prm_vals_dependents_filter is needed here too since wtp is a dependent, equation-derived parameter rather than an independent one). Combined with num_runs and load out_record/out_fmt/out_eqn, out_prm_vals_on_end can build up a per-run summary table (e.g. Cycle, Iter, Rwp, and named parameters) across a whole batch of runs into one results file.
out_prm_vals_per_iteration: out_prm_vals_per_iteration $file [append] and out_prm_vals_on_convergence $file [append] output refined independent parameter values, either every iteration or only on convergence respectively, into the file $file. out_prm_vals_filter can be used to filter which parameters are output; $filter can contain the wildcard character '*' and the negation character '!' -- for example, 'out_prm_vals_per_iteration PRM_VALS.TXT out_prm_vals_filter "* !u*"' outputs every parameter except those starting with 'u'. More than one out_prm_vals_per_iteration/out_prm_vals_on_convergence can be defined at once, letting different filtered subsets of parameters be routed to different files. out_prm_vals_dependents_filter additionally allows dependent (non-independent, equation-derived) parameters to be output according to its $filter_dependents. A related keyword, out_prm_vals_on_end $file [append], outputs only once, at the end of refinement -- for example, 'prm wtp = Get(weight_percent); out_prm_vals_on_end aac2.txt append out_prm_vals_filter wtp out_prm_vals_dependents_filter wtp' appends just the final weight_percent value each run. Combined with num_runs and load out_record/out_fmt/out_eqn, out_prm_vals_on_end can build up a per-run summary table (e.g. Cycle, Iter, Rwp, and named parameters) across a whole batch of runs into one results file.
out_record:
out_record is a repeatable child block (Tout_record) used by out, atom_out/mag_atom_out, phase_out, phase_out_X, and xdd_out to define one output field written to a file. Each out_record has an out_eqn (the equation or parameter to write) and an out_fmt $c_fmt_string (a C-syntax format string with a single double-precision format specifier controlling how it's written); out_fmt_err similarly formats the error of out_eqn. out_fmt can be used without out_eqn to write a plain string; the order out_fmt/out_fmt_err are written in file matches the order they're given. Multiple out_record blocks (often written via 'load out_record out_fmt out_eqn { ... }') build up a row of output field-by-field. For example (see out-1.inp, using the Out_String/Out macros):

xdd ...
out "sample output.txt" append
str ...
  CS_L(cs_l, 1000)
  Out_String("\tCrystallite Size Results:\n")
  Out_String("\t=========================\n")
  Out(cs_l, "\tCrystallite Size (nm):\t%11.5f", "\tError in Crystallite Size:\t%11.5f\n")

Another common pattern uses out_record directly with load syntax, e.g.:

out results.txt append
load out_record out_fmt out_eqn {
  "%d " = Run_Number;
  " %s  " = Files(Run_Number);
}

out_record is used the same way regardless of which parent keyword (out/atom_out/phase_out/phase_out_X/xdd_out) it appears under -- only the scope of what's being written (global, site-level, phase-level, or xdd-level) differs.
out_refinement_stats: out_refinement_stats outputs detailed equation statistics about the refinement, both before and after equation simplification, useful for understanding the computational cost of a refinement's equation graph -- particularly relevant for subject-independent refinements written using fn/noinline/def/return/prm/restraint (computer algebra), where the equation structure isn't implied by conventional subject-dependent keywords. It reports, for each pass, the number of equations, the number of underlying equation-graph nodes, and the number of nodes if those equations were fully expanded (unsimplified) -- e.g. 'Number of equations: 534  Number of nodes: 99751  Number of nodes if expanded: 12070283' -- plus the number of penalties/restraints and independent penalty/restraint parameters, and (in the second pass) the number of objects taking part in refinement and the number of dependent parameters with derivatives with respect to Ycalc. Comparing the before/after node counts shows how much the CAS (computer algebra system) equation simplification reduced the effective computational graph -- for example, one worked case shows node counts dropping from 99766 to 8354 after simplification. See example \functions\alvo4-fn.inp, which performs an entire single-crystal refinement using only these six subject-independent keywords.
out_rwp: Outputs a list of Rwp values encountered during refinement to the file $file in XDD format.
out_sfn4_ycalc: out_sfn4_yobs = E and out_sfn4_ycalc = E output the observed and calculated diffraction data respectively to a binary .sfn4 file at the end of refinement, for xdd data with equal x-axis steps. The file format is: start value, finish value, and number of data points (start/finish as double precision, number of data points as an integer), followed by the data itself in single precision. The two keywords share this exact format, differing only in which array (Yobs vs Ycalc) is written.
out_sfn4_yobs: out_sfn4_yobs = E and out_sfn4_ycalc = E output the observed and calculated diffraction data respectively to a binary .sfn4 file at the end of refinement, for xdd data with equal x-axis steps. The file format is: start value, finish value, and number of data points (start/finish as double precision, number of data points as an integer), followed by the data itself in single precision. The two keywords share this exact format, differing only in which array (Yobs vs Ycalc) is written.
p1_fractional_to_file: p1_fractional_to_file $file [in_str_format] is structure-dependent: it saves the atomic positions of the current structure, expanded to space group P1 (i.e. every symmetry-equivalent position written out explicitly), to the file $file. The original structure can be in any space group -- p1_fractional_to_file performs the expansion to P1 on output. If in_str_format is defined, the structural data is saved in INP format (ready to be pasted back into an INP file as a P1 structure); without it, a plainer fractional-coordinate listing is written instead.
pdb_cif_sites: pdb_cif_sites $sites, a child of pdb_cif_to_str_file, restricts which sites from the CIF file are converted, by matching them against the site-identifying string $sites. It is used, for example, to extract every residue of a particular type from a protein structure (e.g. all LYS residues) -- with the translate keywords of the resulting rigid bodies then set to zero and the individual sites of same-named residues penalized together via atomic_interaction/penalty so that equivalent residues are brought into overlay, as shown in CF-PROTEIN\2pvb-p212121\match.inp.
pdb_cif_to_str: pdb_cif_to_str #0, a child of pdb_cif_to_str_file, is the flag that triggers the actual CIF-to-INP conversion: setting it to 1 causes pdb_cif_to_str_file to generate the rigid-body INP text for the loaded CIF file, inserted into the INP file after the pdb_cif_to_str_file keyword. On termination of refinement it is automatically reset to 0 in the OUT file, so that re-running the (now-populated) INP file refines the generated structure instead of regenerating it.
pdb_cif_to_str_file:
