pdb_cif_to_str_file $file reads a Protein Data Bank (PDB) PDBx/mmCIF file (as downloaded from https://www.rcsb.org/) and converts it into INP text describing the protein structure -- one rigid body generated per residue, with coordinates set relative to that residue's geometric center, ready to be refined against structure-factor data loaded via xdd_scr. The conversion only runs when its child pdb_cif_to_str is set to 1; on refinement termination, pdb_cif_to_str is reset to 0 in the OUT file, and the generated INP text (site/rigid/rotate/translate blocks) is inserted into the INP file immediately after the pdb_cif_to_str_file keyword -- so the normal workflow is to run once with pdb_cif_to_str 1 to generate the structure, then run again (or on the resulting .out) with it left at 0 to refine.

Its other child, pdb_ignode_adps !E0, controls whether the per-atom ADP/B-factor values present in the CIF file are used as-is for each generated site's beq, or ignored in favor of a different default. pdb_cif_sites $sites restricts which sites are considered by matching them against the site-identifying string $sites -- useful, for example, for extracting every residue of a given type (e.g. all LYS residues) so that their sites can be compared or restrained to each other via penalty/atomic_interaction, as shown by the Match macro pattern used in CF-PROTEIN\2pvb-p212121\match.inp. See also CF-PROTEIN\2pvb-p212121\gen.inp and CF-PROTEIN\6y84-c121\Refinement.inp for complete worked protein-refinement examples using pdb_cif_to_str_file.
pdb_ignode_adps: pdb_ignode_adps !E0, a child of pdb_cif_to_str_file, controls how the per-atom ADP/B-factor values present in the loaded CIF file are handled when generating each site's beq. It is used in both worked protein-refinement examples, CF-PROTEIN\2pvb-p212121\gen.inp and CF-PROTEIN\6y84-c121\Refinement.inp, alongside pdb_cif_to_str_file and pdb_cif_to_str when first generating the INP structure from a downloaded CIF file.
pdf_convolute: Convolutes an arbitrary user-defined equation into PDF-type phases, over the x-axis window [min_X, max_X] (with an optional convolute_X_recal flag to force that window's resolution to be recalculated). Only affects PDF (r-space) phases -- an xo_Is/hkl_Is/etc. phase in the same file is left untouched, since pdf_convolute is PDF-specific. Can be declared at several different levels -- global, xdd, str, and pdf_for_pairs (via the Tpdf_convolute mixin at each) -- and several pdf_convolute's can be active at once, each contributing its own convolution; declaring it inside pdf_for_pairs is slower than at the other levels, so prefer placing it outside pdf_for_pairs where possible. Typical use is instrument-resolution damping/ripple correction in PDF refinement, e.g. convoluting a Sinc function for Q-resolution damping -- see test_examples\pdf\sinc-1.inp: `pdf_convolute = Sin(Qmax X+q3)/If(Abs(X) < 0.5 Step_Size, If(X < 0,-q2,q2),X); min_X = -conv_max; max_X = conv_max;`.
pdf_data: A bare xdd-level flag (no argument) that switches that xdd's data from ordinary reciprocal-space diffraction intensity into real-space PDF data -- G(r) rather than a 2-theta/Q pattern. Declaring pdf_data unlocks the whole family of PDF-specific keywords that only make sense in this mode: Tpdf_convolute/pdf_convolute for instrument-resolution damping, pdf_for_pairs/pdf_only_eq_0/pdf_gauss_fwhm for per-pair-type peak widths, pdf_scale_simple/pdf_zero/pdf_ymin_on_ymax/pdf_info at the str level, and the reserved parameter X meaning r (not 2-theta) in any keyword marked with the manual's footnote (1) -- scale_phase_X, fit_obj, rebin_with_dx_of, pdf_zero, pdf_gauss_fwhm. See test_examples\pdf\beq-2.inp, where `pdf_data` is placed right before the str block on the xdd carrying the G(r) data. See references/09-pdf-refinement.md for the full PDF-refinement keyword set, and 08-pdf-generation.md for generating G(r) from raw reciprocal-space data in the first place if it isn't already in hand.
pdf_gauss_fwhm: pdf_gauss_fwhm E (a pdf_for_pairs dependent) supplies the Gaussian FWHM used to write the peak-width equation for the site pairs selected by its parent pdf_for_pairs -- e.g. pdf_for_pairs Al1 Al1 pdf_only_eq_0 pdf_gauss_fwhm 0.1. Pairs fully described this way no longer use their sites' beq values for PDF peak broadening (and TOPAS reports any beq that ends up unused as a result).
pdf_generate:
pdf_generate { ... } is the xdd-scoped block that generates a real-space pair distribution function G(r) from reciprocal-space diffraction data, applying an inverse sine transform to a corrected, 'ideal' diffraction pattern -- one with background removed, atomic scattering factors normalized to constant, and symmetric 2*Theta/peak shapes (see Coelho et al., 2021). It is the second of two operations in the PDF-generation pipeline, typically driven by the Include_PDF_Generate macro: Operation 0 fits the raw reciprocal-space pattern (a peak placed at every data point, plus background and penalty functions, using approximate but NOT further refined peak shapes from a preliminary standard fit); Operation 1 then runs pdf_generate over 4 internal sub-steps (num_runs 4) -- generating the ideal pattern Ideal(2*Theta) from the Operation-0 parameters, converting it to Q-space to form Ideal(Q), fitting and subtracting a polynomial to obtain F(Q) = Ideal(Q) - Poly, and finally generating G(r) from F(Q).

Its children are: dr !E, the r-axis step size (Δr) of the generated G(r); r_max !E, the maximum r value G(r) is generated out to; gr_sst_file = "File", the base filename (an .sst extension is appended) that the generated G(r) is written to; hat !E [num_hats !E]; and gr_to_fq !E. Note that hat here is NOT the same as the ordinary hat convolution used elsewhere in phase-peak generation (the one used by macros like Slit_Width/Specimen_Tilt, which convolutes an impulse function into a diffraction peak in 2*Theta space) -- within pdf_generate, hat instead convolutes an impulse function directly into the generated PDF, G(r) (in real, r-space) typically to represent a termination-ripple or instrumental real-space broadening effect; num_hats sets how many such impulse functions are convoluted in, e.g.:

hat = 4.4934 / (17.5); num_hats = 3; gr_to_fq !E, when non-zero, reverses the usual direction: instead of generating G(r) from reciprocal-space data, it regenerates F(Q) from an already-generated G(r) -- used to verify that the generation round-trip is self-consistent, as demonstrated in LIFEPO4\GR-TO-FQ.INP, which generates G(r) from F(Q) at Run_Number 0 and then reproduces the original F(Q) from that G(r) at Run_Number 1. See also the worked examples Fullerene\DECON.INP, LIFEPO4\DECON.INP, Silicon\DECON.INP and Tungsten\DECON.INP.
pdf_info: pdf_info displays, in matrix form, which site-pair interactions are covered by which pdf_for_pairs definitions (or by beq, if none apply) for every pair of sites -- entries read '-' for beq-derived pairs with no pdf_for_pairs defined, '0'/'1' for a single pdf_for_pairs with/without pdf_only_eq_0, and '2' where two pdf_for_pairs definitions apply (one with, one without pdf_only_eq_0).
pdf_only_eq_0: pdf_only_eq_0 (a pdf_for_pairs dependent) restricts its parent pdf_for_pairs to only equivalent position 0 of the named site sets, rather than every symmetry-equivalent pair. See 09-pdf-refinement.md's worked P-1 example for exactly which atom pairs this includes/excludes.
pdf_partial_1:
pdf_partial_1 $sites, together with pdf_partial_2 $sites and pdf_partial_when !E, lets a partial PDF (the contribution from just one subset of atom-atom interactions) be displayed dynamically in the GUI, either each refinement iteration or only at the end. It's set up using a dummy_str per partial you want to see, each naming the site pair(s) to isolate. pdf_partial_1/pdf_partial_2 are site-identifying strings (can include the '*' wildcard and '!' negation, same rules as pdf_for_pairs) -- both fields let you pick two possibly-different site groups whose mutual interactions form the partial being shown. For example (see BEQ-2.INP):

str ... ' main PDF phase
dummy_str
  phase_name "Al1 Al2 O1 O2 O3"
  pdf_partial_1 "Al1 Al2 O1 O2 O3"
  pdf_partial_2 "Al1 Al2 O1 O2 O3"
  pdf_partial_when 0 ' Only at end of refinement
dummy_str
  phase_name "V1 O4"
  pdf_partial_1 "V1 O4"
  pdf_partial_2 "V1 O4"
  pdf_partial_when = Mod(Cycle_Iter, 2);

pdf_partial_when's default (non-zero) recalculates the partial every iteration; a value of zero defers the calculation to the end of refinement (cheaper, since it's not needed live).
pdf_partial_2:
pdf_partial_2 $sites is the second of the two site-identifying strings (alongside pdf_partial_1) that define a partial PDF -- the calculated contribution from just the interactions between the pdf_partial_1 site group and the pdf_partial_2 site group. Both fields accept the same wildcard ('*') and negation ('!') syntax as pdf_for_pairs; setting them to the same site string (as in the example below) isolates all interactions within that single group. See pdf_partial_1 for the full mechanism and pdf_partial_when for controlling when the partial is (re)calculated. Set up via a dummy_str per partial (see BEQ-2.INP):

dummy_str
  phase_name "Al1 Al2 O1 O2 O3"
  pdf_partial_1 "Al1 Al2 O1 O2 O3"
  pdf_partial_2 "Al1 Al2 O1 O2 O3"
  pdf_partial_when 0 ' Only at end of refinement
pdf_partial_when:
pdf_partial_when !E, a sibling of pdf_partial_1/pdf_partial_2, controls when a partial PDF is (re)calculated. Its default (non-zero) recalculates the partial every refinement iteration, which keeps the displayed partial live but costs extra computation each iteration; a value of zero defers the calculation to the end of refinement only. It can also be an equation, e.g.:

pdf_partial_when = Mod(Cycle_Iter, 2);

to recalculate only every second iteration. See pdf_partial_1 for the full mechanism and worked example (BEQ-2.INP):

dummy_str
  phase_name "Al1 Al2 O1 O2 O3"
  pdf_partial_1 "Al1 Al2 O1 O2 O3"
  pdf_partial_2 "Al1 Al2 O1 O2 O3"
  pdf_partial_when 0 ' Only at end of refinement
dummy_str
  phase_name "V1 O4"
  pdf_partial_1 "V1 O4"
  pdf_partial_2 "V1 O4"
  pdf_partial_when = Mod(Cycle_Iter, 2);
pdf_scale_simple: pdf_scale_simple (a Tpdf keyword) applies a simple scale factor to a PDF calculation, as an alternative to the more detailed scaling machinery elsewhere in the PDF-generation/refinement pipeline.
pdf_ymin_on_ymax: pdf_ymin_on_ymax (default 0.001, a Tpdf keyword) sets a minimum-to-maximum Y-value ratio threshold used internally during PDF calculation/scaling.
pdf_zero: pdf_zero E (a Tpdf keyword, can be a function of the reserved parameter X) sets the PDF's baseline/zero-level correction, applied across the PDF pattern; convergence behavior for pdf_zero is similar to that of coordinates, occupancies and lattice parameters.
peak_buffer_based_on:
[peak_buffer_based_on !E [peak_buffer_based_on_tol !E]]... is a str/hkl_Is/xo_Is/d_Is-phase attribute that exists to mitigate a speed/memory problem: with anisotropic peak shapes the peaks buffer holds as many peaks as there are hkls, which for problems with 100,000s of peaks can make calculation time and storage prohibitive. When peak_buffer_based_on is defined, the usual means of determining the size of the peak buffer is over-ruled -- instead, peaks are grouped according to the peak_buffer_based_on criterion (any function of the reserved parameters H, K, L, M, D_spacing, X, Xo, Th), with peak_buffer_based_on_tol setting the grouping tolerance. For example, to insert a peak into the peak buffer at x-axis intervals of 1:

peak_buffer_based_on = Xo; peak_buffer_based_on_tol 1

Peaks with similar Xo's, within that tolerance, are grouped into a single calculated peak shape. More than one peak_buffer_based_on can be defined at once (e.g. one on Xo and one on a spherical harmonics/march_dollase/hkl-dependent parameter sh), in which case peak groups must obey all of them simultaneously:

peak_buffer_based_on = Xo; peak_buffer_based_on_tol 0.01
peak_buffer_based_on = sh; peak_buffer_based_on_tol 1e-7

Smaller tolerances (e.g. 1e-7) can reduce the number of peaks stored in the peaks buffer by a factor of 15 at times without significantly affecting Rwp. A negative peak_buffer_based_on_tol forces a separate calculation for every peak (independent hkl peak shapes), e.g. 'peak_buffer_based_on 1 peak_buffer_based_on_tol -1'. Defining peak_buffer_based_on disables the peak-stretching procedures and any defined aberration_range_change_allowed.
peak_buffer_step: For computational efficiency, phase peaks are calculated at predefined 2Th intervals and stored in a "peaks buffer"; peaks in between are determined by stretching and interpolating rather than recalculated from scratch -- typically no more than 50 to 100 peaks are needed to accurately describe a whole diffraction pattern this way (see also peak_buffer_based_on, an alternative, grouping-based way of controlling the same buffer). peak_buffer_step determines the maximum x-axis spacing allowed between peaks in the peaks buffer; its default value is 500 * Peak_Calculation_Step. A value of zero forces the calculation of a new peak in the peaks buffer for every single peak of the phase (maximum accuracy, maximum cost). Peaks are not calculated for x-axis regions that are void of phase peaks. Default values are typically adequate; lowering peak_buffer_step (more peaks stored, less stretching/interpolation) trades speed for accuracy -- increase it back toward the default, or beyond, if runtime/memory matters more than peak-shape precision. See also convolution_step, ymin_on_ymax, and aberration_range_change_allowed, which affect peaks-buffer accuracy in related ways.
peak_type:
peak_type $type sets the peak type for a phase (see Chapter 5): fp (Fundamental Parameters), pv (pseudo-Voigt, parameters pv_lor/pv_fwhm), spvii (Split-PearsonVII, parameters h1/h2/m1/m2) or spv (Split-PseudoVoigt, parameters spv_h1/spv_h2/spv_l1/spv_l2).

Phase peaks P are generated as:

P = Get(scale) * Get(all_scale_pks) * EM(peak_type) (x) Convolutions (Eq. 5-1)

where (x) denotes convolution: the emission profile (EM) is generated first using emission lines of the chosen peak_type, then convoluted with any defined convolutions, then multiplied by scale, any defined scale_pks, and an intensity parameter (the I parameter for xo_Is/d_Is/hkl_Is phases, or F^2(hkl) for str phases). Convolutions are normalized and do not change the area under a peak, except for the capillary_diameter_mm and lpsd_th2_angular_range_degrees convolutions; the area under the emission profile is set by the sum of the la parameters, which typically add to 1.

Generating the emission profile is the first step in peak generation: it comprises emission lines EMk, each a Voigt built from la/lo/lh/lg. Lam is assigned the lo value of whichever EMk line has the largest la; that line is called EMREF and is used to calculate d-spacings. For all peak types, the position 2*Theta_k of an emission line, for a Bragg position of 2*Theta, is:

2*Theta_k = ArcSin(EMk,lo / (2d)) * (360/Pi), where 2d = EMREF,lo / Sin(Theta)

(2*Theta for xo_Is phases is the xo parameter; for d_Is phases it comes from the Bragg equation 2*Theta = ArcSin(Lam/(2d)) * 180/Pi with d the site's d value; for str/hkl_Is phases it is calculated from the lattice parameters). When no_th_dependence is defined (via the No_Th_Dependence macro, useful for non-X-ray data or negative 2*Theta values), this simplifies to:

2*Theta_k = 2*Theta + EM(lo, i)

instead. The x-axis extent (x1, x2) an EM line is calculated over is set by:

Intensity_of_EMk(x=x1=x2) / Intensity_of_EMREF(x=0) = ymin_on_ymax

which defaults to 0.001; emission profile data come from Hoelzer et al. (1997), stored in *.LAM files.

Table 5-1 gives each peak type's per-line FWHMk (deg 2Theta):

fp: FWHMk = (EMk,lh / Lam) * Tan(Theta) * (360/Pi)
pv: FWHMk = pv_fwhm * (EMk,lh / EMREF,lh)
spvii: FWHMk = (h1+h2) * (EMk,lh / EMREF,lh)
spv: FWHMk = (spv_h1+spv_h2) * (EMk,lh / EMREF,lh)

-- i.e. pv/spvii/spv scale the user-given FWHM per emission line by that line's Lorentzian half-width relative to the reference line's.

Table 5-2 gives the unit-area functional forms:

Gaussian: GUA(x) = (g1/fwhm) * Exp(-g2 x^2 / fwhm^2), g1 = 2*Sqrt(Ln2/Pi), g2 = 4*Ln2
Lorentzian: LUA(x) = (l1/fwhm) / (1 + l2 x^2/fwhm^2), l1 = 2/Pi, l2 = 4
pseudo-Voigt: PV = eta*LUA(x) + (1-eta)*GUA(x), with eta the PV mixing parameter (pv_lor)
Split-PearsonVII: SPVII = PVIILeft (x<0) + PVIIRight (x>0)
  PVIILeft = a(1+b1 x^2)^(-m1), PVIIRight = a(1+b2 x^2)^(-m2)
  b1=(2^(1/m1)-1)/h1^2, b2=(2^(1/m2)-1)/h2^2, a a Gamma-function normalization constant
Split-PseudoVoigt: SPV combines PVLeft = PV(spv_h1, spv_l1) and PVRight = PV(spv_h2, spv_l2)
  with a = PVLeft(x=0)/PVRight(x=0) matching their heights at x=0

lor_fwhm/gauss_fwhm convolutions, and the first defined hat convolution, are analytically convoluted with fp/pv peak types but numerically (via highly accurate line-segment convolution) with spvii/spv; further hat convolutions are always numerical.

For classic analytical full-pattern fitting, the macros PV_Peak_Type, PVII_Peak_Type and TCHZ_Peak_Type describe profile width as a function of 2*Theta directly rather than via an emission-profile convolution:

PV_Peak_Type: fwhm = ha + hb*Tan(Th) + hc/Cos(Th), lor_fwhm = lora + lorb*Tan(Th) + lorc/Cos(Th)

PVII_Peak_Type: fwhm1 = fwhm2 = ha + hb*Tan(Th) + hc/Cos(Th), m1 = m2 = 0.6 + ma + mb*Tan(Th) + mc/Cos(Th)

TCHZ_Peak_Type (the modified Thompson-Cox-Hastings pseudo-Voigt, Young 1993):

eta = 1.36603 q - 0.47719 q^2 + 0.1116 q^3, where q = L/fwhm
fwhm = (G^5 + A G^4 L + B G^3 L^2 + C G^2 L^3 + D G L^4 + L^5)^0.2
A=2.69269, B=2.42843, C=4.47163, D=0.07842
G = Sqrt(U Tan^2(Th) + V Tan(Th) + W + Z/Cos^2(Th)), L = X Tan(Th) + Y/Cos(Th)

(see example alvo4_tch.inp).

Note: several of these Table 5-1/5-2 equations are reconstructed from the manual's typeset originals and should be cross-checked against the Technical Reference PDF for publication-critical use, particularly the exact operator grouping in the SPVII/SPV normalization constants.
percent_zeros_before_sparse_A:
percent_zeros_before_sparse_A # defines the percentage of the A matrix that must be zero before sparse matrix methods are invoked in place of dense matrix storage/solution, with a default value of 60%. It is relevant when the A matrix is not being explicitly approximated via approximate_A -- in that dense/exact case, this keyword is what decides whether the underlying BCCG solver treats the matrix as sparse or dense based on its actual zero-element content.

This is distinct from use_LU, which instead chooses LU-decomposition over the BCCG method entirely and is intended for A matrices that are not sparse in the first place. Lowering this percentage makes sparse-matrix methods kick in more readily (for matrices that are less densely populated with zeros), which can save memory and time on problems with many structural/xdd parameters. See also A_matrix_memory_allowed_in_Mbytes and A_matrix_elements_tollerance for the separate sparsification controls that apply specifically when approximate_A is used.
phase_MAC: Calculates the mass absorption coefficient in cm2/g for the current phase. See description for mixture_MAC.
phase_dets: phase_dets $name { ... } defines a named, reusable set of phase-level details -- lor_fwhm, gauss_fwhm, th2_offset, scale_pks, transform_X, stretch_pks -- (see Chapter 6, 'Reusing objects in large refinements') that one or more phases can share via use { name }, so the underlying peak-shape/transform calculation and its derivatives are performed only once even when many phases use the same values.
phase_name: The name given to a phase; used for reporting purposes.
phase_out: Used for writing phase dependent details to file. See out for a description of out_record. The Create_hklm_d_Th2_Ip_file uses phase_out.
phase_out_X: Phase dependent keyword that writes phase Ycalc details to a file. The out_eqn can contain reserved parameter names occurring in xdd_out as well as Get(phase_ycalc); for example: phase_out_X Phase.txt load out_record out_fmt out_eqn {
pick_atoms:
pick_atoms $atoms modifies the electron density based on picked atoms during charge flipping. $atom names the atom types to operate on; it can contain the wildcard character '*' and the negation character '!' (see section 19.26). The picking routine locates atoms of the named type(s) based on the intensities of picked atoms and the scattering power of the atoms defined via f_atom_type -- for example:

load f_atom_type f_atom_quantity { Ca 2 O 10 C 12 } pick_atoms "O C"

first picks two Ca atoms, then 10 O atoms, then 12 C atoms, with only the O and C atoms operated on (Ca is ignored, since it wasn't named in pick_atoms). Picked atoms are sorted in decreasing intensity order, and its operations are only invoked when activate evaluates to a non-zero value, e.g.:

pick_atoms "O C" activate = Mod(Cycle_Iter, 20) == 0; More than one pick_atoms can be used, for example to progressively omit and re-insert the highest-intensity atoms as a means of avoiding spurious high-density ('uranium atom') solutions -- see example cf\cf-1a7y-omit.inp.
pick_fwhm: pick_fwhm !E1, a child of pick_atoms (protein charge flipping), sets the FWHM (full width at half maximum) of the Gaussian used when picking atoms from the electron density -- e.g. 'pick_atoms * pick_fwhm 3' in the S1 ab initio structure solution strategy (Coelho, 2021). See omit_fwhm and insert_fwhm for the analogous FWHM controls used when omitting/inserting picked atoms, test_examples\CF-PROTEIN\2erl-C2\solve.inp for a worked example, and pick_atoms for the overall picking mechanism.
pk_xo:
pk_xo E is applied to all phase types except xo_Is phases; it provides a mechanism for transforming a peak's natural position (e.g. d-spacing derived from hkls) into the actual x-axis position used for plotting/fitting. The main use case is neutron time-of-flight (TOF) data, where the peak position is typically calculated in time-of-flight space via:

tof = t0 + t1 * dhkl + t2 * dhkl^2

where t0, t1 and t2 are diffractometer constants and dhkl is the reflection's d-spacing -- pk_xo is set to this tof equation so the phase's peaks land at the correct x-axis (time-of-flight) position rather than a 2Th-based one. See examples TOF_BALZAR_SH1.INP and TOF_BALZAR_BR1.INP. (xo_Is phases don't use pk_xo because their peak position is already given directly via xo.)
point_by_point_beq_fo_etc: point_by_point_beq_fo_etc is a str-dependent keyword for a more accurate structure-factor calculation for powder diffraction data (see section 19.9.6, '2-theta point by point calculation of f0 and beq'). Structure factors for powder data ordinarily write beq and the atomic scattering factor f0 as a function of the Bragg angle 2-theta_o (i.e. one value per reflection); point_by_point_beq_fo_etc instead writes the structure factor in terms of the actual measured 2-theta, calculating f0 and beq on a 2-theta point-by-point basis (one value per data point) rather than a single value per Bragg angle. In routine Rietveld refinement the difference in structure factor values is small and difficult to detect, but it can be useful when analysing nanoparticles where extreme accuracy is required. It only works with X-ray powder data, and results in a slight increase in computational effort of roughly 5%. Reported structure factor values under the reserved parameter names A01, B01, A11 and B11 are still written in terms of the Bragg angle 2-theta_o and are therefore unaffected/unchanged by this keyword.
point_for_site: point_for_site defines a point in space with Cartesian coordinates given by the parameters ux, uy uz. Fractional equivalents can be defined using ua, ub and uc.
primary_soller_angle: primary_soller_angle and secondary_soller_angle define Soller slit angles in degrees. axial_n_beta defines the number of rays emanating from a point X-ray source in the axial plane.
prm:
prm/local declares a refinable parameter (prm) or a local, non-refinable helper value (local), optionally followed by one or more attribute equations: min, max, del, update, stop_when, val_on_continue, and _rem (described separately in section 15.6). Attributes are equations and cannot carry their own parameter name, though they can be a function of other parameter names. min and max limit the parameter's value during refinement, for example:

prm a 0.1 min 0 max = 10;

and are effective for refinement stabilization; max (or min) can reference another parameter, e.g.:

max = a;

del is used for calculating numerical derivatives with respect to the calculated pattern; the internal default del is usually adequate.

Parameter values are updated at the end of each iteration; if update is defined, it replaces the default update rule with:

new_Val = update equation

and can be a function of the reserved parameters Change and Val -- update does not override or negate min/max, which are still enforced afterward. stop_when is a conditional stopping criterion: convergence is only reached once stop_when evaluates to non-zero for every defined stop_when attribute, together with chi2_convergence_criteria being satisfied. val_on_continue is evaluated when continue_after_convergence is defined, providing a way to change a parameter's value after convergence via:

new_Val = val_on_continue

for example, to randomize a parameter and continue refining. Val (the parameter's own numeric value) can be used in min, max, del, update, stop_when, and val_on_continue; Change (the value's change over the last iteration) can only be used in update and stop_when. A parameter referenced via $name (rather than loaded directly) retains its default min/max/del attributes, whereas loading a parameter without min/max in the load block lets it load its already-set attributes instead.
process_times: Displays process times on termination of refinement. (Examples: tof_bank2_1.inp)
push_peak: push_peak and its related keywords (bring_2nd_peak_to_top, bring_n_peak_to_top, add_pop_1st_2nd_peak, scale_top_peak, set_top_peak_area) manipulate TOPAS's internal peak calculation stack, used to build up a final peak shape from a sequence of convolutions. The emission profile P0 of a peak (for a given peak_type) is first placed on the stack; each further-defined convolution is convoluted with the top member of the stack, and the last convolution should leave the stack with a single entry representing the final peak shape. push_peak duplicates the top of the stack. bring_2nd_peak_to_top brings the second stack entry to the top. bring_n_peak_to_top brings the nth peak to the top (n=0 is the top of the stack). add_pop_1st_2nd_peak adds the top entry to the second-most-recent entry and pops the stack. scale_top_peak scales the peak at the top of the stack, and set_top_peak_area sets its area. These are typically used together to build composite peak shapes, such as the back-to-back exponentials required by GSAS time-of-flight peak shape 3.
pv_lor:
pv_lor and pv_fwhm are the parameters of the pseudo-Voigt (pv) peak_type. pv_lor is eta, the PV mixing parameter (the Lorentzian fraction of the peak profile):

PV(x) = eta*LUA(x) + (1-eta)*GUA(x)

where LUA and GUA are the unit-area Lorentzian and Gaussian functions (see peak_type). pv_fwhm is the FWHM of the peak profile; per emission-line component k it is scaled as:

FWHMk = pv_fwhm * (EMk,lh / EMREF,lh)

so emission lines with a larger Lorentzian half-width (lh) than the reference line EMREF are given a proportionally broader instrumental peak shape. Unlike the split peak types (spvii, spv), pv uses a single, non-split profile.
q:
q E is a site-dependent parameter used with grs_interaction/repulsion_refine (TEnergy_minimization) -- it's the site's valence charge, used as a repulsion parameter alongside qi/qj/s and any other parameters appearing in a grs_interaction equation. When a grs_interaction uses the '#m_unique' shorthand (rather than explicit qi/qj), the per-site q values supply those charges directly, letting many separate grs_interaction blocks collapse into one shared equation. For example:

site Al ... q 3 s s1 1
site V ...  q 5 s s2 1
site O ...  q -2 s s3 1
repulsion_refine
grs_interaction * * c = 1/R^9;
penalty = c;

(this reformulates what would otherwise be three separate grs_interaction blocks, one per Al-O/V-O/Al-V pair, into a single shared one). q can also be refined/switched dynamically -- e.g. in GRS-ALVO4\SOLVE-1.INP, q is used together with ok_to_continue and the _rem parameter attribute to periodically re-assign which sites carry the Al+3 vs V+5 charge without including q in the refinement:

macro VQ { _rem 1 val_on_continue = If(Mod(Cycle,10), If(Rand(0,1)<0.5,qal,qv), Val); }
site Al x @ 0.0 y @ 0.9 z @ 0.8 occ Al+3 = OCC; q = q1; s = S_; VV

Get(q) can be used in equations to read the current site's q value, e.g. 'macro S_ { If(Get(q) == qal, sal, sv) }' to pick a different s value depending on which charge is currently assigned. See also the site-dependent g, which reports each site's contribution to the sum of all grs_interactions. Examples: ALVO4-GRS-AUTO.INP, GRS-ALVO4\SOLVE-1.INP, GRS-ALVO4\REP-1.INP.
quick_refine: quick_refine !E speeds up refinement iterations by removing parameters from the A matrix during a refinement cycle, shrinking N and hence the cost of the A matrix dot products (which scale as M(N^2+N)/2). A parameter is removed once the condition of Eq. (4-9) is met for three consecutive iterations; all removed parameters are automatically reinstated at the start of each new refinement cycle unless quick_refine_remove is separately defined to control removal and reinstatement explicitly (enabling a form of block refining). Larger quick_refine values remove parameters more aggressively, which speeds convergence but can hinder reaching the lowest possible chi2 -- a value of 0.1 is reported to work well in most cases -- and larger values also increase the degree of parameter randomization introduced, which randomize_on_errors can compensate for automatically. quick_refine is especially effective for structure solution by simulated annealing (see the Auto_T macro and example ae1-auto.inp), and along with chi2_convergence_criteria and yobs_to_xo_posn_yobs is one of the keywords that most directly trades convergence thoroughness for computational speed, sometimes by a factor of 20 or more.
r_bragg: Reports on the R-Bragg value. R-Bragg is independent of hkl's and thus can be calculated for all phase types that contain phase peaks. (Examples: clay.inp)
r_p:
r_p, r_wp, r_exp, gof, r_p_dash, r_wp_dash and r_exp_dash report the standard Rietveld criteria of fit (Young, 1993; Table 4-2), global and xdd dependent; keywords ending in '_dash' correspond to background-subtracted values. Using Yo,m and Yc,m for the observed and calculated data at point m, Bkgm the background, M the number of data points, N the number of parameters, and wm the weighting given to point m (wm = 1/sigma(Yo,m)^2 for counting statistics):

r_p (R-pattern) = Sum|Yo,m - Yc,m| / Sum(Yo,m)
r_p_dash = Sum|Yo,m - Yc,m| / Sum(Yo,m - Bkgm)

r_wp (R-weighted pattern) = Sqrt[ Sum(wm (Yo,m - Yc,m)^2) / Sum(wm Yo,m^2) ]
r_wp_dash = Sqrt[ Sum(wm (Yo,m - Yc,m)^2) / Sum(wm (Yo,m - Bkgm)^2) ]

r_exp (R-expected) = Sqrt[ (M - N) / Sum(wm Yo,m^2) ]
r_exp_dash = Sqrt[ (M - N) / Sum(wm (Yo,m - Bkgm)^2) ]

gof (Goodness of Fit, also called chi) = r_wp / r_exp = Sqrt[ Sum(wm (Yo,m - Yc,m)^2) / (M - N) ]

See also weighted_Durbin_Watson, a related but distinct criterion of fit reported alongside these that measures serial correlation in the fit residuals rather than their overall magnitude.
rand_xyz:
[rand_xyz !E] is a site attribute used for simulated annealing / structure solution. If continue_after_convergence is defined, rand_xyz is executed at the end of each refinement cycle: it adds a randomly-directed displacement vector u to the site's fractional coordinates, with magnitude in Angstroms given by:

|u| = T * rand_xyz

where T is the current temperature (see the temperature keyword). To add a shift to an atom between 0 and 1 A, the following could be used:

temperature 1
site... occ 1 C beq 1 rand_xyz = Rand(0,1);

Only fractional coordinates (x, y, z) that are independent parameters are considered. The same rand_xyz mechanism also exists as a rigid-body attribute ([rand_xyz !E] under translate), where it displaces the rigid body's independent tx/ty/tz translation parameters by the same T * rand_xyz-scaled random amount instead of individual site coordinates. Outside of continue_after_convergence-driven simulated annealing, rand_xyz can also be triggered directly (e.g. bound to the Break icon/macro during Molecular Dynamics, see MD-3.INP) to kick a site or rigid body to a new random starting position.
randomize_initial_phases_by: randomize_initial_phases_by !E (default Rand(-180,180)) randomizes the charge-flipping phases, in degrees, once at the very start of a run -- distinct from randomize_phases_on_new_cycle_by, which instead re-randomizes phases at the start of every new cycle. Setting it to 0 disables this initial randomization entirely, which is the normal companion setting when starting from an already-known-good phase set via set_initial_phases_to -- e.g. 'set_initial_phases_to already_saved.fc  randomize_initial_phases_by 0' begins the run with those saved phases exactly as-is, rather than perturbing them.
randomize_on_errors:
randomize_on_errors automatically randomizes parameters after convergence (when continue_after_convergence is defined) based on their approximate errors, as given by Eq. (4-10), where T is the current temperature and K corresponds to the K1 weighting of Eq. (4-3); a scaling factor Q is determined internally such that, on average, convergence returns to a previous parameter configuration about 7.5% of the time. It offers an alternative to writing explicit val_on_continue equations for every parameter -- a parameter with val_on_continue defined is not additionally randomized by randomize_on_errors -- which is especially valuable for rigid-body structure solution, where hand-tuning an optimal randomization amount per parameter can be difficult.

Because it derives step sizes from parameter errors rather than fixed values, randomize_on_errors effectively provides an adaptive step size during simulated annealing, meaning only relative (not absolute) temperature values matter, and it can recover from a badly-chosen starting temperature -- example cime-z-auto.inp demonstrates this starting from an intentionally poor temperature of 0.1. The console message 'Breaking - randomize on errors revisit' indicates a previously-seen parameter configuration was revisited and that the internal temperature is being adjusted in response. The Auto_T macro combines quick_refine, randomize_on_errors and a temperature regime, and has proven adequate across a wide range of simulated-annealing examples.
rebin_start_x_at:
rebin_start_x_at !E works alongside rebin_with_dx_of to rebin the observed data (and SigmaYobs if it exists) -- see example CLAY.INP. rebin_with_dx_of can be a function of the reserved parameter X (demonstrated in TOF_BANK2_1.INP); if it evaluates to a constant, the observed data is re-binned to equal x-axis steps, which is useful for converting originally-unequal-step data (e.g. TOF) to equal steps.

rebin_with_dx_of creates a new x-axis with points determined by:
x[i+1] = x[i] + rebin_with_dx_of

The position of the first x[i] value defaults to the start of the original x-axis; rebin_start_x_at changes that starting point instead (used e.g. to align the rebinned x-axis to an integral multiple of the step size, as in test_examples\pdf\beq-2.inp: 'rebin_with_dx_of Rebin_Step rebin_start_x_at Rebin_Step'). Intensities at each new x[i] are determined by integrating Yobs (treated as line segments) from (x[i]+x[i-1])/2 to (x[i]+x[i+1])/2 -- i.e. this is a genuine resampling/convolution of the data, not a simple nearest-point lookup. Total counts and the associated esd's are preserved through the rebin. If rebin_with_dx_of is a constant, the equivalent resampling can also be included directly in Ycalc via a matching hat convolution instead, e.g.:

rebin_with_dx_of 0.02
hat 0.02

Some general points about rebin_with_dx_of: it changes the data; it uses all the data, each point once; resulting errors are similar as long as the fit to the new data is similar; and if a hat convolution is included in Ycalc, the fit is potentially unchanged. For data with equal x-axis steps, rebin_with_dx_of should generally be preferred over x_calculation_step for efficiency.
rebin_with_dx_of: rebin_with_dx_of !E rebins the loaded data (a user_y's data file, or an xdd/PDF pattern, depending on context) onto a regular x-axis grid with step size !E, interpolating as needed. For a user_y specifically, this is useful when the loaded shape's native x-axis spacing is irregular or different from the spacing convenient for the equations that will reference it. rebin_start_x_at (available in some contexts alongside rebin_with_dx_of) sets the x-value the regular grid starts at, rather than defaulting to the data's first x-value.
remove_phase: remove_phase !E (a str/hkl_Is/xo_Is/d_Is dependent) enables automatic phase removal during refinement via the Remove_Phase macro -- typical usage: for strs { Remove_Phase(0.3, 0.5) } removes a phase once its weight percent drops below 0.3% AND its weight-percent error exceeds 0.5 times that weight percent. Phase removal is evaluated at the end of each refinement cycle.
report_on_str: A str-level diagnostic flag (no argument) that prints to the console what anomalous-dispersion values (f1 and f11) -- or, for neutron data, what neutron scattering lengths -- were actually used for each atom type in that structure during the run. Useful for confirming that user-supplied values (via a `load f0_f1_f11_atom ...` block) or the program's default-table lookups (atmscat.TXT for X-ray f0, neutscat.TXT for neutron scattering lengths) are being applied as expected, rather than silently trusting them. No values are reported when d_spacing_to_energy_in_eV_for_f1_f11 is used, since f1/f11 are then computed per-reflection as a function of energy rather than held as the single fixed per-atom-type values report_on_str is built to show.
repulsion_refine:
repulsion_refine places all grs_interactions into a 'repulsion refine' mode, in which each grs_interaction returns the sum of the squared derivatives of the interaction with respect to the atomic coordinates:

Sum((d(grs_interaction)/dfi)^2, i)

rather than the interaction's energy value. In this mode, atomic fractional coordinates are NOT refined; instead, refinement adjusts the repulsion parameters (qi, qj, q, s, and any other parameters in the grs_interaction equation) so that the derivatives of the interactions with respect to those independent repulsion parameters are minimized -- effectively fitting the repulsion model so that the Rietveld-refined structure sits at (or near) a force-balance equilibrium of the interatomic potential.

By default, lattice parameters are NOT included in this derivative minimization. Adding them:

penalty = Get(grs_lp_rep);

The equivalent for normal, non-repulsion_refine refinement is:

penalty = Get(grs_lp_refine);

The site-dependent s parameter scales the equation part of a grs_interaction, which lets several similar interactions be collapsed into one shared grs_interaction equation -- e.g. three separate Al-O/V-O/Al-V grs_interactions, each with its own B-coefficient, become a single:

grs_interaction * * c = 1/R^9;

driven by per-site s1/s2/s3 parameters, with:

B1 = s1*s3, B2 = s2*s3, B3 = s1*s2

this lets the program cache equation values that are independent of the refined repulsion parameters, giving a large speed-up. See examples GRS-ALVO4\solve-1.inp, GRS-ALVO4\Rep-1.inp and GRS-ALVO4\Rep-2.inp.
resample_from_current_ycalc:
resample_from_current_ycalc, used with bootstrap_errors, changes where replacement data comes from during each bootstrap refinement cycle: instead of resampling from the Ycalc determined once at the first refinement cycle (the default), replacement data is instead drawn from the Ycalc of the currently completed refinement cycle. This lets the resampled 'observed' data track the evolving fit as bootstrapping proceeds, rather than staying anchored to the initial fit throughout.

As with the default resampling behaviour, the resulting updated Yobs data is further adjusted so that the change in Rwp is consistent with the current Ycalc. The fraction of data replaced each cycle is still controlled by fraction_of_yobs_to_resample, independent of this keyword. See bootstrap_errors for the overall bootstrap error-determination procedure.
rigid: rigid defines the start of a rigid body. point_for_site defines a point in space with Cartesian coordinates given by the parameters ux, uy uz.
rotate:
rotate E [qx|qa E] [qy|qb E] [qz|qc E] rotates previously-defined point_for_site/z_matrix points of a rigid body by the angle given by the E equation, around the vector (qx, qy, qz) in Cartesian coordinates (or (qa, qb, qc) in fractional coordinates). By default it operates on every point defined so far in the current rigid block; operate_on_points $sites restricts it to a named subset of previously-defined points instead, which is how a deviation applied to only part of a rigid body (e.g. two atoms shifting together as a rigid sub-unit) is expressed. in_cartesian or in_FC signals whether the rotation vector is given in Cartesian or fractional atomic coordinates.

The rotation angle E and the vector components qx/qy/qz (or qa/qb/qc) are all ordinary refinable parameters, so they can carry min/max and other parameter attributes just like any equation. Multiple rotate/translate statements can be layered: an initial rotate/translate positions the rigid body as a whole (this is implied and can be omitted if the body doesn't need repositioning), and further rotate/translate statements later in the rigid block represent additional deviations -- e.g. a local rotation of just a few atoms -- applied on top of the starting model. See rigid and z_matrix/point_for_site for how the points being rotated are defined.
save_best_chi2:
save_best_chi2 changes which set of parameter values is saved when refinement terminates. Without continue_after_convergence and without save_best_chi2, the values saved are those of the last refinement iteration. Without continue_after_convergence but with save_best_chi2 defined, the values saved instead correspond to whichever iteration gave the best chi2. With continue_after_convergence defined but save_best_chi2 not defined, the values saved correspond to whichever cycle gave the best Rwp; with both defined together, the values saved correspond to whichever cycle gave the best chi2.

When there are no penalties or restraints present, the best chi2 and the best Rwp coincide, making save_best_chi2 largely moot in that case -- it matters specifically when penalties/restraints are part of the refinement and can pull chi2 and Rwp in different directions across iterations/cycles. It is used, for example, in the Deconvolution_Init macro ('save_best_chi2 -- We want best Chi2; not best Rwp'), where the penalty-dominated objective function makes best-chi2 the more meaningful criterion than best-Rwp.
save_sequences: save_sequences $file (a generate_stack_sequences dependent) writes the generated stacking sequences out to $file as plain text.
save_sequences_as_strs: save_sequences_as_strs $file (a generate_stack_sequences dependent) writes the generated stacking sequences out as ready-to-use .str phase blocks, one per sequence, to $file.
scale: Rietveld scale factor; can be applied to all phase types.
scale_Aij: scale_Aij (a cf_in_A_matrix dependent) rescales the off-diagonal coefficients of the Pawley-derived A matrix used to partition intensities during charge flipping -- e.g. scale_Aij = Get(Aij); or scale_Aij = Get(Aij)^2;. The default, scale_Aij = 0, is equivalent to using a Pawley-generated hkl file directly (no off-diagonal partitioning).
scale_E: Normalized structure factors (Eh values) are a function of correct_for_temperature_effects and unit cell contents. scale_E allows for an additional scaling of Eh values.
scale_F: scale_F !E (default 1) applies an additional scaling to the normalized structure factors used by charge flipping (which works with normalized structure factors by default). Its default form, scale_F = Exp(-0.2 * Get(d_squared_inverse)), broadens electron density peaks to avoid pixelation effects in the calculated electron density map.
scale_F000: Scale should be set to 1 for compliance with the algorithm of Oszlányi & Süto (2004). When scale_F000 is non_zero, modifications to the electron density produce unfavourable effects.
scale_density_below_threshold: Electron density pixels that are less than the threshold value are scaled by scale_density_below_threshold. Values for scale_density_below_threshold that are less than 1 tends to sharpen the electron density and to reduce large oscillations in R-factors; the latter occurs for bad data, see example cf-sucrose.inp. A value of zero for scale_density_below_threshold results in “low density elimination” similar to that of Shiono & Woolfson (1992).
scale_flipped: scale_flipped !E scales the flipped electron density (ED) charge; it is applied every charge-flipping iteration. It is one of the strategy parameters used in ab initio protein structure solution (Coelho, 2021) -- for example, the S0 strategy uses 'fraction_density_to_flip 0.9 scale_flipped 0.6', while the S1 strategy uses 'fraction_density_to_flip 0.97 scale_flipped 0.2', each tuned for different classes of structure (S0 for large structures with a relatively heavy atom, S1 for non-triclinic structures with symmetry). See test_examples\CF-PROTEIN\ for the worked solve.inp examples demonstrating these strategies.
scale_phase_X: scale_phase_X scales Ycalc point by point. It can be used to define the Lorentz Polarization factor on an x-axis basis rather than on a peak basis (as is the case for scale_pks). It can be a function of X. Multiple definitions are allowed, each applied to the pattern in turn. It can occur at the xdd and/or phase level: an xdd-level scale_phase_X multiplies every phase in that xdd's pattern, while a phase-level one (under str/hkl_Is/etc.) multiplies only that phase, and the two combine when both are present -- for example, with one xdd-level and two phase-level scale_phase_X definitions (one under a str phase, one under an hkl_Is phase), the str phase is multiplied by the first (xdd-level) and second (its own) scale_phase_X, while the hkl_Is phase is multiplied by the first (xdd-level) and third (its own) scale_phase_X.
scale_top_peak: scale_top_peak E (a peaks-buffer stack operation) scales the peak currently at the top of the peak stack by the given equation/value.
secondary_soller_angle: primary_soller_angle and secondary_soller_angle define Soller slit angles in degrees. axial_n_beta defines the number of rays emanating from a point X-ray source in the axial plane.
set_initial_phases_to: set_initial_phases_to $file initializes charge-flipping phases from a previously saved *.FC file, rather than starting from a fresh random or default phase set. It is typically paired with randomize_initial_phases_by 0 (its default) so the saved phases are used exactly as-is without additional randomization -- e.g. 'set_initial_phases_to already_saved.fc randomize_initial_phases_by 0'. This is useful for restarting or refining a process from a known-good phase set, such as one obtained from an earlier successful charge-flipping run, or from a deliberately degraded/reduced-resolution test of an already-solved structure. See use_Fc, a related keyword that achieves the same effect but with the *.FC file name implied (matching the input data file's name) rather than given explicitly.
set_top_peak_area: set_top_peak_area E (a peaks-buffer stack operation) normalizes the peak currently at the top of the peak stack to the given area in situ -- needed because not every aberration convolution is easily normalized by construction, so this lets its resulting area be fixed directly after the fact.
sh_Cij_prm:
Defines a hkl-dependent, symmetry-obeying (symmetrized) spherical harmonics series, named $name -- once declared, using $name in any equation returns that series' value for the reflection currently being calculated, i.e. it's an hkl-direction-dependent scalar function you can drop into whatever equation needs one. Its sub-parameters: sh_Cij_prm $Yij E declares/refines the series' individual expansion coefficients (one per allowed spherical-harmonic term $Yij, filtered down by the space group's symmetry -- this is what 'symmetrized' means: only the terms consistent with the phase's Laue class are free parameters); sh_order # sets the order of the series (even numbers 2-8 for non-cubic, 2-10 for cubic systems -- higher order captures finer angular detail at the cost of more refined parameters); sh_alpha !E is the angle in degrees between the polar axis and the scattering vector, defaulting to 0 (required for symmetric reflection, i.e. ordinary Bragg-Brentano geometry).

Two common uses, both ordinary equation usage once $name is declared: (1) preferred-orientation/texture correction -- multiply scale_pks by $name (`scale_pks = sh;`), which is exactly what the PO_Spherical_Harmonics(sh, order) macro in topas.inc does for you; (2) anisotropic peak-shape/broadening -- feed $name into a broadening-related equation instead, e.g. test_examples\clay.inp uses `spherical_harmonics_hkl sh sh_order 8` then `exp_conv_const = (sh-1);` to make peak broadening vary with hkl direction, typically paired with normals_plot to visualize the resulting anisotropic surface. Since it's a symmetry-aware hkl function, it can equally be used anywhere else an hkl-dependent multiplier obeying the space group's symmetry is needed without hand-rolling the symmetry -- e.g. `spherical_harmonics_hkl sh sh_order 6 ... scale_occ = q sh;` to give an occupancy correction the correct symmetry.

site: site $site [x E] [y E] [z E] defines an atomic site, where $site is a user-defined string identifying it. x, y and z define the site's fractional atomic coordinates (see also section 19.28); each can be a constant, refined parameter, or equation, just like any other equation in TOPAS. A site fully occupied by a single species is written as e.g. 'site Al1 x 0 y 0 z 0.3521 occ Ca+2 1 beq 0.3', and a site occupied by two cations (mixed occupancy) repeats occ (with its own beq) for each species on the same site: 'site Fe2 x 0.9283 y 0.25 z 0.9533 occ Fe+3 0.5 beq 0.25  occ Al+3 0.5 beq 0.25'. Beyond x/y/z, a site also carries occ $atom E [beq E] [scale_occ E] (the occupancy factor and equivalent isotropic temperature factor, with $atom a valid symbol/isotope from ATMSCAT.TXT for X-ray data or NEUTSCAT.TXT for neutron data), num_posns # (the number of unique equivalent positions generated by the space group, updated on refinement termination), rand_xyz !E (random displacement amount used during simulated annealing) and inter !E # (the sum of all GRS interactions that are a function of this site, which can represent the site's electrostatic potential depending on which GRS interactions are defined). The user is responsible for obeying symmetry when defining x/y/z manually for a special position; when not working in P1, the Multiplicities_Sum macro or the spherical_harmonics_hkl keyword can help keep occupancy/scale equations symmetry-consistent.
site_to_restrain: Declares one site in the ordered list of sites that a geometry restraint operates on -- the shared building block behind sites_distance (2 sites), sites_angle (3 sites), sites_flatten (N sites), and sites_geometry (2-4 sites, picking Distance/Angle/Dihedral_Angle by count). Normally populated as a `load site_to_restrain { site1 site2 ... }` block rather than one line per site, e.g. `sites_geometry some_name load site_to_restrain { C1 C2 C3 C4 }`. Each entry is `$site [#ep [#n1 #n2 #n3]]`: $site is the site name; the optional #ep is a symmetry-equivalent-position index and the optional #n1 #n2 #n3 are fractional unit-cell offsets, together letting a restraint reach a specific symmetry mate or a neighboring-cell copy of a site rather than only its own asymmetric-unit copy -- necessary for bonds that cross a special position or a cell boundary. These #ep/#n1/#n2/#n3 values are exactly what append_bond_lengths prints for a real bond, in the form `SiteName:ep n1 n2 n3 distance [angle...]` (e.g. `Zr1:0 O1:20 0 0 -1 2.08772`), so the normal workflow is: run once with append_bond_lengths to see the actual bond geometry table, then copy the printed SiteName:ep/n1/n2/n3 values straight into site_to_restrain entries to set up a restraint on that same bond. See test_examples\sites_geometry_1.inp/_2.inp and benzene.inp (which demonstrates the Distance_Restrain/Angle_Restrain/Flatten macros -- topas.inc wrappers that declare their own sites_distance/sites_angle/sites_flatten and site_to_restrain list for you from a plain list of site names).
sites_angle: When used in equations the name N of sites_distance and sites_angle returns the distance in Å between two sites and angle in degrees between three sites respectively. The sites considered are defined by site_to_restrain.
sites_flatten:
sites_flatten N [sites_flatten_tol !E] defines a named restraint term N (like sites_distance and sites_angle, over the sites listed by site_to_restrain) that decreases toward zero as those sites become coplanar -- useful in penalty equations to restrain a group of atoms to lie in a plane. It is defined as:

sites_flatten = 6/(n(n-1)(n-2)) * Sum_i Sum_j>i Sum_k>j [(|b_i x b_j . b_k| - tol)^2, if |b_i x b_j . b_k| > tol, else 0]

where tol is sites_flatten_tol, n is the number of sites defined by site_to_restrain, and the b's are Cartesian unit-length vectors from each site to the geometric center of all the sites (the triple product |b_i x b_j . b_k| is the scalar triple product, which is zero for three coplanar direction vectors -- summing its excess-over-tolerance, squared, over every triplet of sites penalizes any deviation from a shared plane). #ep, #n1, #n2 and #n3 (as used in site_to_restrain) specify a site's equivalent position and fractional offsets to add, letting the restraint span sites in different unit cells/equivalent positions -- this is useful when the structure is already known and a geometric constraint is needed, as with the bond-length/bond-angle output produced by append_bond_lengths. BENZENE.INP demonstrates sites_flatten alongside the related Distance_Restrain and Angle_Restrain macros (OpenGL viewing recommended). Note: for more than roughly 6 sites, sites_flatten becomes computationally expensive, since the number of triplets summed grows as n^3.
sites_geometry: Declares a named geometric measurement over a small ordered set of sites (given via a nested `site_to_restrain $site ...` list), letting a bond distance, angle, or dihedral angle be read back as an ordinary equation value rather than only being usable as an opaque penalty term. How many sites are loaded under site_to_restrain determines which built-in accessor functions become valid for that $Name: 2 sites makes only Sites_Geometry_Distance($Name) valid; adding a 3rd site also makes Sites_Geometry_Angle($Name) valid; adding a 4th also makes Sites_Geometry_Dihedral_Angle($Name) valid (each level includes the one(s) below it). Each site_to_restrain entry can optionally carry a symmetry-equivalent-position index and a unit-cell offset (`$site [#ep [#n1 #n2 #n3]]]`), so a restraint can reach a symmetry mate or a neighboring-cell copy of a site rather than only its own asymmetric-unit copy. Two typical uses: (1) tie the sites of a rigid body (or any free atoms) to a target bond length/angle/dihedral through a restraint like `penalty = (Sites_Geometry_Distance(name) - target)^2;` -- the topas.inc Distance_Restrain/Angle_Restrain macro family wraps this same idea around the related single-purpose sites_distance/sites_angle/sites_flatten keywords; (2) expose the computed value with no restraint attached, e.g. `prm = Sites_Geometry_Distance(name); : 0`, purely for reporting/monitoring -- see test_examples\sites_geometry_1.inp (builds simulated data from a known z-matrix rigid body, printing its geometry via plain prm statements) and sites_geometry_2.inp (refits that data from a randomized starting geometry, this time using the same Sites_Geometry_* calls inside real penalty restraints). Calling an accessor for a $Name that wasn't loaded with enough sites, or that doesn't resolve at all, fails at solve-time with a bare 'Error in Sites_Geometry_Distance'-style abnormal termination rather than a parse-time error.
siv_s1_s2: Defines the s1 and s2 integration limits for the spherical interaction volume of the GRS series.
sleep: Pause refinement E seconds each iteration; this pause also occurs during molecular dynamics and charge flipping. sleep can be a function of Cycle, Cycle_Iter, etc...
smooth: Performs a Savitzky-Golay smoothing on the observed data. The smoothing encompasses (2 * #num_pts_left_right + 1) points.
smv:
smv (accessed via 'prm = Get(smv);', a str-dependent value) is the current phase's own contribution to the standard quantitative-phase-analysis weight-fraction formula -- Qp = Sp Mp Vp / Bp, where Sp is the phase's Rietveld scale factor, Mp is cell_mass, Vp is cell_volume, and Bp is the phase's Brindley correction (a function of phase_MAC/mixture_MAC and brindley_spherical_r_cm). weight_percent is then:

prm = 100 Get(smv) / Get(sum_smvs); : 0

i.e. 100 times this phase's own smv divided by sum_smvs, the sum of every phase's smv in the xdd. See 11-quantitative-analysis.md.
space_group: If defined, then the cf_hkl_file is assumed to comprise merged hkls corresponding to the defined space group; otherwise, the cf_hkl_file is assumed to be of space group type P1.
