Since it's a symmetry-aware hkl function, it can equally be used anywhere else an hkl-dependent multiplier obeying the space group's symmetry is needed without hand-rolling the symmetry -- e.g. `spherical_harmonics_hkl sh sh_order 6 ... scale_occ = q sh;` to give an occupancy correction the correct symmetry.
spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent: spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent defines the weight percent of a spiked phase. It is used by the xdd dependent weight_percent_amorphous to determine amorphous weight percent.
spv_h1:
spv_h1, spv_h2, spv_l1 and spv_l2 are the parameters of the Split-PseudoVoigt (spv) peak_type, which forms a peak from two independent pseudo-Voigt half-profiles either side of the peak position. The sum of spv_h1 and spv_h2 gives the FWHM of the composite peak:

fwhm1 = 2*spv_h1, fwhm2 = 2*spv_h2, fwhm = spv_h1+spv_h2

spv_l1 and spv_l2 are the left (x<0) and right (x>0) Lorentzian fractions -- i.e. the per-half PV mixing parameters eta1/eta2 used in PVLeft = PV(spv_h1, spv_l1) for x<0 and PVRight = PV(spv_h2, spv_l2) for x>0. The two halves are then combined into the composite SPV profile using a scale factor a = PVLeft(x=0)/PVRight(x=0) that matches their heights at the split point x=0. See peak_type for the full Table 5-2 formulas.
stack: stack $layer, part of TOPAS's supercell approach to stacking faults, applies a stacking vector {sx, sy, sz} to every site previously marked as belonging to the layer named $layer (via the layer keyword). Structure factors are generated in the usual manner, with a shift applied corresponding to the stacking vector; stack operates in any space group. Sites not assigned to any layer are treated as un-stacked and generate structure factors normally, unaffected by any stack definitions. generate_these $sites additionally generates new dummy sites for the named $sites, with coordinates equal to the original sites' positions plus the stacking vector; generate_name_append $append_to_site_name appends that suffix to each generated site's name (e.g. site O1 stacked once becomes O1_1). Generated sites have their occupancy set to zero, marking them as dummy sites: dummy sites take no part in structure-factor calculations (so they don't affect refinement speed), are not displayed graphically, and -- unlike ordinary layer-marked sites, which cannot take part in restraints -- CAN take part in penalties/restraints such as Distance_Restrain, since they were generated via generate_these rather than marked directly with layer. In summary: a site marked with layer cannot take part in restraints and is not displayed graphically; a site generated via generate_these CAN take part in restraints; and an ordinary site not marked with layer can also take part in restraints as normal. Calculation of structure factors and stacking-vector derivatives is very fast; the main speed bottleneck for large supercells is instead summing peaks to Ycalc, which del_approx can help with by grouping nearby peaks in the peaks buffer. See test_examples\stacking-faults\kaolinite.inp (which also demonstrates simplifying layer setup with macros) and test_examples\stacking-faults\debye-new.inp (comparing the layer/stack supercell approach against a Debye-scattering-equation reference pattern, and against the equivalent debye-old.inp which achieves the same result the older way, by explicitly defining layers via site in an enlarged unit cell).
stacked_hats_conv: Defines hat sizes for generating an aberration function comprising a summation of hats. whole_hat defines a hat with an x-axis extent of whole_hat/2. half_hat defines a hat with an x-axis range of half_hat to zero if half_hat<0; or zero to half_hat if half_hat> 0. hat_height defines the height of the hat; it defaults to 1. stacked_hats is used for example to describe tube tails using the Tube_Tails macro.
start_X: start_X !E and finish_X !E define the start and finish x-axis region to fit to. start_X sets the lower x-axis bound and finish_X the upper x-axis bound of that fitted region; data outside the [start_X, finish_X] range is excluded from the refinement.
start_values_from_site:
Rietveld or Pair Distribution Function refinement can comprise rigid bodies. Rigid bodies comprise points in space defined using z_matrix or point_for_site keywords or both simultaneously. Operations can be performed on these points using rotate and translate. Rigid body operations include: Translating a rigid body or part of a rigid body. Rotating a rigid body or part of a rigid body around a point. Rotating a rigid body or part of a rigid body around a line. ua, ub, uc, ta, tb, tc, qa, qb, qc and the parameters of z_matrix are all refinable parameters which can comprise parameter attributes such as min/max.

The directory rigid contains rigid body examples in *.RGD files. These files can be viewed and modified using the Rigid-Body-Editor of the GUI. rigid defines the start of a rigid body. point_for_site defines a point in space with Cartesian coordinates given by the parameters ux, uy uz.
str: Declares a new structure node (`str` for a real, weight-percent-contributing phase; `dummy_str` for one excluded from weight-percent/quantitative-analysis calculations, e.g. an internal-standard-free amorphous or reference phase) -- the container for a phase's cell, space group, sites, and everything derived from a genuine atomic structure (as opposed to xo_Is/d_Is/hkl_Is, which generate peaks without one). Mixes in Tstr_details (site/rigid-body/ADP declarations and structure-level output/interaction settings), Thkl_lat (cell parameters and hkl-dependent settings), Tcomm_1_2_phase_1_2 (shared peak/background/phase-level settings), Tmin_max_r, Trigid, Tspace_group, and, for PDF refinement, Tpdf. Can appear repeatedly under one xdd for a multi-phase refinement -- each str is an independent structure sharing the same diffraction pattern.
str_dets: str_dets $name { ... } defines a named, reusable structural-details block -- a full space_group plus site declarations, the same content an ordinary str would otherwise carry directly (see Tstr_details and Chapter 6, 'Reusing objects in large refinements') -- that one or more phases can share via use { name }. Because the program's automatic search for common items requires identical hkls, phases with similar but not identical lattice parameters normally can't share structure factors; defining the structure once in a str_dets object allows that sharing regardless, cutting memory and recalculation cost sharply when hundreds of thousands of phases are present.
str_hkl_angle: Defines a parameter name N and a vector normal to the plane defined by h, k and l. When the parameter name is used in an equation, it returns angles (in radians) between itself and the normal to the planes defined by hkls.
stretch_pks:
stretch_pks E is a str-dependent keyword that approximates the effect of the lor_fwhm and gauss_fwhm convolutions (e.g. as used via the CS_G/CS_L crystallite-size macros) by stretching already-generated peak shapes, instead of recalculating the peaks buffer for every parameter derivative on every refinement iteration. This is a speed optimization: recalculating the peaks buffer is expensive, and becomes especially costly in refinements with thousands of phases (e.g. XRD-CT refinements), since many peak-aberration parameters would otherwise force a fresh peaks-buffer recalculation for each derivative each iteration. The approximation requires the values of lor_fwhm/gauss_fwhm to already be approximately known -- typically CS_L and CS_G are fixed (not refined) alongside stretch_pks -- and stretch_pks itself is then refined as a small dimensionless correction, e.g. 'CS_L(100) CS_G(100) stretch_pks @ 1 min 0.001 max 10'. For symmetric peaks the stretching approximation is almost exact; for asymmetric peaks, or peaks with asymmetric convolutions, it is not exact, but remains a good approximation provided the fixed lor_fwhm/gauss_fwhm values aren't too far from optimal.

Given a peak's unstretched x-axis limits x1 and x2 and its position Xo, the stretched limits are:

x1_s = Xo - (Xo - x1) * Get(stretch_pks)
x2_s = Xo + (x2 - Xo) * Get(stretch_pks)

In example stretch-pks\stretch-1.inp, using stretch_pks in this way speeds up refinement by a factor of 4.1. In the large-scale xrd-ct-1.inp example (150,000 str's), stretch_pks is applied per phase-shape group rather than per individual str (reported as 'Num stretch_pks/unique: 150000 3000'), consistent with the same object-reuse strategy used by lat_prms/str_dets/phase_dets for large refinements (see section 6, Reusing objects in large refinements).
sum_smvs:
sum_smvs (accessed via 'prm = Get(sum_smvs);') is the sum of every phase's smv (Qp = Sp Mp Vp / Bp, the Rietveld scale-mass-volume-over-Brindley-correction product from the standard quantitative-phase-analysis formula) across all str's of the xdd it's read from -- the denominator of the weight-fraction formula:

prm = 100 Get(smv) / Get(sum_smvs); : 0

Also exposed at the xdd level (not just per-str) as its own equation-accessible value, mirroring mixture_MAC and mixture_density_g_on_cm3. See 11-quantitative-analysis.md.
suspend_writing_to_log_file: When num_runs > 0, then, by default, output to TOPAS.LOG (or TC.LOG if running TC.EXE) is suspended after the first run (Run_Number == 0). suspend_writing_to_log_file changes this behaviour.
sx: sx, sy and sz (str dependents, used with stack) together define the stacking vector {sx, sy, sz} applied to a named layer -- structure factors are generated as usual, with a shift applied corresponding to this stacking vector.
sy: sx, sy and sz (str dependents, used with stack) together define the stacking vector {sx, sy, sz} applied to a named layer -- structure factors are generated as usual, with a shift applied corresponding to this stacking vector.
symmetry_obey_0_to_1:
symmetry_obey_0_to_1 !E; if a space group is defined, controls how strictly charge-flipping electron density adheres to that symmetry. It can be thought of as a real-space electron-density restraint, valued between 0 and 1. If 1, symmetry is obeyed 100%. If 0, no restraint is applied. For an intermediate value: for each set of grid points equivalent under the space group's symmetry, an average density rho_avg is computed, and every grid point's density rho is then adjusted toward it:

rho_new = (1 - symmetry_obey_0_to_1) * rho + symmetry_obey_0_to_1 * rho_avg

The console output 'symmetry error' reported while symmetry_obey_0_to_1 is active is defined as:

symmetry_error = Sum(|rho - rho_avg|) / Sum(|rho|)

(summed over all electron density grid points). symmetry_obey_0_to_1 turns on find_origin by default (origin finding is performed each CF iteration, shifting the electron density to the position that best matches the space group's symmetry before the restraint above is applied) -- find_origin can be used without symmetry_obey_0_to_1, or symmetry_obey_0_to_1 can be used without origin-shifting by explicitly setting find_origin to zero. This restraint is especially useful for powder data / poor-resolution or difficult structures, where it sharpens electron densities; it is commonly ramped up over a CF run, e.g.:

symmetry_obey_0_to_1 = Ramp(0.5, 1, 100);

similar to a simulated-annealing temperature schedule. Note: add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections=90 causes the origin to shift and should not be combined with symmetry_obey_0_to_1 (which prevents origin shifting); use:

add_to_phases_of_weak_reflections = Rand(-180,180);

instead when both are needed.
system_after_save_OUT: system_after_save_OUT { $system_commands } executes the operating-system commands given in $system_commands immediately after the *.OUT file has been written/updated (the counterpart to system_before_save_OUT, which runs just before). It is used, for example, to concatenate per-run OUT files together across multiple num_runs iterations -- in the File_Variable macro worked example, 'system_after_save_OUT { #if (Run_Number) type Out_File >> aac.out #else type Out_File > aac.out #endif }' appends (or, on the first run, creates) a combined aac.out file containing every run's OUT file content, using the '>'/'>>' shell redirection operators together with the #if (Run_Number) preprocessor test to distinguish the first run from subsequent ones. Like system_before_save_OUT, $system_commands can contain any operating system command and is run from the INP file's directory.
system_before_save_OUT: system_before_save_OUT { $system_commands } executes the operating-system commands given in $system_commands, run from the directory of the INP file, immediately before the *.OUT file is written. $system_commands can contain any operating system commands (e.g. copy, del, or any external program invocation). It is used, for example, by the standard Backup_INP macro (defined in Topas.inc) to keep a backup copy of the INP file each time it's about to be overwritten: 'macro Backup_INP { system_before_save_OUT { copy INP_File##.inp INP_File##.backup } }', where INP_File is the reserved macro returning the current INP file's name (without path or extension). See also system_after_save_OUT for the equivalent hook that runs immediately after the *.OUT file is written/updated instead.
sz: sx, sy and sz (str dependents, used with stack) together define the stacking vector {sx, sy, sz} applied to a named layer -- structure factors are generated as usual, with a shift applied corresponding to this stacking vector.
tangent_max_triplets_per_h: tangent_max_triplets_per_h and tangent_min_triplets_per_h defines the maximum and minimum number of triplets per reflection h.
tangent_min_triplets_per_h: tangent_max_triplets_per_h and tangent_min_triplets_per_h defines the maximum and minimum number of triplets per reflection h. Reflections with less than tangent_min_triplets_per_h are not included for tangent formula updating.
tangent_num_h_keep: tangent_num_h_keep defines the number of highest h reflections to include for tangent formula updating. tangent_max_triplets_per_h and tangent_min_triplets_per_h defines the maximum and minimum number of triplets per reflection h.
tangent_num_h_read:
tangent_num_h_read !E and tangent_num_k_read !E, used with the tangent formula in charge flipping, define the number of highest-h and highest-k reflections read when determining triplets. tangent_num_h_keep defines how many of the highest-h reflections are included for tangent-formula updating; tangent_max_triplets_per_h and tangent_min_triplets_per_h define the maximum and minimum number of triplets considered per reflection h, with reflections having fewer than tangent_min_triplets_per_h excluded from tangent-formula updating. tangent_scale_difference_by (called S below) blends the charge-flipping-derived phase with the tangent-formula-derived phase:

phi_h,new = phi_h,cf + S * alpha_h * (phi_h,tf - phi_h,cf)

where the tangent-formula phase is tan(phi_h,tf) = T_h / B_h, with:

T_h = Sum_k[ E_h E_k E_(h-k) Sin(phi_k + phi_(h-k)) ]
B_h = Sum_k[ E_h E_k E_(h-k) Cos(phi_k + phi_(h-k)) ]

(the classic Karle-Hauptman/Sayre tangent-formula triplet sums over reflections k), and alpha_h = M_h / M_h,max is a reliability weight built from:

M_h = Sqrt(T_h^2 + B_h^2)

normalized against the largest M_h seen across all h. Using a large number of triplets per h (tangent_max_triplets_per_h greater than 100) reduces perturbation and increases the chance of finding a solution after an initial phase randomization, but also increases the occurrence of spurious high-density ('uranium atom') solutions -- appropriate for poor-resolution data, but should be paired with a flipping regime that dampens high electron densities. tangent_scale_difference_by is often ramped down over the course of a run, e.g.:

tangent_scale_difference_by = Ramp(0, 1, 100);

gradually shifting weight from the raw charge-flipping phase toward the tangent-formula phase as the solution converges, similar in spirit to a simulated-annealing temperature schedule.
tangent_num_k_read: tangent_num_h_read and tangent_num_k_read defines the number of highest h and highest k reflections to read in determining triplets. tangent_num_h_keep defines the number of highest h reflections to include for tangent formula updating.
tangent_scale_difference_by:
tangent_scale_difference_by !E (called S in the manual) controls how strongly the tangent-formula phase pulls the charge-flipping phase toward it during CF's tangent-formula phase refinement (see also tangent_num_h_read, tangent_num_k_read, tangent_num_h_keep, tangent_max_triplets_per_h and tangent_min_triplets_per_h, which control which reflection triplets are used). The blended phase is:

phi_h,new = phi_h,cf + S * alpha_h * (phi_h,tf - phi_h,cf)

where phi_h,cf is the current charge-flipping phase, phi_h,tf is the tangent-formula phase (tan(phi_h,tf) = T_h / B_h, with T_h and B_h built from Karle-Hauptman/Sayre triplet sums E_h E_k E_(h-k) over reflections k), and alpha_h = M_h / M_h,max is a per-reflection reliability weight. S = 0 leaves the charge-flipping phase untouched; S = 1 replaces it entirely with the tangent-formula phase. tangent_scale_difference_by is often ramped from 0 to 1 over the course of a run, e.g.:

tangent_scale_difference_by = Ramp(0, 1, 100);

gradually shifting weight from the raw charge-flipping phase toward the tangent-formula phase as the solution converges -- similar in spirit to a simulated-annealing temperature schedule (see also tangent_num_h_read for the full derivation of T_h, B_h and alpha_h).
tangent_tiny: tangent_tiny (default 0.01) is a small-value cutoff used internally by the tangent-formula phase-extension calculation (Tcf_tangent_formula) during charge flipping, alongside tangent_num_h_read/tangent_num_k_read/tangent_num_h_keep/tangent_max_triplets_per_h/tangent_min_triplets_per_h/tangent_scale_difference_by -- guarding against division by (or otherwise treating specially) near-zero structure-factor magnitudes in the triplet-phase calculation.
tb: ta, tb define the stacking vector's x and y coordinates in terms of the crystallographic a and b axes. a_add, b_add define the stacking vector's x and y coordinates relative to the previous stacking vector, in terms of the crystallographic a and b axes.
temperature: temperature !E defines a temperature regime for simulated annealing. It has no effect unless the reserved parameter T (which returns the current temperature) is used in val_on_continue attributes, or unless the temperature-dependent keywords rand_xyz or randomize_on_errors are used (randomize_on_errors automatically determines parameter displacements from the current temperature without needing rand_xyz or explicit val_on_continue equations, and performs well across a wide range of problems). The first temperature defined becomes the starting temperature; each subsequent temperature value defined becomes the new current temperature. If chi2/Rwp increases relative to a previous cycle, refinement advances to the next defined temperature; if it decreases relative to previous temperatures of lesser value, the current temperature is rewound to an earlier, higher one. move_to_the_next_temperature_regardless_of_the_change_in_rwp forces an advance to the next temperature unconditionally, ignoring the change in Rwp. save_values_as_best_after_randomization saves the current parameter set with the status of 'best solution' for this purpose (note: this does not affect the global 'best solution' saved at the end of the refinement); use_best_values replaces the current parameter set with whichever was marked 'best solution'. A typical manually-written temperature regime starts high and steps down through a series of annealing temperatures, e.g. 'temperature 2  move_to_the_next_temperature_regardless_of_the_change_in_rwp  temperature 1 temperature 1 temperature 1'; for most problems, the ready-made temperature regime in the Auto_T macro is sufficient without needing to hand-write one.
to:
to $to_transition_name !E, a child of transition within generate_stack_sequences, defines a possible "to" transition -- $to_transition_name must be the name of another transition already defined via transition $transition_name. The equation !E gives that transition's relative probability. Children of a given 'to' line (ta/tb/tz or a_add/b_add/z_add) define the resulting stacking-vector shift; n reports the number of times that particular transition was generated (useful for recovering empirical probabilities after the fact). For example, from test_examples\stacking_faults\fit-1.inp:

Transition(1, lpc)
  to 1 = pa;   a_add = 2/3;  b_add = 1/3;   n !n1 349984
  to 2 = 1-pa; a_add = 0;    b_add = 0;     n !n2 149781
Transition(2, lpc)
  to 1 = 1-pa; a_add = 0;    b_add = 0;     n !n3 149781
  to 2 = pa;   a_add = -2/3; b_add = -1/3;  n !n4 350254

Here each 'from' transition (1, 2) has two possible 'to' transitions with complementary probabilities pa/(1-pa), and the generated n1-n4 counts let the probability parameter pa be recovered as (n1+n3)/(n1+n2+n3+n4). See examples FIT-1.INP, FIT-2.INP, FIT-3.INP.
track_buffer: A str-level setting (a plain integer, e.g. `track_buffer 100`) that sizes the history buffer used to graphically track atomic movement across iterations/cycles -- it works together with the site-level `track` keyword, which is a boolean-valued equation deciding, on each iteration, whether that site's current position gets recorded into the buffer (e.g. `track = Mod(Cycle_Iter, 2) == 0;` records every other iteration). Used both in ordinary Rietveld refinement, to watch a site migrate as it refines (see test_examples\alvo4a.inp), and in molecular-dynamics runs, to watch an offset atom relax back toward its lowest-energy position over the simulation (see the MD chapter's md-2.inp/md-3.inp discussion, test_examples\md\). The recorded positions are what the GUI's 'tracking atomic movements graphically' display draws from. The exact meaning of the numeric value -- presumably a cap on how many recorded positions are kept -- isn't spelled out in the Technical Reference manual beyond the bracket listing and these worked examples, so treat that detail as inferred rather than confirmed manual text.
transition: transition defines a "from" transition with the name $transition_name; the transition uses the layer defined in use_layer. to defines the "to" transition; $to_transition_name must be a defined $transition_name.
translate:
translate [tx|ta E] [ty|tb E] [tz|tc E] translates previously-defined point_for_site/z_matrix points of a rigid body by the amount (tx, ty, tz) in Cartesian coordinates, or (ta, tb, tc) in fractional coordinates. By default it operates on every point defined so far in the current rigid block; operate_on_points $sites restricts it to a named subset of previously-defined points instead. in_cartesian or in_FC signals whether the translation is given in Cartesian or fractional atomic coordinates. tx/ty/tz (or ta/tb/tc) are ordinary refinable parameters and can carry min/max/equations like any other parameter; start_values_from_site $unique_site_name initializes ta/tb/tc from the coordinates of an existing named site, which is a convenient way to position a rigid body at a known starting location.

When continue_after_convergence is defined, rand_xyz processes are triggered after each convergence, introducing a random displacement to any translate fractional coordinates (tx, ty, tz) that are independent parameters -- the displacement size is the current temperature multiplied by #displacement (in Angstrom), making translate the natural target for simulated-annealing-driven rigid-body placement during structure solution. As with rotate, an initial translate/rotate positions the whole rigid body (implied/omittable if not needed), and further translate statements later in the same rigid block layer additional, more localized deviations on top of the starting model.
try_space_groups: try_space_groups $, used during indexing (TIndexing), defines which space groups are searched for each candidate lattice found. Rather than listing individual space groups by hand, it is typically given one of the lowest-symmetry Bravais space groups defined by the Bravais_*_sgs macros in Topas.inc (e.g. Bravais_Monoclinic_sgs for monoclinic Bravais lattices of lowest symmetry) -- using these lowest-symmetry representatives is normally sufficient, since higher-symmetry space groups for the Bravais lattices corresponding to the 10 best solutions are automatically searched again at the end of an indexing run. For example, 'try_space_groups 3' searches primitive monoclinic, 'try_space_groups 5' searches C-centered monoclinic of lowest symmetry, and the Unique_Orthorhombic_sgs macro searches all orthorhombic space groups individually. Choosing a narrower, more targeted try_space_groups set (when something about the likely symmetry is already known) reduces the search space and speeds up indexing, just as index_min_lp/index_max_lp do for the lattice-parameter range.
tz: tz defines the stacking vector's z coordinate along the crystallographic c axis, in Å. add_z defines the stacking vector's z coordinate along the crystallographic c axis, in Å, relative to the previous stacking vector.
use: use { $names } pulls one or more previously-defined lat_prms, str_dets and/or phase_dets bins into the current phase (see Chapter 6, 'Reusing objects in large refinements'), e.g. str scale @ 1 load use { l0 s0 pd0 ze0 } -- the phase then shares whatever common lattice parameters, structural details and phase details those named bins hold with every other phase that also uses them, rather than recalculating and storing its own copy.
use_Fc: Sets initial phases to those saved in a previous *.FC file. The FC file used corresponds to the same name as the data file, defined using cf_hkl_file or cf_in_A_matrix, but with a FC extension. use_Fc is similar-to set_initial_phases_to except that the file is implied.
use_LU: use_LU invokes LU-decomposition to solve the normal equations Eq. (4-4), in place of the default Bounds Constrained Conjugate Gradient (BCCG) method (Coelho, 2005). It is intended for use when the A matrix is not sparse. Unlike the BCCG routine, LU-decomposition does not incorporate parameter min/max limits during the solution process, and it requires the full (dense) A matrix, which can be memory-intensive for problems with thousands of parameters and can also become slow once the number of parameters exceeds roughly one thousand. percent_zeros_before_sparse_A determines the percentage of zero elements in the A matrix required before sparse matrix methods are used instead (default 60%), which is a separate consideration from the BCCG-versus-LU choice made by use_LU. See also use_LU_for_errors, which applies the same LU-decomposition choice specifically to the end-of-refinement error calculation rather than to the iteration-by-iteration solve.
use_LU_for_errors: use_LU_for_errors forces the use of LU-decomposition, rather than the default Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), specifically for the end-of-refinement error calculation triggered by do_errors (or its do_errors_include_restraints/do_errors_include_penalties variants) -- it does not affect which method (BCCG vs use_LU) is used to solve the normal equations during refinement itself. SVD-based errors closely resemble those obtained by the bootstrap method (bootstrap_errors) and are generally preferred, since LU-decomposition produces very large errors for intensities that are 100% correlated, which is common in Pawley-type refinements with strongly overlapping reflections. The three means of error determination available -- default SVD, use_LU_for_errors, and bootstrap_errors -- are directly compared in a Pawley refinement of Y2O3 across the examples y2o3a-lu.inp, y2o3a-svd.inp and y2o3a-boot.inp, found in test_examples\svd-errors.
use_extrapolation:
use_extrapolation invokes Parameter Extrapolation, which uses parabolic extrapolation of each parameter as a function of iteration number to adjust it such that chi2 is minimized. For a particular parameter pi at iteration k, the last six sets of parameter values are used to form:

y1 = (pi,k-5 + pi,k-4)/2, y2 = (pi,k-3 + pi,k-2)/2, y3 = (pi,k-1 + pi,k)/2

from which parabola coefficients:

ai = (y1 - 2y2 + y3)/2, bi = (y3 - y1)/2, ci = y2

are formed and used to extrapolate the next parameter value.

When both use_extrapolation and line_min are defined, Parameter Extrapolation reduces possible oscillatory behaviour in chi2 introduced by line minimization. Parameter Extrapolation combined with line minimization can increase the rate of convergence when refining on penalties only. Like line_min, it has a small memory footprint and cannot be used together with approximate_A.
use_layer: use_layer $layer (a transition dependent, stacking-fault modeling) tells a named transition which layer type it operates on -- since a transition matrix commonly describes several unique layer types, each transition points back to its own layer via use_layer.
use_tube_dispersion_coefficients: Forces the use of Laboratory tube anomalous dispersion coefficients, see section 19.9.
user_defined_convolution:
user_defined_convolution E min E max E [...] convolutes an arbitrary user-written response function into phase peaks; it can be a function of the reserved parameter X. The min/max equations are mandatory -- they define the x-axis extents of the convolution, and must satisfy min <= 0 and max >= 0 (the convolution kernel has to straddle zero). For example, a sinc function can be convoluted into phase peaks (see example au111.inp) as follows:

str ...
prm k 10 min 0.001 max 100
user_defined_convolution = If(Abs(X) < 10^(-10), 1, (Sin(k X) / (k X))^2);
min -3 max 3

(the If-branch avoids a 0/0 division exactly at X = 0, where the sinc-squared function's true limiting value is 1). user_defined_convolution is one of the response functions whose convolution has discontinuities in 2Th space (along with capillary_diameter_mm and lpsd_th2_angular_range_degrees), so it is convoluted as straight-line segments rather than analytically.
user_defined_starting_transition: user_defined_starting_transition $transition_name (a generate_stack_sequences dependent) forces generation to begin at the named transition; if omitted, generation instead starts at whichever transition has the greatest probability in the transition probability matrix.
user_threshold: By default, Get(threshold) is determined using fraction_density_to_flip. When defined then user_threshold overrides fraction_density_to_flip. Electron density pixels are normalized to have a maximum value of 1, thus typical values for user_threshold range between 0 and 0.1.
user_y_exp_conv_const: user_y_exp_conv_const E [user_y_exp_limit E] convolutes an exponential aberration function into a user_y's data, identical in form to the ordinary exp_conv_const convolution applied to phase peaks, but scoped specifically to the user_y it is defined under; user_y_exp_limit is its dependent, analogous to exp_limit. It is used, for example, in USER_Y\USER_Y_CONVOLUTION.INP to apply an exponential aberration to a learnt peak shape loaded via user_y, refined alongside user_y_gauss_fwhm with val_on_continue randomization when fitting the convolved shape to simulated data. See exp_conv_const for the underlying convolution mechanics and the equation of the aberration function.
user_y_exp_limit: user_y_exp_limit E is the dependent of user_y_exp_conv_const, giving the boundary condition for the exponential aberration function convoluted into a user_y's data, analogous to exp_limit for the ordinary phase-peak exp_conv_const convolution. See exp_conv_const/user_y_exp_conv_const for the underlying equation and mechanics.
user_y_gauss_fwhm: user_y_gauss_fwhm E convolutes a Gaussian of the given FWHM into a user_y's data, identical in form to the ordinary gauss_fwhm convolution applied to phase peaks, but scoped specifically to the user_y it is defined under. It is used, for example, in USER_Y\USER_Y_CONVOLUTION.INP to broaden a learnt peak shape loaded via user_y so that it matches a simulated or measured pattern's instrumental broadening -- there it is refined alongside user_y_exp_conv_const with val_on_continue randomization to fit the convolved shape to simulated data. See gauss_fwhm for the underlying convolution mechanics, and user_y_hat/user_y_lor_fwhm/user_y_exp_conv_const for the other user_y-scoped convolutions.
user_y_hat: user_y_hat E applies a hat (top-hat) convolution to a user_y's data, identical in form to the ordinary hat convolution applied to phase peaks, but scoped specifically to the user_y it is defined under rather than to a phase. It is one of four such user_y-scoped convolutions -- alongside user_y_gauss_fwhm, user_y_lor_fwhm and user_y_exp_conv_const -- that let a learnt shape loaded via user_y be further broadened or shaped before being used in fit_obj/equation expressions. See example USER_Y\USER_Y_CONVOLUTION.INP, and see hat for the underlying convolution mechanics.
user_y_lor_fwhm: user_y_lor_fwhm E convolutes a Lorentzian of the given FWHM into a user_y's data, identical in form to the ordinary lor_fwhm convolution applied to phase peaks, but scoped specifically to the user_y it is defined under. It is one of four user_y-scoped convolutions -- alongside user_y_hat, user_y_gauss_fwhm and user_y_exp_conv_const -- available for broadening or shaping a learnt shape loaded via user_y before it is referenced in fit_obj/equation expressions. See lor_fwhm for the underlying convolution mechanics.
verbose: verbose # (default 1), used in charge flipping, controls how much text output is produced each iteration: a value of 1 outputs text verbosely on every iteration, while a value of 0 only outputs text when the R-factor improves on the best value seen so far within the current Cycle. Lower verbosity is commonly used in long simulated-annealing-style runs (e.g. via the Simulated_Annealing_1 macro, which sets verbose to -1) to avoid exhausting memory from saving large volumes of Rwp/text output.
view_cloud:
view_cloud !E (default 1), used in the GUI, tells a detected GUI to display the electron density cloud -- for example:

view_cloud 1

updates the cloud display every charge-flipping iteration, while:

view_cloud = Mod(Cycle_Iter, 10) == 0;

updates it only every 10th iteration, which reduces display overhead during long runs.
view_structure: Informs the GUI to display the structure.
weight_percent: cell_mass, cell_volume and weight_percent correspond to the unit cell mass, volume, and weight percent of the phase within the mixture. spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent defines the weight percent of a spiked phase.
weight_percent_amorphous: Determines the amorphous content in a sample. The phase dependent spiked_phase_measured_weight_percent needs to be defined for weight_percent_amorphous to be calculated.
weighted_Durbin_Watson:
weighted_Durbin_Watson reports the Durbin-Watson d statistic (Durbin & Watson, 1971; adapted for Rietveld refinement by Hill & Flack, 1987), global and xdd dependent, as:

d = Sum_{m=2}^{M}( (dYm - dYm-1)^2 ) / Sum_{m=1}^{M}( dYm^2 )

where dYm = Yo,m - Yc,m is the residual at data point m, and M is the number of data points. Unlike r_p/r_wp/r_exp/gof, which quantify the overall magnitude of the fit residuals, the Durbin-Watson statistic measures serial correlation between consecutive residuals -- that is, whether residuals at neighbouring data points tend to have the same sign rather than varying randomly. A value close to 2 indicates no significant serial correlation (residuals behave randomly), whereas values well below 2, approaching 0, indicate strong positive serial correlation, meaning runs of consecutive points are systematically over- or under-fitted -- a common symptom of an inadequate peak-shape or background model even when r_wp/gof look acceptable.
weighting: Used for calculating the xdd dependent weighting function in . Can be a function of the reserved parameter names X, Yobs, Ycalc and SigmaYobs. The default is as follows:
whole_hat: whole_hat (a stacked_hats_conv dependent) defines one hat-shaped term in a summation-of-hats aberration convolution, with an x-axis extent of whole_hat/2 either side of center. hat_height sets the hat's height (default 1). stacked_hats_conv -- built from any number of whole_hat/half_hat terms -- is used, for example, by the Tube_Tails macro to describe X-ray tube tails.
with_symmetry: with_symmetry !E, a child of pick_atoms (protein charge flipping), extends atom picking to also consider symmetry-equivalent positions of the picked atoms, rather than only the atoms as found in the asymmetric unit. It is used, for example, in the S1 ab initio structure solution strategy ('pick_atoms * pick_fwhm 3 choose_randomly = If(Mod(Cycle_Iter, 50), 0, 10); with_symmetry 1 insert 10 ...', see Coelho, 2021). See test_examples\CF-PROTEIN\2erl-C2\solve.inp for a worked example, and pick_atoms for the overall picking mechanism.
x_angle_scaler: x_angle_scaler #0.1, used during indexing (TIndexing), is a scaling factor that determines the number of angular steps searched for monoclinic and triclinic space groups (which, unlike higher-symmetry systems, have refinable inter-axial angles). Small values, 0.05 for example, increase the number of angular steps searched, giving a finer angular search at the cost of speed; the default value of 0.1 is usually adequate. See also x_scaler, the equivalent scaling factor for the number of lattice-parameter steps searched.
x_calculation_step: Calculation step used in the generation of phase peaks and fit_obj’s. Peak_Calculation_Step is the actual step size used. For an x-axis with equidistant steps and x_calculation_step not defined then: Peak_Calculation_Step =  “Observed data step size” / convolution_step
x_scaler: x_scaler #, used during indexing (TIndexing), is a scaling factor that determines the number of steps searched in parameter space; it must be less than 1, and increasing x_scaler searches parameter space in finer detail (at the cost of a slower search). Default values depend on the crystal system being searched: Cubic 0.99, Hexagonal/Trigonal 0.95, Tetragonal 0.95, Orthorhombic 0.89, Monoclinic 0.85, Triclinic 0.72 -- lower-symmetry systems default to a coarser (smaller) x_scaler since they already require searching a much larger parameter space. See also x_angle_scaler, the equivalent scaling factor for the angular steps searched in monoclinic and triclinic space groups.
xdd: xdd $file declares one experimental powder-diffraction pattern to be fit against a calculated pattern -- the central top-level object most other keywords (str phases, background, peak shape, convolutions, ...) hang off of, either directly or via one of the many type-mixins pulled in alongside it (Tcomm_1, Tcomm_2, Txdd__xdd_scr, ...). $file can be a real data file (with an optional range N to select one range from a multi-range file, and xye_format/gsas_format/fullprof_format to force a specific reader), or data can be given inline: xdd { 1 1 10 ... } for equidistant x/step/finish data, or xdd { _xy 0.1 1 0.2 2 ... } for explicit x-y pairs. gui_reload/gui_ignore control how the GUI treats this pattern on reload.
xdd_array:
xdd_array !E calculates and stores an array of values from an equation that can be a function of the reserved parameter names X, Yobs, Ycalc and SigmaYobs. For example, applying a Si atomic scattering factor correction to an xo_Is phase:

xo_Is ...
xdd_array si_f0 =
  2 ( ' atomic scattering data from atmscat.txt
  5.275329 Exp(-2.631338 (Sin(X Pi/360)/Lam)^2) +
  3.191038 Exp(-33.730728 (Sin(X Pi/360)/Lam)^2) +
  1.511514 Exp(-0.081119 (Sin(X Pi/360)/Lam)^2) +
  1.356849 Exp(-86.288643 (Sin(X Pi/360)/Lam)^2) +
  2.519114 Exp(-1.170087 (Sin(X Pi/360)/Lam)^2) +
  0.145073);
scale_phase_X = si_f0; ' apply the atomic scatter factor

This gives the same result as replacing xdd_array with a plain prm -- the difference is that prm does not store the array, so its equation is recalculated every time si_f0 is used, whereas xdd_array stores the array and automatically tracks its dependencies, recalculating only when the equation changes (e.g. a refinable parameter it depends on changes value), and only when the array is next referenced. xdd_array therefore produces faster, more efficient INP files than the equivalent prm-based approach whenever the same array is reused many times. See also xdd_sum, which is similar but stores only the summed value of the array rather than the array.
xdd_out: Used for writing xdd dependent details to file. The out_eqn can contain the reserved parameter names of X, Yobs, Ycalc and SigmaYobs. See out for a description of out_record. The Out_Yobs_Ycalc_and_Difference macro is a good example of using xdd_out.
xdd_scr: xdd_scr defines single crystal data from the file $file. The file can have extensions of *.HKL for ShelX HKL4 format or *.SCR for SCR format.
xo: Defines a phase type that uses x-axis space for generating peak positions, see example xois.inp. xo corresponds to the peak position, and I is the intensity parameter before applying scale_pks equations. (Examples: xois.inp)
xo_Is: Declares a phase type that generates peaks directly from user-supplied x-axis positions rather than from a crystal structure or hkls -- each member is a `[xo E I E]...` pair: xo is the peak position (in the pattern's x-axis units) and I is the intensity parameter, both before any scale_pks equation is applied. Useful for simulating or fitting a pattern as a plain sum of peaks with no structural model behind them (no cell, no space group, no sites) -- e.g. peak-fitting a raw pattern before indexing, or reproducing a reference pattern for testing. See test_examples\xois.inp. Also mixes in Tcomm_1_2_phase_1_2 (so it can carry its own peak-shape/background/phase-level settings like any other phase type) and supports create_pks_fn/create_pks_name for exporting the generated peaks.
xye_format: xye_format indicates that the file loaded by a user_y is in XYE format (x, y and estimated error/weight columns) rather than the plain XY format otherwise assumed. It only affects how the loaded data file is parsed; it does not change how the resulting user_y shape is used in equations once loaded.
ymin_on_ymax: ymin_on_ymax determines the x-axis extents of a peak (see also section 5.1). aberration_range_change_allowed describes the maximum allowed change in the x-axis extent of a convolution aberration before a new peak is calculated for the peaks buffer.
yobs_eqn: Observed data is created via an equation; this is useful for approximating functions. The name !N given to the equation is used for identifying the plot in the GUI. (Examples: test_examples\mag\occ-merge.inp)
yobs_to_xo_posn_yobs:
At the start of refinement, yobs_to_xo_posn_yobs decomposes an X-ray diffraction pattern into a new pattern comprising at most one data point per hkl. Fitting to the decomposed pattern in a normal Rietveld refinement manner is then possible due to the ability to refine data of unequal x-axis step sizes. This normal Rietveld manner of fitting is important in structure solution from simulated annealing, as the background can still be refined and the problem of peak overlap avoided.

These new data points are not extracted intensities and thus the problem of peak overlap, as occurs in intensity extraction, is avoided. The much smaller number of data points in the new diffraction pattern can greatly improve speed in structure solution; in other words, the calculation time in synthesizing the diffraction pattern becomes close to that of when dealing with single crystal data. (Examples: cime-decompose.inp, test_examples\occ-merge.inp)
z_matrix:
z_matrix atom_1 [atom_2 E] [atom_3 E] [atom_4 E] defines a point in space belonging to a rigid body using Z-matrix internal coordinates -- bond length, bond angle and dihedral angle -- rather than absolute Cartesian/fractional coordinates. atom_1 names the site the new Z-matrix point represents; the E after atom_2 is the bond distance in Angstrom between atom_2 and atom_1 (atom_2 must already exist if atom_1 is preceded by at least one point); the E after atom_3 is the bond angle in degrees between atom_3-atom_2-atom_1 (atom_3 must already exist if atom_1 is preceded by at least two points); and the E after atom_4 is the dihedral angle in degrees between the atom_3-atom_2-atom_1 plane and the atom_4-atom_3-atom_2 plane, using the right-hand rule with the thumb pointing from atom_3 to atom_2 (atom_4 must exist if atom_1 is preceded by at least three points). Placement is anchored progressively: the first point of the rigid body is placed at Cartesian (0,0,0); the second point is placed on the positive z-axis at (0,0,E) using the atom_2 distance; the third point is placed in the x-y plane -- every subsequent point is then fully determined by its own distance/angle/dihedral.

Z-matrix parameters are ordinary parameters -- they can be equations, refined, and given min/max attributes, e.g. constraining several bond lengths to a single shared parameter c1c2 so they refine together, or making a bond length a function of a site's occupancy. Benzene, for example, is typically built from two dummy atoms (sites with occ fixed to 0, which take no part in structure-factor calculations but DO take part in penalties) via 'load z_matrix { X1  X2 X1 1.0  C1 X2 1.3 X1 90  C2 X2 1.3 X1 90 C1 60  ... }'. z_matrix can be freely mixed with point_for_site within the same rigid block, and the resulting points can then be operated on with rotate/translate, either as a whole rigid body or restricted to a subset via operate_on_points.
number_independent_parameters: Returns the number of independent parameters.
